A machine learning-based discriminative framework for mild cognitive 
impairment risk in middle-aged and elderly Chinese patients with 
depression: evidence from CHARLS and CLHLS

Keywords:
Depression
Mild cognitive impairment
Machine learning
ABSTRACT
Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the application value of machine learning (ML) techniques in the 
discrimination of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) among middle-aged and elderly Chinese patients with 
depression and to determine the major factors associated with MCI.
Methods: This study is based on the data from the 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study 
(CHARLS), which are divided into a training set and an internal testing set in a 7: 3 ratio. In addition, data from 
the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Life Survey (CLHLS) cohort are selected for external validation. Eight ML 
methods are adopted to construct a discriminative model for MCI in middle-aged and elderly patients with 
depression. Five-fold cross-validation was used to confirm the robustness of the model. Decision curve analysis 
(DCA) was implemented to quantify the net clinical benefit of predictive models across threshold probabilities. 
The significant contribution of the discriminant results is elucidated through the SHapley Additive exPlanation 
(SHAP) values.
Results: From the CHARLS dataset, 1964 participants were selected for model training and internal testing, while 
6782 participants from CLHLS comprised the external validation set. In internal testing, the random forest (RF) 
achieved the best predictive performance (AUC = 0.826 in training and 0.801 in internal validation), with 
balanced accuracy, recall, and specificity. Five-fold cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.791 (95 % CI: 
0.771 – 0.810), confirming the model ’ s robustness. DCA showed RF yielded greater clinical net benefit than other 
models at practical thresholds. In external validation, the RF model demonstrates moderate discriminative 
ability. SHAP analysis identified education, loneliness, household registration, Instrumental Activities of Daily 
Living disability and dyslipidemia as the most influential predictors of MCI risk.
Conclusion: ML algorithms can effectively discriminate MCI in middle-aged and elderly Chinese patients with 
depression and identify the important factors associated to MCI.
1. Introduction
Depression is a mental disorder characterized mainly by a significant 
and persistent low mood, accompanied by a decrease in interest and a 
loss of pleasure ( McCarron et al., 2021 ). The global prevalence rate of 
major depressive disorder among the elderly is 13.3 %( Abdoli et al., 
2022 ). In China, the lifetime prevalence rate of depression among the 
entire population is 3.4 %, and the annual prevalence rate is 2.1 % 
( Huang et al., 2019 ). Between 1990 and 2017, the Disability-Adjusted 
Life Year rate per 100,000 individuals in China increased from 525.1 
to 607.4, with a notable rise in prevalence among those over 55 years of 
age. This trend clearly indicates that depression has progressively 
emerged as a significant public health concern in China ( Ren et al., 
2020 ). Beyond emotional and physical symptoms, an increasing body of 
evidence suggests that cognitive impairment is a core, yet often over -
looked, feature of depression — especially in older adults ( Malhi and

Mann, 2018 ). These impairments typically involve executive dysfunc -
tion, attention deficits, memory loss, and slowed information processing 
( Lim et al., 2013 ; Semkovska et al., 2019 ). Cognitive symptoms are 
common across all stages of depression — from prodromal to acute and 
remission phases — with prevalence rates ranging from 76.9 % to 94 % 
during acute episodes, and persisting in 32.4 % to 44 % of patients even 
during remission ( Conradi et al., 2011 ; Wang et al., 2019 ). These re -
sidual deficits not only impair daily functioning but also markedly 
elevate relapse risk ( Porter and Douglas, 2019 ), highlighting the 
persistent link between depression and cognitive decline.
Among the various cognitive impairments observed in depression, 
mild cognitive impairment (MCI) has attracted particular attention due 
to its potential role as a transitional state between normal aging and 
dementia. Notably, depression and MCI frequently co-occur, especially 
in middle-aged and older adults, forming a clinically significant co -
morbidity. Emerging evidence suggests a complex and bidirectional 
relationship: late-life depression may increase the risk of MCI and de -
mentia( Knight et al., 2020 ), while in some cases, depressive symptoms 
themselves may reflect early neurodegenerative changes( Panza et al., 
2010 ). Regardless of the directionality, numerous longitudinal studies 
have confirmed the high comorbidity between depression and MCI in 
older adults, with the two conditions interacting and exacerbating each 
other over time( Butters et al., 2004 ; Rhee et al., 2024 ). In addition, this 
comorbidity is clinically significant, as it can severely impair functional 
capacity, increase caregiver burden, accelerate cognitive decline, 
worsen prognosis, and raise mortality and suicide risk( Divers et al., 
2022 ; Knight et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2019 ). Despite these consequences, 
it remains controversial whether antidepressants alone can improve 
cognitive outcomes( Culpepper et al., 2017 ; Zuckerman et al., 2018 ). 
Therefore, early identification of middle-aged and elderly patients with 
depression at high risk of developing MCI is critical for timely inter -
vention and improved outcomes.
However, current clinical practice lacks effective tools to meet this 
need. Machine learning (ML) can early identify and capture complex and 
potential relationships in data by integrating multiple variables, 
including demographic and clinical information, and make high- 
precision predictions or complex decisions( Patton and Liu, 2023 ). In 
recent years, numerous studies have applied ML methods to identify 
individuals with MCI, most of which have focused on the general elderly 
population. For example, ML have been widely used to predict MCI 
based on neuroimaging features( Lin et al., 2024 ) and transcriptomics 
( Huang et al., 2025 ), while deep learning models have shown great 
potential in detecting MCI from multimodal data such as images( Yue 
et al., 2025 ), and videos( Sun et al., 2023 ). Although these approaches 
have achieved satisfactory predictive performance, their dependence on 
costly and specialized data collection restricts their practical use in 
primary care and large-scale screening. Moreover, most existing studies 
have treated depression merely as a predictor of MCI or dementia ( Song 
et al., 2024a ), rather than targeting depressed individuals as the primary 
population of interest. To date, few studies have developed and vali -
dated ML-based models specifically designed to predict MCI among 
middle-aged and older adults with depression.
Consequently, this study targets depressed middle-aged and elderly 
individuals and employs eight ML algorithms to construct and validate 
an applicable, low-cost MCI risk discriminative framework specific to 
this cohort. Meanwhile, considering the key role of model interpret -
ability in clinical decision support, this study incorporates the SHapley 
Additive exPlanation (SHAP) method. SHAP analysis aims to provide 
multi-level explanations: (1) quantifying the degree and direction of 
each feature ’ s contribution to the discriminant outcomes for individual 
patients, helping to understand the basis for individualized discrimi -
nant; (2) identifying the most significant feature variables for discrimi -
nating MCI in the ultimately selected optimal model. These analyses are 
expected to significantly enhance the clinical comprehensibility and 
application value of the model.
2. Method
2.1. Data source
This study utilizes data from two nationally representative aging 
tracking surveys conducted by Peking University. The China Health and 
Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) has conducted five waves of 
surveys on individuals aged 45 and above since 2011, systematically 
collecting information on health status, healthcare service utilisation, 
economic conditions, family structure, and work and retirement status; 
The China Longitudinal Health and Retirement Study (CLHLS) has 
completed nine waves of surveys since 1998, focusing on elder in -
dividuals. It has collected data on physiological health indicators, 
cognitive function, activities of daily living, lifestyle, social support, and 
survival outcomes. Both surveys employ a multistage stratified sampling 
method and include detailed variables on individual characteristics, 
family background, and community environment, providing compre -
hensive and reliable longitudinal data support for research on China ’ s 
aging population.
The inclusion criteria for participants in both datasets were consis -
tent: 1. Age ≥ 60 years; 2. Complete cognitive dimension-related data; 3. 
Complete depression scale responses; 4. Patients with depression. 
Finally, in the 2018 CHARLS, we identified 1964 participants, while in 
the 2018 CLHLS, 6782 participants were identified. The participant 
screening workflow and the overarching research design are illustrated 
in Fig. 1 .
2.2. Data collection
2.2.1. Assessment of depression
Both CHARLS and CLHLS utilize the 10-item Center for Epidemio -
logic Studies Depression (CESD-10) scale to evaluate depressive symp -
toms. The CESD-10 comprises 10 items, each rated as: rarely or never, 
sometimes, most of the time, or always. Each item is scored 0, 1, 2, or 3, 
yielding a total range of 0 – 30, with higher scores denoting greater 
depressive severity. Research suggests that a CESD-10 score threshold of 
10 demonstrates good sensitivity and specificity for Chinese older adults 
( Cheng et al., 2016 ), so a score of ≥ 10 is classified as clinically signifi -
cant depression( Zhao et al., 2025 ).
2.2.2. Assessment of mild cognitive impairment
CHARLS evaluate cognitive performance using the identical meth -
odological framework adopted by the U.S. Health and Retirement Study 
( Crimmins et al., 2011 ). This method encompasses four dimensions of 
assessment: Orientation ability is assessed using a cognitive status 
telephone interview scale that includes items such as date and season, 
with a maximum score of 5 points. Calculative ability is assessed through 
a calculation test involving subtracting 7 from 100 continuously, capped 
at 5 points. Memory is tested through immediate and delayed word - 
recall tasks, with a maximum score of 20. Visual - spatial ability is 
assessed through a graphic copying task, with a maximum score of 1 
point. The total score for cognitive function is the sum of the scores 
across these four dimensions, with a maximum total score of 31 points 
( Cao et al., 2021 ).
CLHLS assesses cognition with the Chinese version of the Mini- 
Mental State Examination (CMMSE), a culturally adapted instrument 
that demonstrates satisfactory reliability and validity in mainland Chi -
nese older adults( Ma et al., 2020 ). The CMMSE comprises five domains: 
temporal and spatial orientation (0 � 12), immediate recall (0 – 3), 
attention and calculation (0 – 5), delayed recall (0 – 3), and language 
function (0 – 7), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 30, with higher 
score denoting superior cognitive performance( Folstein et al., 1975 ).
At present, no consensus exists on the diagnostic criteria for MCI. In 
this study, we used age - associated cognitive decline (AACD) as the 
diagnostic criterion, specifically defined as a CMMSE score ≥ 1 SD below 
the age - stratified mean( Levy, 1994 ; Richards et al., 1999 ). To

standardise assessment, participants aged 60 years and older were 
stratified into five-year age bands. Individuals who met the AACD 
criteria within each age group were classified as MCI patients. This 
diagnostic method has been previously applied and validated in prior 
studies( Song et al., 2025 ).
2.3. Covariate
The sociodemographic characteristics included in this study were 
age, gender, education, marital status, household registration type, 
residence, number of people living in the household, and participation 
in public medical insurance. Behavioural variables encompassed 
smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical exercise, social 
participation, and nightly sleep duration. In terms of health status, we 
included self - reported health status, Katz activities of daily living (Katz 
ADL), Lawton instrumental activities of daily living (Lawton IADL), and 
physician - diagnosed chronic conditions: hypertension, diabetes, pul -
monary disease, heart disease, stroke, arthritis, dyslipidaemia, and liver 
disease. Mental - health measures comprised loneliness experience and 
self - reported quality of life. Operational definitions of ADL and IADL 
are provided in Supplementary materials Part I.
2.4. Data preprocessing
After excluding variables with a missing data rate greater than 20 %, 
24 variables were ultimately retained for analysis. The missing data for

the retained variables are shown in Table S1. Subsequently, we imputed 
the missing data. We randomly split the 1964 participants from CHARLS 
(1634 non - MCI, 330 MCI) into a training set and an internal validation 
set at a 7:3 ratio, while the 6782 participants from CLHLS (5636 non - 
MCI, 1146 MCI) served as an independent external validation cohort. 
Due to the significant class imbalance in the training set, which could 
affect the performance of ML models, we applied the Synthetic Minority 
Over - sampling Technique (SMOTE) method. This technique generates 
synthetic samples by linearly combining existing minority class neigh -
bours, thereby over - sampling the minority class. SMOTE is an effective 
algorithm for addressing class imbalance and reducing model overfitting 
( Liu et al., 2024 ).
2.5. Variable selection and model building
Feature selection was accomplished with least absolute shrinkage 
and selection operator (LASSO) regression. This method considers the 
magnitude of coefficients during training and parameter estimation by 
adding a penalty term to the loss function (i.e., the optimisation objec -
tive) ( Pavlou et al., 2015 ). By setting a reduction factor (penalty factor), 
the coefficients of less influential features are attenuated to 0. Thus, only 
important features are retained, which helps reduce the possibility of 
overfitting in ML models. Candidate features identified by LASSO were 
subsequently reviewed against clinical expertise and prior literature to 
finalise the model covariates. To verify the robustness of feature selec -
tion and capture potential nonlinear relationships, we additionally 
applied decision tree (DT) - based feature screening. DT recursively split 
the dataset based on feature thresholds to maximize class purity, and 
feature importance is quantified by the total reduction in impurity 
attributable to each variable( Yu et al., 2024 ). DT - based selection 
effectively captures nonlinear effects and interactions, is robust to 
correlated predictors, and provides an intuitive importance ranking that 
complements LASSO results.
This study utilised eight ML algorithms to discriminat the risk of MCI 
in individuals with depression, namely: DT, K - nearest neighbor (KNN), 
Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Logistic regression (LR), 
Naive Bayes (NB), RF, Support vector machine (SVM), and Extreme 
gradient boosting (XGBoost), An overview of each algorithm is provided 
in the supplementary materials, Part II. We plotted the Receiver oper -
ating characteristic (ROC) curve and computed the area under the ROC 
curve (AUC) to assess the discriminatory performance of the models. The 
Delong test was employed to assess differences in AUC between models. 
Precision - recall (PR) curve was further used to assess the discrimina -
tory ability of models. The decision curve (DCA) was used to illustrate 
the net clinical benefits at different threshold probabilities. The “ treat- 
all ” approach labels every instance as positive, risking overtreatment 
and resource depletion, whereas the “ treat-none ” strategy classifies all 
cases as negative, potentially resulting in undertreatment and height -
ened patient harm. Additionally, confusion matrices were used to assess 
model performance, with accuracy, recall, and specificity. Brier scores 
were calculated to measure the discrepancy between predicted proba -
bilities and observed outcomes.
2.6. Cross-validation
To evaluate the stability and generalizability of the model, a five-fold 
cross-validation was performed within the training dataset. The mean 
and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) of the AUC across folds were 
calculated to assess model robustness, followed by independent vali -
dation using the CLHLS cohort.
2.7. Model interpretation
To enhance interpretability, we applied the Shapley Additive Ex -
planations (SHAP) framework, a game - theoretic approach that assigns 
each feature a consistent, locally accurate contribution (SHAP value) to 
every individual prediction( Lundberg et al., 2020 ). These values quan -
tify the direction and magnitude of each variable ’ s influence on the 
model output, thereby increasing transparency and facilitating 
comprehension of the decision process.
2.8. Statistical analysis
Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation 
(SD) for normally distributed data and as median with interquartile 
range for non - normally distributed data. Between - group differences 
were examined using independent - samples t - tests for normally 
distributed variables and Wilcoxon rank - sum tests for skewed variables. 
Categorical variables are expressed as counts (percentages). Intergroup 
comparisons of continuous variables were performed using χ
2 
tests or 
Fisher ’ s exact tests, while categorical variables were analysed using chi - 
square tests. All statistical tests were two - sided, and P < 0.05 was 
considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses and data vi -
sualizations were performed using R (version 4.4.2) and JD_DCPM 
(V6.11, Jingding Medical Technology Co., Ltd.).
3. Result
3.1. Baseline characteristics of the training set, validation set, and 
external validation set populations
This study enrolled 1964 participants from CHARLS, including 1473 
non - MCI cases and 491 MCI cases. A total of 6782 individuals from the 
CLHLS were ultimately included, including 5636 non - MCI cases and 
1146 MCI cases. The baseline characteristics are presented in Supple -
mentary Table S1.
3.2. LASSO regression and variable selection
LASSO regression was first employed to preliminarily screen cova -
riates. We used ten - fold cross - validation to determine the optimal λ 
value. We selected λ .se (0.028) as the optimal value and screened out 
five variables ( Fig. 2 ). To further verify the robustness of feature selec -
tion, DT analysis was performed, yielding a ranking of the top 15 fea -
tures that largely overlapped with those selected by LASSO regression 
(Fig. S1), confirming consistency between the two methods. Impor -
tantly, the final set of predictive variables remained unchanged, 
demonstrating the stability and reliability of the selected covariates. In 
addition, based on clinical knowledge and previous studies, we included 
three variables: diabetes, hypertension, and exercise( Jia et al., 2020 ). 
Ultimately, eight discriminative variables were identified: education, 
household registration, loneliness, IADL, diabetes, hypertension, and 
exercise.
3.3. Model construction and discriminative power
Based on the selected discriminative variables, we developed eight 
ML models. In the training set, discriminant analysis revealed the AUC 
values of eight ML algorithms, with DT (0.780, 95 % CI: 0.762 – 0.799), 
KNN (0.683, 95 % CI: 0.665 – 0.702), LGBM (0.796, 95 % CI: 
0.777 – 0.814), LR (0.796, 95 % CI: 0.778 – 0.814), NB (0.776, 95 % CI: 
0.757 – 0.795), RF (0.826, 95 % CI: 0.809 – 0.843), SVM (0.794, 95 % CI: 
0.776 – 0.812), XGB (0.809, 95 % CI: 0.792 – 0.827) ( Fig. 3 A). Among 
these, RF demonstrated the highest AUC. In the validation set, RF 
(0.801, 95 % CI: 0.760 – 0.841) showed a higher AUC value compared to 
other ML models, while XGBoost (0.789, 95 % CI: 0.743 – 0.834) and 
SVM (0.788, 95 % CI: 0.744 – 0.832) also demonstrated comparable AUC 
values, with KNN (0.665, 95 % CI: 0.613 – 0.716) having the lowest AUC 
( Fig. 3 B). Except for KNN, all models had an AUC greater than 0.7 in the 
validation set.
In the training set, Delong ’ s test confirmed that the ROC curve per -
formance of the RF model differed significantly from that of the

3.4. Cross-validation and model stability
In the five-fold cross-validation conducted on the training dataset, 
the random forest (RF) model achieved AUCs of 0.819 (95 % CI: 
0.778 – 0.860), 0.818 (95 % CI: 0.777 – 0.858), 0.775 (95 % CI: 
0.729 – 0.820), 0.747 (95 % CI: 0.699 – 0.794), and 0.807 (95 % CI: 
0.764 – 0.850) across the five folds, with a mean AUC of 0.791 (95 % CI: 
0.771 – 0.810). These results indicate that the model maintained stable 
performance across resampling iterations, supporting its robustness and 
reliability (Fig. S2).
3.5. Clinical utility assessment
The DCA values for both the training set and the validation set 
indicate that RF achieves a significantly higher clinical net benefit 
within a certain threshold range compared to other models ( Fig. 5 A). 
The PR curve and PRAUC of the validation set are presented in the 
Fig. S3. DCA curve analysis on the validation set revealed that, for 
predicted-probability thresholds spanning 0 to 0.28 ( Fig. 5 B), RF pro -
vides greater clinical benefit within a certain risk range compared to 
both extreme cases and other discriminant models, underscoring its 
clinical applicability. Furthermore, given that RF has the highest AUC in

3.6. External validation
Using the cohort from CLHLS for external validation, the AUC 
(0.653, 95 % CI: 0.636 – 0.670) of RF did not reach the level of the 
validation set, and only showed moderate discriminative ability 
(Fig. S4). However, DCA indicates that within the predicted probability 
threshold range of 0.07 to 0.20, the static benefit of RF is still superior to 
the two extreme strategies (Fig. S4).
3.7. Variable importance and interpretability analysis
Firstly, we employed the built - in function of the RF algorithm to 
calculate the variable importance within the model. Fig. 6 A illustrates 
the ranking of variable importance for discriminating MCI in the 
depressed population using the RF model. The five most significant 
variables are education, feeling lonely, household registration, IADL, 
and abnormal blood lipids. Subsequently, we applied SHAP values to 
interpret the RF model. The results of SHAP are shown in the Fig. 6 B, 
with the vertical axis indicating the features sorted by their accumulated 
SHAP values ’ influence. The top five important variables in the SHAP 
plot align with those previously identified, although the ranking of 
dyslipidemia has increased. The horizontal axis represents the SHAP 
values, with colors indicating high (yellow) and low (purple) variable 
assignments. The greater the distance from the SHAP value of 0, the 
more significant the impact on discriminant. For instance, in the case of 
education, yellow dots correspond to a value of 3, signifying an educa -
tion level of junior high school or above. An increase in education level 
negatively impacts the discriminant, steering it towards a non - MCI 
outcome. The distance between yellow dots and the SHAP value of 0 is

We also generated SHAP force plots to elucidate the contribution of 
each feature to the discriminant of each specific instance in RF model. In

model discriminates a lower risk of MCI than the baseline. The main 
factors influencing this discriminant are higher education, urban 
household registration, and absence of loneliness.
4. Discussion
Leveraging data from the CHARLS and CLHLS cohorts, this study 
developed and assessed eight ML models for discriminating MCI among 
Chinese middle - aged and elder patients with depression. Among these 
models, the RF model demonstrated the highest performance within the 
study ’ s framework. Eight indicators were employed to construct and 
validate the model, resulting in a commendable discriminative perfor -
mance and relatively accurate discriminative ability. We applied SHAP 
values to elucidate the discriminant results of the model. The findings 
indicated that key features associated with MCI discrimination included 
education, household registration, loneliness, IADL disability, and 
dyslipidemia.
When constructing this framework, eight key features were selected 
as discriminant variables, including demographic characteristics, past 
medical history and neuropsychological assessment. Previous studies 
have developed risk prediction models for MCI in various populations; 
however, these often rely on features that are difficult to obtain at the 
first visit or require invasive procedures. For instance, Wang et al. 
constructed a diagnostic model for MCI in elderly Chinese patients based 
on urine proteomics( Wang et al., 2023 ). In the ML model constructed by 
Mieling et al., cerebrospinal fluid status, hippocampal volume, etc. are 
important features for predicting MCI( Mieling et al., 2025 ). In contrast, 
this study focuses on indicators that are widely used in clinical practice 
and can be quickly obtained through inquiry at the first visit. Recent 
studies have also explored deep learning approaches. For example, Yue 
et al. developed a deep learning framework based on structural magnetic 
resonance imaging data to identify individuals with MCI( Yue et al., 
2025 ). Nevertheless, in this study, we chose classical ML algorithms due 
to considerations of data characteristics, interpretability, and clinical 
applicability. First, our predictors were structured tabular variables, for 
which classical models are particularly well suited. Moreover, 
combining classical algorithms with SHAP analysis provides interpret -
able outputs that facilitate clinical understanding and decision-making, 
and these models require less computational power, making them 
feasible for primary care settings. By leveraging this model, first - visit 
doctors can rapidly screen middle-aged and elderly patients with 
depression for MCI risk and promptly arrange detailed neuropsycho -
logical evaluations for high - risk individuals. This enables early diag -
nosis and intervention, optimizing subsequent management strategies. 
Consequently, the model ’ s favorable clinical feasibility positions it as a 
promising tool for risk screening of MCI in this population.

XGBoost while maintaining rapid training, making it a preferred base -
line in clinical discriminant tasks. This model has been widely applied in 
previous medical prediction studies( Liu et al., 2024 ; Maroco et al., 
2011 ). AUC is a key metric for evaluating the discriminative perfor -
mance of a model. In the training set, Delong’s test shows that RF has 
significantly higher AUC than other models, indicating that it has a 
stronger ability to discriminate on the training data and a more robust 
model fitting. In the validation set, the RF model similarly attained the 
highest AUC, demonstrating good generalization. Compared with a 
previously constructed model for predicting the progression of Chinese 
elderly people to MCI, the optimal AUC was 0.761 ( Song et al., 2025 ). 
The multiple ML models we developed have all achieved higher AUC 
values, indicating superior discriminative performance. External vali -
dation using the CLHLS cohort showed moderate discriminative ability. 
Although the internal training/testing set (CHARLS) was smaller than 
the external validation set (CLHLS), this design choice was driven pri -
marily by data quality and construct validity considerations rather than 
sample size alone. Specifically, the CHARLS questionnaire was devel -
oped with reference to international standards and provides detailed 
cognitive, psychological, and socio-demographic information, offering a 
richer and more comprehensive dataset for model training( Meng et al., 
2019 ). In contrast, the CLHLS employs the CMMSE, which is shorter and 
subject to a ceiling effect, limiting its sensitivity for MCI identification 
( Jia et al., 2021 ; Zhuang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the CLHLS dataset was 
considered more appropriate for evaluating the model’s generalizability 
among a broader and more heterogeneous elderly population. This 
approach ensured that the model was trained on high-quality, infor -
mation-rich data and validated on an independent dataset, thereby 
enhancing its robustness and external applicability. DCA is a method for 
evaluating the clinical practicability of predictive models. The DCA 
values of the training set and validation set in this study indicate that 
within a certain threshold range, RF achieves higher clinical net benefits 
than other models. The results of the two core evaluation indicators, 
namely the discriminative ability and clinical practicality of the 
comprehensive model, show that the RF model has the best compre -
hensive performance in this study and has clear clinical value. There -
fore, this study established an RF model as the best candidate model for 
discrimnating MCI risk in middle - aged and elderly individuals with 
depression.
While ML can uncover complex interactions and achieve prediction 
and decision - making, its “black box” nature complicates interpretation 
( Li et al., 2023 ). Consequently, explainable artificial intelligence has 
gained prominence, with the SHAP algorithm emerging as a preferred 
choice due to its distinct advantages( Song et al., 2024b ). This study 
quantifies the contribution intensity and direction of each feature to the 
individual discrimination results through SHAP values. It should be 
emphasized that this method reveals feature correlations rather than 
causal mechanisms. Analysis shows that the key features discriminated 
by the RF model for MCI include education, loneliness, household 
registration, IADL and dyslipidemia. Prior research consistently dem -
onstrates a positive association between education level and cognitive 
performance( Opdebeeck et al., 2016 ), and multiple cohort studies have 
identified that lower educational level is a risk factor for the progression 
of MCI( Angevaare et al., 2022 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ). 
Wang et al. ( Wang et al., 2022 ) further established that limited educa -
tion synergistically accelerates cognitive decline and AD progression 
with depression through miRNA expression modulation. Residential 
disparities significantly impact cognition in middle - aged and older 
adults( Jia et al., 2020 ), potentially due to the lower frequency of leisure 
activities and the scarcity of medical and social resources in rural areas 
( Xu et al., 2017 ). Compared with younger individuals, old adults are 
more susceptible to feeling lonely( Hoang et al., 2022 ). A meta - analysis 
has demonstrated that loneliness markedly elevates the risk of Alz -
heimer’s disease and overall dementia( Qiao et al., 2022 ). Dabiri et al. 
( Dabiri et al., 2024 ) reported that brain gray matter volume and 
depression may sequentially mediate the pathway linking loneliness to 
cognitive decline. IADL is significantly related to multiple cognitive 
domains, such as executive function, attention, and working memory 
( Raimo et al., 2024 ). A prospective cohort study demonstrated that each 
one - point increase along the three risk trajectories—depressive 
symptoms, comorbidity burden, and impaired instrumental activities of 
daily living—was associated with a 49 % higher incidence of cognitive 
impairment( Du et al., 2024 ). Although most current studies suggest that 
dyslipidemia is a risk factor for MCI( Lu et al., 2022 ; Montero-Odasso 
et al., 2025 ), evidence from CHARLS reported that patients with 
abnormal lipid diagnoses scored higher in comprehensive cognitive 
function measurements, indicating better cognitive function( Pan et al., 
2022 ). This suggests a more complex relationship between blood lipids 
and MCI. In addition, we have generated SHAP graphs to visually 
demonstrate the impact of each feature in a single sample on discrimi -
nation results in individual samples and enhance the interpretability of 
the model. For example, although a patient may not have an IADL dis -
order, the combined contribution of low education level and rural 
household registration may classify them as high risk. Such individual -
ized explanations can provide auxiliary clues for doctors to identify high 
- risk patients, but clinical decisions should still be combined with 
medical assessments.
To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first risk- 
discrimination framework for MCI tailored to middle-aged and elder 
Chinese patients with depression, thereby addressing the unmet need for 
early screening instruments for MCI comorbid with depression. This 
framework requires only demographic and neuropsychological in -
dicators obtainable in regular outpatient clinics, eliminating the need for 
expensive imaging or biomarker tests, which aligns with the resource 
constraints of primary health institutions under China’s hierarchical 
medical system. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates excellent 
discriminative performance and clinical practicability. By identifying 
key driving factors through SHAP interpretability analysis, it offers a 
low-burden and high-efficiency decision support tool for the cognitive 
health management of middle-aged and elderly patients with depres -
sion. However, this study still has certain deficiencies. Firstly, we only 
achieved moderate discriminative ability in external validation. This 
might be because the MCI diagnosis in the CHARLS and CLHLS cohorts 
employed different cognitive assessment tools, among which CMMSE 
had a strong age dependence. The AACD diagnostic criteria we use 
essentially reduce the weight of age-related predictors, which may 
weaken the cross-cohort applicability of the model. Furthermore, in the 
CLHLS cohort, the standardized depression assessment using the CES - D 
scale was only implemented in 2018, while previous survey waves used 
non-standardized items. Therefore, to ensure the consistency of the 
measurement and the comparability of the data, we limited the analysis 
to the dataset of 2018 instead of conducting a longitudinal analysis. 
Further longitudinal research in the future will help extend our findings 
to a true risk prediction framework. In addition, the included indicators 
such as IADL score and loneliness were baseline single measurements, 
without considering the dynamic impact of functional decline or 
changes in social support (such as bereavement or relocation) over time 
on the risk of MCI, which limited the diacriminative value of long-term 
risk. Finally, due to the lack of screening for factors such as hypothy -
roidism and vitamin B12 deficiency in the questionnaire, some inter -
ventionable cases may be misjudged as high-risk.
5. Conclusion
Employing eight ML algorithms, we developed a discriminative 
framework for MCI in Chinese middle-aged and elder individuals with 
depression. Among these, the RF model achieved the highest

to survival modelling in residential aged care

School of Mathematical and Computational Sciences, Massey University, Albany, Auckland, 0632, New Zealand
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Explainable AI (XAI) in geriatric palliative care
Survival analysis machine learning aged care
mortality prediction
Explainable clinical decision support systems
for end-of-life care
Time-to-event analysis
A B S T R A C T
Background and Objective: Scalable, flexible and highly interpretable tools for predicting mortality in
residential aged care facilities for the purpose of informing and optimizing palliative care decisions, do not
exist. This study is the first and most comprehensive work applying machine learning to address this need
while seeking to offer a transformative approach to integrating AI into palliative care decision-making. The
objective is to predict survival in elderly individuals six months post-admission to residential aged care facilities
with patient-level interpretability for transparency and support for clinical decision-making for palliative care
options.
Methods: Data from 11,944 residents across 40 facilities, with a novel combination of 18 features was used
to develop predictive models, comparing standard approaches like Cox Proportional Hazards, Ridge and Lasso
Regression with machine learning algorithms, Gradient Boosting (GB) and Random Survival Forest. Model
calibration was performed together with ROC and a suite of evaluation metrics to analyze results. Explainable
AI (XAI) tools were used to demonstrate both the cohort-level and patient-level model interpretability to enable
transparency in the clinical usage of the models. TRIPOD reporting guidelines were followed, with model
parameters and code provided publicly.
Results: GB was the top performer with a Dynamic AUROC of 0.746 and a Concordance Index of 0.716 for
six-month survival prediction. Explainable AI tools provided insights into key features such as comorbidities,
cognitive impairment, and nutritional status, revealing their impact on survival outcomes and interactions
that inform clinical decision-making. The calibrated model showed near-optimal performance with adjustable
clinically relevant thresholds. The integration of XAI tools proved effective in enhancing the transparency
and trustworthiness of predictions, offering actionable insights that support informed and ethically responsible
end-of-life (EoL) care decisions in aged care settings.
Conclusion: This study successfully applied machine learning to create viable survival models for aged care
residents, demonstrating their usability for clinical settings via a suite of interpretable tools. The findings
support the introduction into clinical trials of machine learning with explainable AI tools in geriatric medicine
for mortality prediction to enhance the quality of EoL care and informed discussions regarding palliative care.
1. Introduction
Predicting death is easy. Everybody will die. Estimating the precise
probability of death for an individual within a specific time period is
more difficult. An accurate estimate of expected survival time helps
people choose treatments that align with their goals of care [1]. A
falsely optimistic prognosis reduces the quality of death experienced
by a patient and their loved ones [2].
Palliative care in people with a terminal diagnosis focuses on with-
drawing treatments that cause pain or suffering and offering care that
enhances the quality of remaining life. Many people are willing to

a point when sacrificing quality for quantity is no longer justifiable. For
some, this realization comes just days before death, while for others, it
may be recognized several months prior [3].
People entering residential aged care do not usually have a specific
terminal illness. Rather, they are undergoing the inexorable decline
in function that accompanies chronic illness and natural ageing [4].
Shifting from an active treatment model to a palliative approach in this
setting is a nuanced decision and is not always clearly communicated
with residents or their families [5]. However, more than one-third

of older people admitted to residential aged care will die within six
months of admission [6]. In most healthcare settings, this prognosis
would prompt discussions about the patient’s care preferences in view
of their short life expectancy. Yet these vital conversations occur less
frequently than many older people would prefer [7].
In gerontological research, prognostic tools in mortality prediction
with the potential to inform palliative care options can be broadly cate-
gorized into prognostic indices, statistical methods, and machine learn-
ing approaches. Prognostic indices aggregate multiple clinical variables
correlated with mortality into a single value, and have been the most
popular tool for predicting mortality in aged care contexts [8]. These
indices, particularly those utilizing the Minimum Data Set (MDS),
have played a pivotal role in predicting mortality in residential aged
care. Notable tools such as the MDS Mortality Risk Index (MMRI) and
its various adaptations [9–13] have provided valuable insights into
mortality risks. However, new technologies have emerged which can
address many of the shortcomings of earlier approaches. For instance,
machine learning methods offer the potential for greater accuracy and
the capacity to manage complex, non-linear data relationships [14].
The application of machine learning in medical contexts has increased
rapidly, with some hospitals already integrating this technology into
their everyday decision-making processes [15].
Palliative care has yet to significantly benefit from advancements
in machine learning, despite the recognized potential of these tech-
nologies to enhance the quality of end-of-life (EoL) care by facilitating
timely and informed palliative treatment decisions [16]. Current ap-
plications of machine learning for mortality prediction and palliative
care decision-making are predominantly confined to hospital environ-
ments and terminally ill patients [16], leaving a notable gap in their
application to residential aged care settings. This gap is particularly
significant given the need for predictive tools that address the complex-
ities of aged care populations while ensuring transparency and clinical
usability. Furthermore, the lack of explainability behind many machine
learning models’ predictions, presents a major barrier to their adop-
tion in healthcare. The opaque nature of these models often obscures
the reasoning behind their predictions, undermining clinician trust
and impeding their integration into decision-making processes [15].
To address these challenges, recent advancements in eXplainable AI
(XAI) techniques, such as SHAP and LIME, have introduced methods
to enhance the transparency of machine learning models [17–19].
However, their application in mortality prediction for residential aged
care remains unexplored. This study fills this critical gap by combining
machine learning with XAI tools to predict six-month mortality in aged
care residents, delivering a transparent and actionable framework for
supporting palliative care decision-making in this underserved context.
Study contributions and novelty
The contributions of this study are as follows:
1. This work is the first comprehensive study to develop machine
learning models for predicting survival probabilities for a gen-
eral population of adults in residential aged care facilities.
2. This research is novel in that it integrates machine learning
into supporting palliative care, tailored specifically for aged care
settings, addressing existing gaps in the literature [15,16] by
providing actionable insights that can improve the timing and
quality of EoL care decisions.
3. This study pioneers the use of XAI tools in survival analysis
models specifically designed for residential aged care, offering
both cohort-level model interpretability and individual-level pre-
diction explanations to enhance overall transparency and trust
in AI-driven clinical decision-making where current literature
shows a significant lack of XAI integration in survival analysis
models [20].
4. Our extensive comparative benchmarking analysis demonstrates
the superior performance and interpretability of machine learn-
ing models over state-of-the-art statistical models and prognostic
indices, thus validating its practical relevance in real-world aged
care settings.
5. Our study leverages both a unique combination of features and
a large dataset to develop models capable of supporting person-
alized care, which aligns with the latest trends in biomedical AI
research.
6. Our workflow and the set of technologies used significantly
advance EoL care in aged care settings, enabling more in-
formed, transparent, and ethically responsible decision-making
that aligns with patient preferences, thus bridging the gap be-
tween theoretical models and real-world clinical utility [15].
2. Methods
This study is reported according to the TRIPOD (Transparent Re-
porting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or
Diagnosis) guideline [21].
2.1. Data source and participants
Healthcare data used in this study were collected during the pro-
vision of routine care to older individuals admitted for long-term care
between 1st July 2017 and 30th August 2023 to facilities owned by
a single large Australasian private residential aged care provider. Data
from residents at 34 New Zealand and 6 Australian aged care facilities
were included. Individuals were eligible for inclusion if they were
admitted for long-term care on or after 1st July 2017.
2.2. Outcome variable and problem formulation
The primary model prediction outcomes were twofold:
1. The development of a survival function 𝑆(𝑡|𝑥), where 𝑡 repre-
sents the time since admission to an aged care facility and 𝑥
denotes the set of covariates or features. This function provides
a continuous probability curve of survival from admission up to
six years, offering a comprehensive longitudinal risk assessment,
that also enables relative risk comparisons between patients.
2. The generation of calibrated, time-specific survival probabil-
ities at the key intervals 𝑡 = 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-
admission. These intervals represent time points for clinical
decision-making, with the 6-month forecast being particularly
vital in the context of this study.
For each individual 𝑖 in our dataset 𝐷, consisting of 𝑛 subjects, we
observe the time-to-event 𝑇𝑖 and an event indicator 𝛿𝑖, where 𝛿𝑖 = 1 de-
notes the event occurrence (death) and 𝛿𝑖 = 0 indicates censoring (sur-
vival). The dataset is represented as 𝐷 = {(𝑇1, 𝛿1, 𝑥1), … , (𝑇𝑛, 𝛿𝑛, 𝑥𝑛)},
where 𝑥𝑖 are the features. The trained model generates a survival
probability 𝑆(𝑡|𝑥𝑖) for each patient 𝑖 at any given time 𝑡, effectively
quantifying the risk of the event (death) across the entire timeframe.
Post-training, model calibration is a necessary step in survival anal-
ysis that aligns the above-predicted probabilities with actual observed
outcomes, ensuring the reliability and accuracy of the predictions for a
specific point in time of interest. To calibrate the survival probabilities
predicted by our model at any time point 𝑡, we used Platt scaling [22,
23]. This involved fitting a logistic regression model to the survival
model’s output, where 𝑃 (𝑇 > 𝑡|𝑥) represents the calibrated survival
probability beyond time 𝑡, given features 𝑥. The calibration is formally
expressed as:
𝑃 (𝑇 > 𝑡|𝑥) = 1
1 + exp(𝐴 ⋅ 𝑓 (𝑥, 𝑡) + 𝐵) , (1)

2.3. Features
A total of 18 features were used for modelling, drawn from de-
mographic and clinical data recorded by registered nurses during the
initial clinical evaluation of newly admitted residents. Medication data
were taken from the electronic medicine chart. The earliest instance
of each specific feature following admission was used. Any feature
recorded more than 31 days after admission was excluded since our
objective was to predict survival probability from the time of admis-
sion. Therefore, data collected more than one month post-admission
was discarded.
Tables 1 and 2 list all features included in the model and the values
assigned to each level. Table 1 details the demographic attributes of the
study cohort, including reasons for discharge and Rx-Risk Co-morbidity
Index diagnostic categories [24]. Table 2 reports clinical variables
drawn from the initial nursing assessment. Domain expertise was used
to assign ordinal values representing the degree of severity for each
level of the features. High values represent a state associated with
worse function or clinical status (higher mortality risk) and low values
represent states associated with better function or clinical status (lower
mortality risk).
Features relating to nutrition, mobility, smoking, sleep, skin in-
tegrity and continence correspond to the standardized set of questions
and answers based on the InterRAI long-term care facilities assess-
ment [25]. Features relating to current health status, cognition, mood
and pressure ulcers are drawn from validated InterRAI-based composite
measures (respectively, the CHESS scale (Changes in Health, End-
Stage Disease, Symptoms and Signs) [26,27], cognitive performance
scale [28], depression rating scale [29], pressure ulcer risk scale [30]).
Co-morbidities are assessed in two ways. The presence of a specific
diagnosis was established by filtering the diagnosis fields in the resident
clinical record for terms that captured dementia of any type, ischemic
cardiac disease and heart failure of any type, any malignant neoplasm,
any non-cancer pulmonary disease and any form of diabetes, excluding
glucose intolerance. The sum of the scores for these items (1 = ANY
diagnosis of this type present, 0 = ALL diagnoses of this type absent),
rather than the individual diagnosis, was used as a feature in the
final model (minimum value = 0, maximum value =5). The Rx-Risk
Co-morbidity Index was included as a second comorbidity item. This
index provides a weighted score for each specific diagnosis based on
prescription data. The scores are summed for an individual resident to
provide the final Rx-Risk score. The falls feature was a bespoke question
used by the provider about the frequency of falls in the past six months
prior to admission.
During the preliminary stages of our data processing, a pairwise
correlation coefficient threshold of 0.7 was used as a guide for eliminat-
ing highly correlated variables to ensure model parsimony and reduce
multicollinearity [31]. The decision on which one of the variables to
exclude from the model was made by examining data quality and
completeness, the relative univariate predictive power of the variable,
and potential interpretability.

Gradient boosting machine (GBM). Conceptualized by [37], employs an
optimization strategy for a differentiable loss function 𝐿 in survival
analysis. This is achieved through the iterative addition of regression
trees, with each tree addressing the residuals of the model up to that
point. In each iteration 𝑡, GBM adapts the model by adding a new
regression tree, specifically targeting the negative gradients (denoted as
−∇𝐿) of the loss function—reminiscent of the steepest descent method
in optimization. The ensemble model is updated according to:
𝐹𝑡(𝑥) = 𝐹𝑡−1(𝑥) + 𝜈 ⋅ Tree(𝑥, −∇𝐿), (2)
where 𝐹𝑡(𝑥) represents the model’s prediction at iteration 𝑡, 𝐹𝑡−1(𝑥)
is the prediction from the previous iteration, 𝜈 is a shrinkage pa-
rameter introducing regularization to control model complexity, and
Tree(𝑥, −∇𝐿) signifies the regression tree added in the current iteration,
tailored to the negative gradient of the loss. This methodical enhance-
ment at each step incrementally refines the model, contributing to a
more robust and accurate predictive performance.

Interpretation of evaluation metrics. The C-index measures the model’s
ability to rank survival times correctly. A value of 1.0 indicates perfect
discrimination, meaning the model perfectly ranks all survival times,
while 0.5 reflects random performance. Values above 0.7 are typically
considered indicative of strong predictive ability. Harrell’s C-index
can be interpreted on the same basis, but it extends this metric to
account for censored data, making it robust for incomplete survival
information. Meanwhile, the Dynamic AUROC evaluates the model’s
ability to distinguish between individuals experiencing events at spe-
cific time points. Values close to 1.0 indicate excellent discrimination,
while values below 0.7 suggest limited utility. This metric helps track
the model’s reliability over time-specific predictions. IBS on the other

2.7. eXplainable AI tools
Machine learning models are often categorized based on their trans-
parency into interpretable or ‘‘black-box’’ models. Interpretable models,
such as Linear Regression and Decision Trees, are inherently under-
standable without additional tools, allowing their global behaviour
(i.e. across the entire dataset) to be directly interpreted. Black-box mod-
els, such as Gradient Boosting and Neural Networks, require post-hoc
methods for understanding their mechanics. In this study, we define the
term interpretability as understanding the global behaviour of a model,
which includes how input features and their values influence predic-
tions and which features are most important in driving the model’s
decisions. Explainability, we define as understanding instance-specific
(i.e. patient-level) predictions using post-hoc methods like SHAP. Model
transparency captures both interpretability of its mechanics and the
explainability of its individual predictions.4
Balancing predictive strength and model transparency is a specific
challenge in contemporary machine learning research, especially in
sensitive fields such as healthcare where decisions based on model
outputs must adhere to ethical and regulatory standards. XAI aims
to address this challenge by enhancing the transparency of machine
learning models. Among various XAI tools, SHapley Additive exPla-
nations (SHAP) is prominent for its effectiveness in elucidating the
decision-making processes of complex models [45]. SHAP provides
both the model interpretability at the global (cohort-level) and ex-
plainability at the local (patient-level) dimensions. At the cohort-level,
SHAP Summary plots depict the ranked impact of features on survival
probability, while SHAP Dependence plots reveal interactions between
features. These plots offer a macroscopic view of the key factors influ-
encing model predictions. On the patient-level, SHAP Waterfall plots
detail each feature’s contribution to a specific prognosis, enhancing

3. Results
3.1. Overview
The study’s results are presented in two sections: The first part
details the performance of uncalibrated models predicting survival
probability up to six years post-admission, including insights from indi-
vidualized survival curves and SHAP plots. The second part focuses on a
calibrated model’s performance at the six-month mark, complemented
by ROC analyses.
3.2. Final study participants
Data from 12882 individuals were extracted from the database.
407 individuals lacked requisite assessment data within 31 days of
admission from the cohort and were removed. Reconciling duplicate
data from residents with one or more consecutive admissions resulted
in 11945 unique individuals. One resident was excluded due to a neg-
ative value for length of stay. The final study cohort comprised 11944
individuals. The mean age in the cohort was 86 years (SD=7), with
the majority being women (n=7200, 60%). Just over half the cohort
(n=6739, 56%) were discharged due to death (the modelled outcome)
and approximately 30% were current residents (n=3465). When all
categories were combined, in total 57% (n=6740) were represented de-
ceased and 43% (n=5205) comprised censored (survived) (see Table 1).
Three-quarters of residents had an electronic medicine chart initiated
within 31 days of admission, enabling the estimation of the Rx-Risk
Comorbidity Index for these individuals (n=9065, 76%) [24]. The most
common diagnostic categories based on prescription data were pain, a
psychotic disorder (most likely behavioural and psychological symp-
toms of dementia), congestive heart failure and gastro-oesophageal
reflux. The distribution of Rx-Risk Comorbidity Index categories is
reported5 in Table 1.

Here, we transition from theoretical high-level modelling and in-

3.5. Operationalization for clinical decision-making
The ROC curve illustrated in Fig. 67 for the calibrated 6-month GBM
model shows both the performance characteristics of the model as well
as an operational tool clinicians can use to adjust the decision-making
threshold for identifying high-risk patients of mortality within 6 months
that is suitable for different clinical contexts. It illustrates the balance
between the true negative rate (TNR or specificity) and the true positive
rate (TPR or sensitivity) achieved at various thresholds. As an example,
the figure shows the clinical implications of adopting a 0.2 survival
probability threshold (x-axis), equating to an 80% risk of death within
the 6-month timeframe and the associated misclassification tradeoffs.
• NPV: quantifies the model’s accuracy in predicting mortality. It
is defined as the ratio of true non-survivors correctly predicted,
to the total number of individuals predicted as non-survivors.
Formally, NPV is given by:

𝑇 𝑁 + 𝐹 𝑁 , (8)
where 𝑇 𝑁 represents the true negatives, i.e., individuals cor-

i.e., individuals who survived despite being predicted not to. At a
specified threshold of 0.2, our model achieves an NPV of 74%,
indicating that 74% of the residents predicted not to survive
beyond six months at this threshold, indeed did not.
• TNR: measures the model’s precision in identifying non-survivors.
Although 0.29 is low, this level of caution is appropriate in a
situation where under-estimating the likelihood of death within
six months carries potentially less clinical and ethical risk than
an over-estimation of risk.

with an example threshold of 0.2 model output probability yield-

4. Discussion
Our study represents a significant contribution in gerontological
research, notably for predicting survival rates in the residential aged
care settings via advanced machine learning and XAI. Our approach
goes beyond the current traditional methods, predominantly based on
multivariate prognostic indices, by leveraging sophisticated predictive
models whose evaluation metrics indicated satisfactory discriminatory
power and robust statistical stability. Although prognostic indices have
a long-standing history, one drawback is that their computation ne-
cessitates in-person consultations [16]. Since these consultations are
inherently resource-intensive and thus do not scale effectively for iden-
tifying individuals requiring palliative care across a larger population
such as those in aged care facilities, automated solutions such as ma-
chine learning are more appropriate. Results from our machine learning
models generally surpassed existing prognostic models in residential
aged-care populations reported in literature [8,46,47], while offer-
ing superior insights, reasoning and explainability for individualized
patient predictions. The calibrated GBM models have demonstrated
clinically useful predictive accuracy, which can be adjusted at dif-
ferent decision points on the ROC curve, in conjunction with model
transparency through the integration of SHAP tools. These advance-
ments facilitate a deeper understanding of individual patient prognoses,
thereby enabling healthcare professionals to engage in more meaning-
ful and informed discussions regarding end-of-life care preferences with
residents and their families. A recent systematic literature review [48]
has confirmed that machine learning is becoming more embedded
within aged-care contexts. The study identified 70 studies conducted
over a span of 12 years, exploring the application of machine learning
techniques for the classification of various age-related health outcomes
in older populations, including mortality. Neurodegenerative diseases
were the primary focus in over 30% of studies, followed by mental
health and the tracking of cardiovascular diseases, with both being the
focus of 10% of studies each. However, notably, despite the extensive
reliance on machine learning methods, only two studies employed XAI
tools.
4.1. Ethical implications of AI use in palliative care decisions
Ethical considerations are central to the application of predictive
AI-driven technologies in palliative care, particularly in ensuring fair-
ness, accountability and respect for patient autonomy. XAI tools, such
as SHAP used in this study, address these concerns by bringing to
light the contribution of individual factors, such as comorbidities or
cognitive impairment, to model predictions. The lucidity these tools
offer mitigates biases inherent in machine learning models, fostering
equitable and trustworthy decision-making. Medical literature is replete
with examples where opaque AI systems, even when well-intentioned,
perpetuate inequalities in healthcare access and outcomes [49,50],
therefore, traceability characteristics of AI systems represent a core
ethical requirement rather than simply a mere curious technological
feature.
While it is relatively recent, XAI is not an unknown and untested
technology, already having been successfully used in various fields in
healthcare. [51] utilized XAI with machine learning on a large colorec-
tal cancer registry, thereby identifying the ASA score and comorbidities
such as COPD, asthma, hypertension, and myocardial infarction as
key predictors of postoperative mortality which outperformed tradi-
tional scores. Meanwhile, [52] also reported that risk predictions from
machine learning models for dementia and cognitive impairment are
supported by the XAI tools in identifying variables that contribute to
the prediction outcome.
In the palliative care context, by providing clinicians with explain-
able risk probabilities and insights, XAI enhances patient autonomy,
enabling patients and families to make informed decisions aligned with
their care preferences. This is an essential component, as in the context
of palliative care, insights from these AI systems are not only for the
care provider but also for patients and their families, allowing for truly
shared decision-making. From the perspective of care providers, in the
field where patient data and mortality risk prediction are complex, XAI
provides a pathway to identify and address algorithmic bias at the level
of individual cases. By exposing decision pathways, XAI helps ensure
that predictions are non-discriminatory and clinically meaningful, and
by instilling trust, these tools prove to be critical for a field where
empathy and understanding are essential.
Collectively, both the findings and the suite of AI technologies
used in this study, point to the potential to transform decision-making
surrounding palliative care within aged care facilities, advocating for
their role as primary providers of palliative services. The real-world
applicability and impact of this study on the clinical adoption of these
advanced tools, hold the promise of meaningfully improving decision-
making processes in end-of-life care. Therefore, we believe that by
integrating the workflow comprised of the set of technologies used
in this study, a gap is bridged between theoretical models and their
real-world application in end-of-life care, ensuring that decisions are
transparent and aligned with patient preferences for delivering a higher
level of care.
4.2. Future research
Subsequent studies should incorporate dynamic, time-varying fea-
tures (such as new falls) to bolster both accuracy and responsiveness
to changes. Crucially, validating these models across varied datasets
and through clinical trials is essential to establish their generalizability.
Research should also explore integrating novel features. Future work
should also perform clinical trials using these patient-focused clinical
decision tools with the aim of quantifying effects on the quality of end-
of-life care, ensuring they are safe, effective, and aligned with patient
needs.
4.3. Study limitations
The dataset contained missing data, which, despite sophisticated
imputation, may cast some uncertainty on certain features and their
interpretability, especially in SHAP analyses. The sole reliance on cross-
sectional data at admission overlooks dynamic health changes which
are potentially more indicative of mortality risks than static admission
data. The patient cohort’s homogeneity, sourced from a single provider,
may to some degree limit the model’s applicability in varied clini-
cal settings. Furthermore, the study’s technical validation requires an
exploration into a real-world clinical integration which can only be sat-
isfied in subsequent pragmatic clinical trials and user-centred designs
to ensure the model’s practical utility and effective incorporation into
clinical workflows.
5. Conclusion
This study is the first comprehensive undertaking into developing
machine learning models to predict survival probabilities for a general
population of adults in residential aged care facilities, in combination
with interpretable AI tools. This work conducted extensive experiments
using numerous algorithms on a large dataset as well as a unique set
of features, demonstrating the feasibility of developing robust predic-
tive survival models in this setting which can be used by clinicians

learning suitable for clinical decision-making, where trust in the AI-
driven prognostic tools is provided. Predictive models were calibrated
for multiple time horizons, with an emphasis placed on the six-month
survival probabilities post-admission to a residential aged care facility.
TRIPOD reporting was adhered to and both the model parameters
and code have been made publicly available. The proposed predictive
framework, comprising the models and AI tools represents a signif-
icant step forward, offering a comprehensive approach to AI-driven
healthcare for survival analysis in residential aged-care contexts and
beyond.

ABSTRACT
Backgrounds: Preserving intrinsic capacity (IC) is essential for healthy aging. This study examined the associa -
tions between longitudinal changes in IC and subsequent adverse health outcomes.
Methods: Participants were community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 60 years from the China Health and Retirement 
Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Changes in IC between 2011 and 2013 were classified as consistently well, 
improved, worsened, or consistently declined. Logistic regression assessed associations with falls and hospital -
ization (2015), and Cox models evaluated all-cause mortality (2020).
Results: Changes in IC were significant predictors of adverse outcomes. Worsened (OR = 1.674, 95 % CI: 
1.163 – 2.411, P = 0.006) and consistently declined changes in IC (OR = 1.914, 95 % CI: 1.373 – 2.668, P < 0.001) 
were both associated with an increased risk of falls, while domain-specific changes, such as worsened locomo -
tion, consistently declined in cognition and fluctuations in psychology or vision, were also linked to increased fall 
risk (all P < 0.017). Both consistently declined IC (OR = 1.513, 95 % CI: 1.079 – 2.122, P < 0.017) and worsened 
locomotion were independent predictors of hospitalization (OR = 1.837, 95 % CI: 1.265 – 2.670, P = 0.001). 
Declines in locomotion were also strongly associated with mortality, with higher risk observed in the worsened 
group (HR = 1.571, 95 % CI: 1.088 – 2.267, P < 0.017).
Conclusions: Monitoring intrinsic capacity changes, especially locomotion decline, enables early identification of 
vulnerable older adults and supports timely, targeted interventions to reduce adverse outcomes.
1. Backgrounds
Population aging has become a common challenge worldwide. Aging 
is a natural stage of life involving physical, psychological, and social 
changes. To age actively and healthily, individuals need strategies that 
maintain or improve quality of life ( Sanchis-Soler et al., 2025 ). In the 
World Report on Ageing and Health released by the World Health Orga -
nization in 2015, the concept of “ intrinsic capacity ” (IC) was introduced. 
IC refers to the composite of an individual's physical and mental ca -
pacities. Together with the surrounding environment and their in -
teractions, it influences functional ability in older adults. This provides 
theoretical support for the goal of “ healthy aging ” ( WHO, 2015 ). IC 
includes locomotion, cognition, vitality, psychology, and sensory (vision 
and hearing). This concept moves beyond a disease-centered 
perspective, emphasizing functional status in older adults ( Cesari et al., 
2018 ).
Building on this framework, empirical studies have demonstrated 
that impairments in IC are associated with disability ( Stolz et al., 2022 ; 
Zeng et al., 2021 ), falls ( Liu et al., 2021 ), hospitalization ( S ´anchez- 
S ´anchez et al., 2022 ), and mortality ( Locquet et al., 2022 ). However, the 
level of IC in older adults is not fixed. With increasing age, IC may 
deteriorate, remain stable, or improve. For instance, while some older 
adults maintain stable cognition or locomotion, others may experience 
accelerated decline despite being of similar age. This heterogeneity re -
flects the combined effects of individual health reserves, environmental 
support, and disease burden ( Zhou et al., 2024 ). Within this interplay, 
leisure activities provide social support and enhance emotional well- 
being, forming a fundamental component of quality of life that may

tivity, thereby fostering active and healthy aging ( Parra-Rizo et al., 
2022 ). IC represents the integration of multiple dimensions, its dynamic 
changes may affect health gradually and accumulate over time. Most 
existing evidence focuses on the association between IC levels measured 
at a single cross-sectional time point and adverse health outcomes. 
Given China's rapidly aging population, examining changes in IC in this 
context is particularly relevant. Limited evidence exists on how longi -
tudinal changes of IC and its dimensions relate to short-term and long- 
term outcomes in community-dwelling older adults in China.
This study was based on a nationally representative prospective 
cohort of community-dwelling older adults in China. We applied a two- 
period analysis. The short-term follow-up (2 years) focused on acute 
events such as falls and hospitalization, reflecting immediate losses of 
adaptive capacity. The long-term follow-up (7 years) examined all-cause 
mortality, capturing the cumulative impact of sustained IC deterioration 
across multiple systems. By linking IC changes with key short- and long- 
term health outcomes, this study advances the understanding of aging 
processes and supports strategies for early intervention and long-term 
health promotion in older adults.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Data source and study population
The data for this study were obtained from the China Health and

Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). The CHARLS study, orga -
nized by the National School of Development at Peking University 
(IRB00001052-11015), is a nationwide longitudinal survey of adults 
aged 45 and older in China. Detailed information on the study design, 
survey methods, and data quality has been described in previous 
research ( Zhao et al., 2013 ). The sample includes over ten thousand 
households from 28 provinces and 150 counties, making it broadly 
representative. The survey collected information on health, medical 
insurance, income and spending, work, and retirement at both the 
household and individual levels. Data were gathered through face-to- 
face and proxy interviews. The database is updated every two years 
and has conducted multiple follow-ups since the national baseline sur -
vey in 2011. The study analyzed the trends of IC changes between 2011 
(Wave 1) and 2013 (Wave 2), and further examined their associations 
with short-term outcomes in 2015 (Wave 3) ( N = 1777) and with out -
comes at the last follow-up in 2020 (Wave 5) ( N = 1672).
Inclusion: adults ≥ 60 years, complete IC and outcome data.
Exclusion: missing data, death before 2015 ( Fig. 1 ).
2.2. Variable selection and definition
2.2.1. IC
According to the WHO ICOPE guidelines, IC includes six dimensions 
( WHO, 2017 ). Each dimension is scored 1 if the function is intact and 0 if 
it is impaired, giving a total score from 0 to 6. Higher scores mean better 
IC status, while a total score of 5 or below is considered IC decline. The 
assessment methods for each dimension were the same as a previous 
study ( Zhou et al., 2024 ). Locomotion: five times sit-to-stand tests; vi -
tality: BMI, cognition: TICS (Telephone Interview of Cognitive Status); 
psychology: 10-items CES-D (Center for epidemiologic studies depres -
sion scale); hearing and vision: self-reported impaired. IC was assessed 
at the baseline survey (2011) and at the 2-year follow-up (2013). The 
patterns of IC change were divided into four categories ( Jia et al., 2023 ): 
(1) Consistently well: 5 – 6 points at both baseline and 2-year follow-up; 
(2) Improved: ≤ 4 points at baseline and 5 – 6 points at 2-year follow-up; 
(3) Worsened: 5 – 6 points at baseline and ≤ 4 points at 2-year follow-up; 
(4) Consistently declined: ≤ 4 points at both baseline and 2-year follow- 
up. The changes of locomotion, cognition, psychology, vitality, vision, 
and hearing were also classified into four categories:(1) consistently 
well: 1 point at both baseline and 2-year follow-up; (2) improved: 
0 points at baseline and 1 point at 2-year follow-up; (3) worsened: 1 
point at baseline and 0 points at 2-year follow-up; (4) consistently poor: 
0 points at both baseline and 2-year follow-up.
2.2.2. Adverse health outcomes
2.2.2.1. Falls. Since the time span of IC changes in this study was from 
2011 to 2013, the short-term outcome of falls was assessed based on the 
2015 follow-up question: “ Have you fallen in the past two years? ” Par -
ticipants who answered “ yes ” were classified into the fall group.
2.2.2.2. Hospitalization. Hospitalization was defined as staying in a 
hospital for at least one night. Because IC changes in this study covered 
the period from 2011 to 2013, the short-term outcome of hospitalization 
was assessed in the 2015 follow-up. Participants were asked, “ Have you 
been hospitalized in the past year? ” Those who answered “ yes ” were 
classified into the hospitalization group.
2.2.2.3. All-cause mortality. From baseline to the end of the 2020 
follow-up, all-cause deaths were recorded. However, the exact dates of 
death were available only in Wave 2 (2013) and Wave 5 (2020). This 
study examined the association between IC changes from baseline 
(Wave 1, 2011) to Wave 2 (2013) and short-term outcomes in Wave 3 
(2015). Therefore, individuals who died during these three waves were 
excluded, and only deaths recorded in Wave 4 (2018) and Wave 5 
(2020) were included. For participants with an exact date of death, 
survival time was calculated as the time from the baseline survey date to 
the date of death. If the exact date of death was unavailable, survival 
time was estimated from the baseline interview date to the survey wave 
date when death was last recorded.
2.2.3. Covariates
2.2.3.1. Sociodemographic. Data were obtained from the CHARLS 
baseline survey (2011), including age, sex, education level, marital 
status, and income level.
2.2.3.2. Chronic conditions. Diseases included self-reported physician- 
diagnosed chronic conditions, such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, dia -
betes or hyperglycemia, cancer or malignant tumor, heart disease, 
stroke, chronic lung disease, liver disease, kidney disease, stomach or 
other digestive diseases, arthritis or rheumatism, emotional or mental 
disorders, memory-related diseases, and asthma.
2.2.3.3. Frailty. Baseline frailty status was assessed using the Fried 
frailty phenotype ( Fried et al., 2001 ), which includes weakness, slow -
ness, exhaustion, inactivity, and shrinking. The cut-off points validated 
in the CHARLS study were applied ( Wu et al., 2017 ).
2.3. Statistical analysis
Data processing and statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 
(version 27.0) and R software (version 4.4.1). For normally distributed 
data, results were presented as mean ± standard deviation (x ± s); for 
non-normally distributed data, results were presented as median 
(interquartile range) [M (IQR)]. Statistical analyses were conducted 
using the Student's t -test and the Mann – Whitney U test, respectively. 
Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, 
and analyzed using the chi-square test. Logistic regression models were 
used to examine the associations between the four IC change patterns 
and short-term outcomes of falls and hospitalization. Adjusted odds 
ratios (ORs) with 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Cox 
proportional hazards models were used to assess the relationship be -
tween the four IC change patterns and all-cause mortality. Collinearity 
was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs) and tolerance sta -
tistics. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using 
Schoenfeld residuals; detailed results are provided in Supplementary 
Fig. S1. The main exposure variable was categorized into four trend- 
based groups, with the first group serving as the reference. As three 
pairwise hypotheses were tested against the reference group, Bonferroni 
correction was applied to control for multiple testing, and a two-sided P 
< 0.017 (0.05/3) was considered statistically significant.
3. Results
3.1. Baseline characteristics of short-term outcomes
The mean age of participants was 66.6 years, and 42.6 % were 
women. Among the 1777 participants, 343 (19.3 %) had a history of falls 
and 306 (17.2 %) had a history of hospitalization ( Table 1 ). Baseline 
comparison showed that, compared with the non-fall group, the fall 
group had more women, more urban and low-income participants, more 
with two or more diseases, and more with frailty at baseline. The fall 
group showed higher proportions of worsened and consistently declined 
IC compared with the non-fall group ( P < 0.001). Higher proportions of 
worsened or consistently declined status were also observed in loco -
motion, cognition, psychology, and vision (all P < 0.05). The hospital -
ization group was older than the non-hospitalization group and had 
more participants with two or more diseases and with frailty at baseline. 
They also had higher proportions of worsened and consistently declined
