3.3. Baseline characteristics of long-term outcomes
At the 7-year follow-up, 105 participants were lost to follow-up, 
leaving 1672 included in the study. Among them, 236 (14.1 %) had 
died. The mean age was 66.6 years, and 41.1 % were women. Compared 
with the survival group, the death group was older, included fewer 
women, and were more likely to be widowed or single (all P < 0.05). 
They also had more participants with two or more chronic diseases and 
with frailty (all P < 0.05). In the death group, more participants showed 
worsened or consistently poor IC, as well as worsened or consistently 
poor locomotion, vitality, cognition, hearing, and vision (all P < 0.05) 
( Table 3 ).
3.4. Associations of IC and domain-specific change patterns with long- 
term all-cause mortality
Table 4 presents the associations between changes in IC and all-cause 
mortality. In the univariate analysis, no concerning multicollinearity 
was detected (all VIFs < 3.0; all tolerances > 0.30), and worsened and 
consistently poor IC patterns, as well as worsened and consistently poor 
locomotion, consistently poor vitality, consistently poor cognition, and 
consistently poor hearing, were all associated with a higher risk of 
mortality (P < 0.05).
After adjusting for covariates associated with mortality in univariate 
analyses, worsened locomotion (HR = 1.571, 95 % CI: 1.088 – 2.267, P =
0.0158) remained significant indicating higher 7-year all-cause mor -
tality ( Table 4 ).
4. Discussions
4.1. The role of IC changes in falls, hospitalization, and mortality
Contemporary geriatric medicine emphasizes risk prevention and 
functional preservation. This study shows that changes in IC and its 
domains of locomotion, cognition, psychology, and vision are important 
predictors of falls, hospitalization, and mortality. By dynamically 
monitoring these changes, clinicians can identify high-risk populations 
in advance and develop personalized intervention strategies. This 
approach is valuable for reducing adverse health events, improving 
quality of life in older adults, and optimizing the allocation of healthcare

4.2. Association with short-term adverse outcomes
Worsened and consistently poor IC was significantly associated with 
short-term adverse events of falls after adjustment, consistent with ev -
idence from both cross-sectional ( Liu et al., 2021 ) and longitudinal 
cohort studies ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) demonstrating that impaired IC is 
linked to subsequent fall risk.
Within the IC framework, worsened locomotion and consistently 
poor cognition were further identified as independent risk factors for 
falls. These associations may be attributable to a progressive loss of 
functional reserve, including reduced lower-limb strength and proprio -
ception, as well as a slower and more variable gait, all of which reduce 
recovery capacity after unexpected events ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Mahoney, 
1998 ; Thomas et al., 2025 ). In addition, lower performance in attention 
and executive function has been associated with gait slowing, insta -
bility, and future falls ( Montero-Odasso and Speechley, 2018 ). An as -
sociation between consistently poor IC and falls was observed in our 
study, aligning with results from the National Health and Aging Trends 
Study (NHATS), in which persistently low IC was associated with higher 
fall risk ( Chen et al., 2025 ). The agreement across cohorts with differing 
IC definitions, follow-up structures, and care settings suggests that low 
or persistently poor IC captures a common vulnerability relevant to fall 
susceptibility. These convergent findings reinforce the usefulness of IC 
trajectories and levels for risk stratification in community-dwelling 
older adults. Consistently poor psychology and worsened or consis -
tently poor vision were each associated with a higher risk of falls after 
multivariable adjustment. These findings are consistent with prior re -
ports linking sustained psychological problems ( Gambaro et al., 2022 ) 
and visual impairment ( Seresirikachorn et al., 2025 ) to later falls in 
community-dwelling older adults.
It is noteworthy that improvement in the psychology and vision 
domains was also associated with an increased risk of falls. This pattern 
may arise when increased activity following improvement is not 
matched by physical capacity, or when perception and coordination are 
disturbed during the adaptation period after treatment or functional 
change. These observations suggest that functional change in any di -
rection may temporarily disrupt the balance between physical capacity 
and behavioral demands in older adults, leading to a new period of

vulnerability. Practical implications follow directly. Structured strength 
and balance training should be provided to improve lower-limb function 
and postural stability. Vision rehabilitation combined with fall- 
prevention education can address sensory deficits and unsafe behav -
iors. Psychological support can help patients adapt to change, reduce 
fear of falling, and encourage safe participation in daily activity.
From a public health perspective, these findings support integrating 
IC monitoring into primary care. Routine screening of IC and simple 
tracking of changes can identify people at higher risk earlier, guide 
timely referrals to rehabilitation and mental health services, and inform 
community programs for fall prevention. Aligning these practices with 
policies on healthy aging may help reduce adverse events and improve 
quality of life in older adults.
Consistent with the NHATS findings ( Chen et al., 2025 ), consistently 
poor IC was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization. 
Although some studies have classified IC change into decline, stable, and 
improvement and reported a higher hospitalization risk in the decline 
group ( Hwang et al., 2024 ), our study did not observe an increased risk 
associated with IC worsening. Shorter follow-up and differing opera -
tional definitions may also have captured declines that had not yet 
reached a threshold to precipitate hospitalization. Finally, adjustment 
for multimorbidity and frailty and variation in hospitalization defini -
tions may have reduced the apparent independent effect of IC 
deterioration.
Worsened locomotion was also an independent risk factor for hos -
pitalization. This may be related to the increased risk of falls and frac -
tures, as well as pulmonary diseases, caused by musculoskeletal and 
neurological decline. In terms of disease progression, loss of muscle 
strength and mass limits effective training of cardiopulmonary function, 
which accelerates the progression of chronic conditions such as car -
diovascular disease ( Damluji et al., 2023 ) and neurological disorders 
( Yang et al., 2022 ). These factors act together to increase the likelihood 
of hospitalization. For older adults with these worsened changes, 
personalized comprehensive intervention plans can be developed. 
Similarly, a study in Jinan, Shandong Province, which included 756 
community-dwelling older adults aged 60 years and above, identified IC 
change patterns over one year. The group with rapid declines in loco -
motion, psychology, cognition, and vitality had twice the risk of hos -
pitalization after one year compared with the relatively healthy group 
( Yu et al., 2022 ). Compared with cross-sectional classifications that 
focus on combinations of domain-specific status, this study used a 
nationwide database covering older adults with different economic 
levels, healthcare environments, and lifestyles. IC was assessed not only 
as an overall functional trajectory but also further refined into specific 
domain trajectories such as locomotion and cognition.

4.3. Association with long-term adverse outcomes
After adjusting for disease number and baseline frailty status, this 
study still found that worsened locomotion was significantly associated 
with 7-year all-cause mortality, with risks increased by 57.1 %. This 
finding is generally consistent with results from the same population 
showing that immobility increased the risk of all-cause mortality over 2 
years ( Wang et al., 2024 ). This study, with a longer 7-year follow-up, 
further confirmed the sustained impact of worsened locomotion on 
long-term all-cause mortality. Compared with other dimensions such as 
cognition, vitality, psychology, hearing, and vision, locomotion is more 
vulnerable to adverse events such as falls and being bedridden, which 
are major contributors to mortality in older adults. This is consistent 
with our findings that worsened locomotion was also associated with 
short-term falls and hospitalization. Therefore, locomotion shows 
unique sensitivity and predictive value in assessing the risk of all-cause 
mortality. From a clinical intervention perspective, the assessment and 
management of locomotion should be a central component of health 
care in older adults. In 2024, the WHO released the second edition of the 
Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) guidelines, which emphasize 
person-centered care. The guidelines highlight the importance of 
providing long-term care based on IC monitoring and changes to opti -
mize health outcomes, improve equity, enhance health security, and 
increase cost-effectiveness, consistent with primary health care ( WHO, 
2024 ). Our results support WHO's 2024 ICOPE recommendations to 
prioritize IC, particularly locomotion, as a key indicator for designing 
personalized interventions. We suggest an annual IC screen and 3 to 6 
month follow up for those with decline, using standardized brief tools 
and predefined referral pathways. Program performance can be evalu -
ated by reductions in falls and hospitalizations and by preservation of 
functional ability. These steps align with primary health care priorities 
and can inform healthy aging initiatives in community settings.
4.4. Strengths and limitations
This study has several strengths. It applied a nationally representa -
tive cohort to track IC changes over time, providing evidence beyond 
single time-point assessments. It examined both short-term outcomes 
(falls and hospitalization) and long-term outcomes (7-year mortality), 
which allowed evaluation of both immediate and cumulative effects. 
Furthermore, it explored domain-specific changes, showing that loco -
motion deterioration had a distinct predictive value for adverse health 
outcomes.
This study also has several limitations. First, since data were ob -
tained from the CHARLS database, the way IC was measured may not 
fully reflect the actual condition of older adults. Second, participants 
with missing follow-up data were excluded when determining IC 
changes; these individuals may have experienced severe declines in IC 
that prevented follow-up, potentially leading to an underestimation of 
the impact of IC deterioration. Finally, chronic diseases were self- 
reported without laboratory verification, and their control status was 
not available, which may have reduced the reliability of the findings.
5. Conclusions
Compared with the consistently well IC group, worsened and 
consistently poor IC were significantly associated with falls, and 
consistently poor IC was also associated with hospitalization. Worsened 
locomotion was a strong predictor of short-term falls, hospitalization, 
and long-term all-cause mortality. This suggests that the assessment of 
older adults' health should shift from static measurement to dynamic 
monitoring. Early identification of specific longitudinal changes of IC 
and its dimensions may facilitate targeted interventions and help pre -
vent adverse health outcomes. In addition, clinical interventions should 
not only focus on older adults with functional decline but also remain 
alert to those showing “improvement.” Providing appropriate adaptive 
training and safety education may help them transition smoothly and 
ultimately translate functional improvement into tangible health 
benefits.

Abstract
OBJECTIVES: The concept of ‘intrinsic capacity’ (IC) offers a new 
way to approach another concept, that of ‘healthy aging’. The first 
objective of the present study was to assess the ability of the construct 
of ‘intrinsic capacity’ to predict death. The second objective was to 
assess whether deteriorations in intrinsic capacity, measured over 1 and 
2 years, are predictive of death. 
DESIGN: The present analysis was based on a prospective cohort 
study.
SETTING: Community-dwelling participants.
PARTICIPANTS: The study recruited older adults aged 65 years and 
older.
MEASUREMENTS:  Intrinsic capacity (IC) encompasses five 
domains: sensorial (not evaluated here), cognition (Mini-Mental 
State Examination), nutrition (Mini-Nutritional Assessment), mobility 
(Short Physical Performance Battery), and psychological (Geriatric 
Depression Scale). Each domain was considered satisfactory when 
its assessment, for an individual, was above the threshold defined by 
the initial validation of the domain assessment tool. To explore the 
relationship between IC and mortality risk, a Cox model was applied. 
The predictive value of the dynamic aspects (i.e., changes over 1 year 
and 2 years) was investigated using the following categorization of IC: 
stable, deteriorated, improved.
RESULTS: The sample was composed of 481 volunteers aged 
73.4±6.12 years (60.1% women). Two satisfactory IC domains 
appeared to be significantly associated with reduced mortality risk: the 
satisfactory mobility domain (adjusted HR=0.45 [0.26-0.79]) and the 
satisfactory psychological domain (adjusted HR = 0.56 [1.04-3.09]). 
When considering intrinsic capacity as a whole construct, using a 
composite Z-score, we noticed that the risk of death was decreased by 
49% for an increase of 1 standard deviation in IC. Changes in intrinsic 
capacity in the mobility and psychological domains led to an increased 
risk of death (from 2.74 to 4.18-fold). 
CONCLUSION:  The concept of intrinsic capacity seems highly 
relevant in order to assess older adults’ health and well-being. This 
concept should be considered for integration into clinical practice. 
Key words: Healthy Ageing, World Health Organization, epidemiology. 
Introduction
I
ntrinsic capacity (IC), a new concept for assessing mental 
and physical functioning, was recently launched by the 
World Health Organization (WHO) in its World Report 
on Aging and Health as a strategy towards healthy aging (1). 
IC, a multidimensional indicator, is defined as “the composite 
of all the physical and mental capacities of an individual”. This 
concept searches to shift focus from the negative approach of 
disability to a positive approach of capacity. IC encompasses 
five domains of functioning: cognition, vitality (including 
energy/metabolism aspects), sensory, locomotion, and 
psychosocial (2).  
The WHO encourages efforts worldwide aligned with their 
Healthy Ageing program, and has published guidelines on 
integrated care for older people (ICOPE), detailing community-
level interventions to manage declines in IC (3). The WHO 
proposes a paradigm shift in care priorities for older people, 
away from episodic needs (diseases, frailty, disability...) and 
towards care trajectories that focus on the preservation of 
physical and mental capacity in the long-term (4, 5). 
Evidence of the association of each individual domain of 
IC and health outcomes is accumulating (2, 6–8), and IC has 
recently been applied in a nursing home population, where 
a reduced IC was associated with a higher risk of mortality 
during its 3-year follow-up (9). Before adopting the positive 
approach of IC of the WHO guidelines, it seems crucial to 
statistically investigate the relationship between a satisfactory 
IC and its potential consequences on the reduction of the 
occurrence of health adverse outcomes and confirm that the 
new construct is meaningful (10), particularly in community-
dwelling older people, which is the target population of the 
WHO guidelines.  
The WHO has suggested that the concept of IC should be 
considered a dynamic construct, evolving over time (11). This 
means that the course of a patient’s IC (i.e., its trajectory over 
time: a decline, an improvement, or a stabilization) should be 
monitored by clinicians and researchers, at the individual level 
but also for populations (12). 
Based on these observations, we hypothesize that: 1) A 
satisfactory IC (as a whole construct) at baseline is associated 
with a reduced risk of mortality in community-dwelling 
older people over 5 years of follow-up; 2) The five domains 
represented in the concept of IC provide a different predictive 
value for the association of IC with mortality; 3) IC is a 
dynamic condition and a decrease in IC from baseline to the 
first year of follow-up, as well as from baseline to the second 
year of follow-up, is proportionally associated to a higher risk 
of mortality at the end of the 5-year follow-up period.

INTRINSIC CAP ACITY DEFINED USING FOUR DOMAINS AND MORTALITY RISK
Methods
Design
The present article presents the results of a post-hoc 
analysis of a prospective population-based cohort, part of 
the SarcoPhAge study, which included 534 older adults in 
Belgium who were seen annually from 2013 to 2019. A 
detailed description of the procedures and data collection in the 
SarcoPhAge study has been previously published (8, 13). 
Population 
The population consisted of community-dwelling healthy 
volunteers, 65 years of age or older. Participants with a body 
mass index (BMI) ≥50 kg/m
2 or an amputated limb were 
excluded.
Intrinsic capacity 
Four domains of IC were evaluated in this study: cognition, 
nutrition, mobility, and psychosocial. We were unable to 
evaluate the sensory domain due to a lack of available data. The 
four domains were assessed using the following procedures, and 
thresholds were established according to previous literature:
• Cognitive domain: The Mini-Mental State Examination 
(MMSE) (14) has been used to assess cognitive function, and 
considered satisfactory when >26 points (out of a maximum 
of 30 points) (15).
• Nutritional domain: The Mini-Nutritional Assessment 
(MNA) (16) has been administered. A score higher than 
17 points (maximum 30 points) indicates no risk of 
malnutrition, and consequently a satisfactory nutritional 
domain. 
• Mobility domain: The Short Physical Performance Battery 
(SPPB) test, scored on a maximum of 12 points (17, 18) 
has been used. A score > 8 points indicates the absence of 
mobility-related disability (19), thus a satisfactory mobility 
domain.
• Psychological domain: The Geriatric Depression Scale 
(GDS), composed of 15 items, has been employed to 
evaluate this domain. A score of <5 points indicates the 
absence of depression and was thus considered satisfactory 
in this study (a score comprised between 12 and 15 indicates 
severe depression, between 9 and 11 indicates moderate 
depression, between 5 and 8 indicates mild depression, and 
between 0 and 4 indicates normal functioning) (20).
Most of the thresholds have been based on what was 
proposed as satisfactory cutoffs during the initial validations 
of the tools (for the MNA, the GDS, and the SPPB) while the 
MMSE satisfactory threshold has been defined according to 
more recent literature.
Unfortunately, the sensorial domain was not assessed in our 
study. Our analysis focused on the four domains separately 
(i.e., 4 dichotomous variables) but also on the IC as a whole, 
by combining the values obtained in the four domains. For this 
summary score, representing IC, we calculated Z-scores (which 
are the distance to our studied population mean expressed in 
standard deviations). The Z-score can be interpreted as follow: a 
positive z-score indicates that the raw score of the individual is 
higher than the mean. A negative Z-score indicates that the raw 
score of the individual is below the mean. The z-score indicates 
the number of standard deviations by which the individual’s 
raw score deviates from the population mean. In this study, 
we first calculated z-scores for each of the four domains and 
then calculated a composite Z-score that is the sum of the 
four domains Z-scores divided by four. This methodology 
places each of the four domains on the same scale before 
calculating a summary measure. Cognitive, nutritional and 
mobility domains were identically weighted, with higher scores 
indicating improvement on this domain. The psychosocial 
domain was negatively weighted, with higher scores indicating 
a deterioration.  
The dynamic nature of the IC concept was investigated as 
follows:
• Evolution of each of the four IC domains separately (stable, 
deteriorated, improved) between baseline (T0) and 1 year of 
follow-up (T1). We consider the evolution as stable when the 
individual presented a not satisfactory domain at T0 and at 
T1 or a satisfactory domain at T0 and at T1. The evolution 
was considered deteriorated when the individual had a 
satisfactory domain at T0 but had a not satisfactory domain 
at T1. Finally, the evolution was considered as improved 
when the individual presented a not satisfactory domain at 
T0 and a satisfactory domain at T1.
• Evolution of each of the four IC domains separately (stable, 
deteriorated, improved) between baseline (T0) and the 2nd 
year of follow-up (T2). We consider the evolution as stable 
when the individual presented a not satisfactory domain at 
T0 and at T2 or a satisfactory domain at T0 and at T2. The 
evolution was considered deteriorated when the individual 
had a satisfactory domain at T0 but had a not satisfactory 
domain at T2. Finally, the evolution was considered as 
improved when the individual presented a not satisfactory 
domain at T0 but no longer at T2.
Outcome measure
The main outcome measure was the mortality risk in 
individuals with satisfactory IC or without satisfactory IC. 
Regarding the dynamic evolution at baseline during the 5-year 
follow-up, comparison of individuals with without satisfactory 
IC or satisfactory IC were also performed. Mortality was 
collected annually by interview or phone call to the relatives of 
the participants of the SarcoPhAge study and confirmed by the 
medical record. The date of death was also recorded. 
General characteristics of the population and 
covariates
The following demographic and clinical characteristics were 
used to describe the population:
• Age: employed as a covariate because known to significantly

impact mortality risk.
• Sex, employed as a covariate because known to significantly 
impact mortality risk.
• Body mass index (BMI); calculated as height divided by 
weight-squared (kg/m²). 
• Number of concomitant diseases per participant: self-
reported and employed as a covariate because known to 
significantly impact mortality risk. 
• Number of drugs per participant: self-reported.  
• Quality of life: using the SF-36 (21) which was self-
administered. The SF-36 is a generic questionnaire assessing 
the quality of life of the individual in its physical (PCS) and 
mental (MCS) aspects, generating scores ranging from 0 
(worst quality of life) to 100 (better quality of life). 
Statistical procedures  
All the statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 24 
software (IBM Corporation, Armonk; NY , USA) and R version 
3.6.2. The distribution of numeric variables was checked 
using four methods: examining the histogram, examining 
the quantile-quantile plot, performing the Shapiro-Wilk test 
and comparing mean and median values. When normally 
distributed, data is presented as mean ± standard deviation 
(SD). When skewed, data are presented as median (percentile 
25 – percentile 75). Binary variables are expressed in absolute 
(N) and relative (%) frequencies. Regarding the association 
between a satisfactory IC domain and mortality risk, we applied 
the Cox proportional hazards model to examine the effect of 
a satisfactory IC on time to mortality, yielding a hazard ratio 
(HR) and its 95% confidence interval. An HR significantly 
greater than 1 indicates higher risk, and an HR smaller than 1 
indicates lower risk. The model was adjusted for age, sex, and 
number of comorbidities. Survival curves were constructed 
by the Kaplan-Meier method to visualize the time-to-event 
relationship. Log-rank tests were performed. All results were 
considered statistically significant at the 5% critical level. 
Results
Description of the studied population
After 5 years of follow-up of the SarcoPhAge cohort, 
initially constituted of 534 older individuals, only 53 
participants were impossible to contact and thus considered lost 
to follow-up, making a total sample of 481 volunteers.
In our sample of 481 community-dwelling older people, 
the mean age was 73.4 ± 6.12 years. Most of the participants 
were female (n=289; 60.1%). The individuals in our cohort 
had a mean body mass index of 26.6 ± 4.76 kg/m2. Individuals 
consumed 4 (3-6) drugs and had 5 (3-8) concomitant conditions 
(i.e., median scores). Quality of life in the sample, measured 
by the mental and the physical component scores of the SF-36, 
did not reach higher than 44.9 (35.4 – 53.2) points and 44.8 
(37.05 – 51.9) points, respectively. Complete characteristics are 
described in Table 1.

Intrinsic capacity
The concept of IC encompasses 4 domains. Table 2 provides 
a detailed overview of the domains, for both participants with 
satisfactory or without results. The prevalence of satisfactory IC 
reached 84% for the cognitive domain, 86.3% for the nutritional 
domain, 72.8% for the mobility domain and 68% for the 
psychological domain.
After one year of follow-up, data was available for 366 
volunteers. The 1-year follow-up showed that fewer participants 
presented not satisfactory domains of IC than at baseline, with 
the prevalence of not satisfactory domains varying, depending 
on the domain, from 5.7% (cognition and nutrition) to 27.2% 
(psychosocial) (Table 2). The same finding was established at 
the 2-year follow-up (n=318 individuals), with a prevalence 
of not satisfactory IC domains ranging from 6.0% (nutrition) 
to 27.4% (cognition). After 1 year of follow-up, a decrease 
in the prevalence of limitation was noted, the prevalence 
ranging from 1.9% of older individuals (cognition) to 6.8% 
of older individuals (psychosocial). Interestingly, an increase 
in the prevalence of satisfactory IC domains must also be 
highlighted, varying from 6.8% of the sample (psychosocial) 
to 9.0% (mobility). The same pattern between stabilization, 
deterioration and improvement was found for the evolution of 
IC domains after two years of follow-up (Table 2).
Association between IC and 5-year mortality risk
Subsequently, we observed the relationship between having a 
satisfactory score for each of the 4 domains of IC with mortality 
risk in our cohort. The first observation to be made is that two 
IC domains appear to have an outsized impact on mortality. 
Indeed, presenting with good physical abilities (i.e., satisfactory 
mobility) entailed a lower risk of death (which was decreased 
by 55%) (adjusted HR = 0.45 [0.26-0.79]). Likewise, good 
psychological health (i.e., satisfactory psychosocial domain) 
engendered a 44% lower risk of death (adjusted HR =0.56 
[0.32-0.96]) (Table 3). No statistically significant association 
between having a satisfactory score for the other two domains

established. Figure 1 depicts the time-to-event association 
between these satisfactory IC domains and mortality occurring 
during the 5-year period of follow-up.
When looking at the association between the composite 
Z-score and the occurrence of deaths within the 5-year follow-
up period, we observed that when the Z-score  was increased 
(i.e., better IC), the risk of death within 5 years was reduced 
(-49% risk) as shown in Table 3. 
Further analysis demonstrates that the observed changes 
for the 4 domains of IC were also of determining importance. 
Indeed, when we looked at the 1-year and 2-year decline of 
SPPB (decreased mobility), a significant increase in the risk 
of death was found (respectively, HR = 2.74 [95%CI: 1.09-
6.9] and HR = 3.61 [95%CI: 1.23-10.6]). We also made the 
observation that a psychological decline (via GDS) in the 2-year 
period of follow-up was highly determinant of the risk of death 
at 5 years: the risk of death was effectively increased 4.18-fold 
(Table 4).

Discussion 
Our study sought to assess the predictive power of IC (as 
a single construct or as its separate domains) on mortality 
risk. Two main findings emerged. First, three indicators were 
predictive of a lower risk of death: a satisfactory mobility 
domain, a satisfactory psychosocial domain and the composite 
IC Z-score (i.e., IC as a whole construct). Second, considering 
IC as a dynamic entity is important given the relationship 
between the short-term (i.e., over 1 year or 2 years) decline in 
mobility and psychosocial IC domains with higher mortality 
risk.
Although few other studies have been carried out on this 
topic, they confirm our overall conclusions: the concept of IC 
is relevant, and has a degree of predictive power regarding 
mortality (2, 22, 23). A different study has focused on the 
topic of the individual IC domains: Charles et al. evaluated

Another important element in this study was the analysis of 
IC as a whole, using the composite Z-score. When we applied 
this method, we noticed that the risk of death decreased by 49% 
for a 1 SD increase in the z-score (i.e., by improving the IC as a 
whole). 
Considering IC as an indicator in itself seems judicious and 
clinically relevant. IC can therefore be considered as a whole 
construct and not a collection of separate entities.
We cannot conclude, on the basis of our results, that a 
specific determinant of IC (i.e., satisfactory mobility domain, 
satisfactory psychological domain or composite IC) was better 
adapted than the others. Indeed, even if the magnitude of 
the association seemed greater for the mobility domain (i.e., 
risk reduction of 55% compared to a risk reduced by 44% 
for the psychosocial domain and 49% for the IC composite 
score), confidence intervals overlapped. The three elements 
therefore appear to be of roughly equal importance in our 
study. Previous studies interested in each domain separately 
(mobility, psychosocial) have  also shown the importance of 
these domains in predicting the all-cause mortality in older 
adults (26, 27).
An important aspect that our analysis highlights is the need 
to take a dynamic view of the notion of IC. Indeed, we have 
found that a short-term decline (i.e., over 1 or 2 years) in 
the IC mobility and psychosocial domains was associated 
with an increased risk of death. The finding is all the more 
startling when we focus on the magnitude of the association: 
HR ranging from 2.74 to 4.18, which reinforces the idea of a 
strong association. Note also that we confirmed our hypothesis 
that an initial decrease in IC from baseline to the first year of 
follow up and from baseline to the second year of follow-up 
was proportionally associated to a higher risk of mortality, 
when considering the mobility domain (over 1 year, HR = 2.74 
and over 2 years, HR = 3.61). 
The IC model definitely seems promising, and health actors 
are called upon to refocus their geriatric practice on function 
and to move away from a strict disease-oriented approach, 
which would represent a paradigm-shift in the way older 
patients are thought of. 
Our study is original, in that only one study has previously 
evaluated the predictive capacity of the recently introduced 
concept of IC on mortality. It also brings a new vision to bear 
on the subject, namely that a dynamic approach to the concept 
of IC is essential, this being key to assessing mortality risk. 
However, our analysis has some weaknesses. Our population 
consists mainly of older people who are still in good health, 
and is thus not representative of older people on the whole. 
In the same vein, a selection bias and selective survival could 
potentially be present: participants in better health are the 
ones who, presumably, come back for the in-person yearly 
interviews during the five years of follow-up. This is confirmed 
by the following observation in our results: We have observed, 
in our population, a higher prevalence of older adults who 
improved their IC, in any domain, compared to those with 
declining IC. These findings are probably linked to a potential 
selection bias. Indeed, those who were not seen again one 
year after baseline (n=115) were significantly older than those 
who participated in the follow-up interview (respectively, 72 
years old versus 75 years old, p-value = 0.001), presented 
more often with a limited cognition domain (27% versus 12%, 
p-value <0.001), a limited nutrition domain (24% versus 11%, 
p-value <0.001), a limited mobility domain (43% versus 22%) 
and a limited psychosocial domain (43% versus 28%, p-value 
= 0.004). Therefore, a limited IC at baseline was more often 
encountered in individuals who were ultimately lost-to-follow 
up. Consequently, our analysis was carried out on a greater 
number of individuals in better health than those less healthy.
Another potential bias is linked to the choice of measurement 
instruments: although several are suggested by the WHO, the 
choice for one or another evaluation method may impact the 
final results. Finally, we were unfortunately not able to assess 
the entire concept of IC, an important area that we lack: the 
sensory area. Evaluating the link between this domain and 
the risk of death is of great importance and would allow more 
definitive conclusions to be drawn regarding IC.
Using fixed thresholds to define satisfactory or declining 
IC has also some limitations. Indeed, we can assume that the 
transition towards and away from the declining group could 
have been done even with a small change, potentially non 
clinically relevant. The inverse is also true.

In addition, for resource reasons, some areas of IC were not 
investigated in their entirety (e.g., psychological based only on 
depression score only, vitality based only on nutrition…). This 
represents a weakness in having a global understanding of the 
whole IC of older persons and in future comparisons of future 
other works on the topic. However, our results already show the 
importance of the 4 domains of the IC in predicting mortality, 
and, the sensory domain, studied separately (28), also predicted 
deaths. Therefore, by combining them, the predictive power 
of the whole IC will probably be increased. Future works will 
have to take this aspect into account and propose a more holistic 
approach of the concept.
Conclusion 
The concept of IC, newly developed by the WHO, could be 
a valuable tool to integrate into clinical practice, in light of the 
relationship between limitations in IC and risk of mortality. The 
mobility and psychosocial domains have been shown to have a 
major impact on mortality risk in this study.

ABSTRACT
Background: Hip fracture poses a substantial threat to the quality of life in older adults. Evidence regarding the 
association between intrinsic capacity (IC) and hip fracture is limited. This study aimed to investigate the 
relationship between IC and hip fracture risk in older populations.
Methods: This multi-cohort study included five nationally representative aging cohorts: the China Health and 
Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the Mexican Health and 
Aging Study (MHAS), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), and the English Lon -
gitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). Participants aged 60 years and older with baseline IC assessments and at least 
two follow-ups were included. Individuals with baseline hip fracture, missing hip fracture data, missing covariate 
data, or lost to follow-up were excluded. IC was comprehensively evaluated across five domains: cognition, 
locomotion, vitality, sensory function, and psychological function. Hip fractures were identified through self- 
report or physician diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate the associa -
tion between IC and hip fracture, and results were pooled across cohorts using a common-effects meta-analysis.
Results: A total of 37,267 participants were included, with hip fracture prevalence ranging from 1.40% in SHARE 
to 4.64% in CHARLS. Higher IC was significantly associated with lower hip fracture risk in all cohorts: CHARLS 
(HR = 0.75, 95% CI [0.67 – 0.84]), HRS (HR = 0.65, 95% CI [0.53 – 0.78]), MHAS (HR = 0.77, 95% CI 
[0.63 – 0.95]), SHARE (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.72 – 0.95]), and ELSA (HR = 0.74, 95% CI [0.57 – 0.98]). The pooled 
estimate from the common-effects model was HR = 0.76 (95% CI [0.71 – 0.81], I² = 10.7%). In addition, 
Sensitivity analyses further supported the robustness of these findings.
Conclusions: Higher IC is associated with a lower risk of hip fracture among older adults. IC may serve as an early 
predictive indicator of hip fracture, supporting preventive strategies to reduce the economic and societal burden 
of hip fractures and to preserve quality of life in aging populations.
1. Introduction
With the accelerating trend of global population aging, the propor -
tion of older adults is steadily increasing, posing substantial challenges 
to public health systems worldwide. Among the geriatric syndromes that 
threaten healthy aging, hip fracture is considered a catastrophic health 
event. Characterized by high rates of disability and mortality, hip frac -
ture is often referred to as “ the last fracture of life ” [ 1 ]. Although ad -
vances in surgical treatment have led to a decline in mortality over the 
past decades, the one-year mortality rate after hip fracture remains as 
high as 14% – 58% [ 2 ]. Moreover, most survivors experience irreversible 
functional decline, including persistent pain, impaired mobility, and loss 
of independence [ 3 – 5 ]. Driven by population aging, the global number 
of hip fractures is projected to reach 6.26 million by 2050 [ 6 ].
Currently, risk stratification for hip fracture primarily relies on 
established factors such as bone mineral density, age, sex, and history of 
falls [ 7 – 9 ]. However, this approach is often confined to isolated clinical 
phenotypes and fails to capture the complexity of older adults as dy -
namic adaptive systems. As a result, it does not adequately quantify 
physiological reserve or biological resilience. Consequently, individuals

with comparable risk profiles under traditional models (e.g., similar 
bone mineral density) may still exhibit marked heterogeneity in fracture 
risk due to unmeasured factors such as balance, cognitive function, or 
muscle strength. The poor prognosis following hip fracture underscores 
the inherent limitations of current stratification strategies, which tend to 
identify high-risk individuals only at advanced stages of functional 
decline. Therefore, there is an urgent need for predictive tools that can 
detect risk earlier and with greater precision, thereby shifting the win -
dow of prevention forward.
To promote healthy aging, the World Health Organization (WHO) 
introduced the concept of Intrinsic Capacity (IC), which provides a ho -
listic framework for assessing overall health status in older adults [ 10 ]. 
IC is defined as the composite of an individual ’ s physical and mental 
capacities, encompassing five core domains: cognition, locomotion, vi -
tality, sensory, and psychological function [ 11 ]. These domains together 
form a multidimensional foundation for the comprehensive assessment 
of health in later life. A growing body of evidence indicates that IC is a 
powerful predictor of adverse health outcomes, including disability, 
frailty, and mortality [ 12 – 14 ]. Although impairments in specific do -
mains such as locomotion and psychological health have been identified 
as independent risk factors for hip fracture [ 15 , 16 ], direct evidence 
linking IC as a whole — a reflection of multisystem functional integra -
tion — to hip fracture risk remains scarce. Furthermore, most existing 
studies are restricted to single regions or countries, limiting their 
generalizability across populations.
Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the association between IC 
and hip fracture risk in older adults aged 60 years and above, drawing on 
five large, multinational aging cohorts (CHARLS, HRS, SHARE, MHAS, 
and ELSA).
2. Methods
2.1. Study design and population
Data were obtained from five longitudinal aging cohorts: the China 
Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) [ 17 ], the Health 
and Retirement Study (HRS) [ 17 , 18 ], the Mexican Health and Aging 
Study (MHAS) [ 19 ], the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in 
Europe (SHARE) [ 20 ], and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing 
(ELSA) [ 21 ]. The present study used data from selected waves of these 
cohorts: CHARLS waves 1 – 5 (2011 – 2020), HRS waves 11 – 15 
(2012 – 2020), MHAS waves 5 – 6 (2018 – 2021), SHARE waves 6 – 8 
(2015 – 2020), and ELSA waves 6 – 9 (2012 – 2019).
Participants younger than 60 years or with missing data on intrinsic 
capacity, hip fracture, or covariates were excluded. Ultimately, 3,857 
participants from CHARLS, 3,433 from HRS, 6,359 from MHAS, 19,488 
from SHARE, and 4,130 from ELSA were included in the analyses 
( Fig. 1 ). This study followed the STROBE guidelines.
These five cohorts were chosen as they are large-scale, nationally 
representative longitudinal studies with similar study designs and 
follow-up waves (repeated measures) and harmonized functional health 
measures corresponding to intrinsic capacity. Taken together, the

North America and Europe to increase the generalizability of the find -

2.2. Assessment of intrinsic capacity
Intrinsic capacity (IC) was assessed using the Integrated Care for 
Older People (ICOPE) framework developed by the World Health Or -
ganization (WHO), which provides standardized screening tools and 
assessment guidance for key functional domains. In accordance with the 
WHO definition and previous studies [ 22 – 24 ], IC was evaluated across 
five domains: cognitive function, locomotion, vitality, sensory function 
(hearing and vision), and psychological status. Each domain was 
dichotomously scored (0 = impaired, 1 = preserved). Sensory function 
comprised two components (hearing and vision), each contributing one 
point. Consequently, the total IC score ranged from 0 to 6, with higher 
scores indicating better intrinsic capacity.
2.3. Cognitive function
Cognitive function was evaluated through assessments of memory 
and mental status. Memory was measured using immediate and delayed 
recall of 10 unrelated words, yielding a maximum score of 20 when all 
words were correctly recalled. Mental status was assessed through 
multiple components, including time orientation (assessment of day, 
month, year, day of the week, and season, depending on the cohort), 
calculation ability (serial subtraction of 7 from 100 for five consecutive 
trials), and visuospatial construction (copying a figure of two inter -
secting five-pointed stars, available in CHARLS). Cognitive impairment 
was identified based on established criteria within each cohort.
2.4. Locomotion
Locomotion was assessed using either performance-based tests or 
self-reported functional difficulty, depending on the cohort. In CHARLS 
and ELSA, mobility was evaluated using the five-time chair stand test. A 
completion time of ≤ 14 seconds was scored as 1 point, indicating pre -
served locomotor capacity, whereas a time > 14 seconds was scored as 
0 points, indicating mobility limitation. In MHAS, HRS, and SHARE, 
locomotion was assessed using two self-reported questions regarding 
difficulty or need for assistance in getting in or out of bed and walking 
across a room. Participants who reported no difficulty in both activities 
were assigned 1 point; any reported difficulty resulted in a score of 0.
2.5. Vitality
Vitality was represented by body mass index (BMI). A BMI threshold 
of 18.5 kg/m
2 
was used to indicate nutritional adequacy. Participants 
with a BMI > 18.5 kg/m
2 
were assigned 1 point, reflecting preserved 
vitality, whereas those with a BMI ≤ 18.5 kg/m
2 
were assigned 0 points, 
indicating reduced vitality.
2.6. Sensory function
Hearing function was assessed using self-reported hearing status. 
Participants who rated their hearing as “ fair, ” “ good, ” “ very good, ” or 
“ excellent ” (with hearing aids if normally used) were assigned 1 point; 
those reporting “ poor ” hearing were assigned 0 points.
Vision was evaluated using self-reported eyesight. In CHARLS, HRS, 
SHARE, and ELSA, participants rated their ability to see both near and 
distant objects (with corrective lenses if applicable). A score of 1 point 
was assigned if both near and distance vision were rated as “ fair ” or 
better; if either was rated as “ poor, ” the score was 0. In MHAS, vision 
was assessed using a single self-reported question, with responses of 
“ fair ” or better scored as 1 point and “ poor ” scored as 0.
2.7. Psychological status
Psychological status was assessed using validated depression scales. 
Depressive symptoms were measured using the Center for Epidemiologic 
Studies Depression scale (CES-D) in CHARLS (CESD-10), HRS (CESD-8), 
MHAS (CESD-9), and ELSA (CESD-8), and the Euro-Depression scale 
(Euro-D) in SHARE. Total scores ranged from 0 to 30, 0 to 8, 0 to 9, 0 to 
8, and 0 to 12, respectively. Depressive symptoms were identified using 
established cutoff values: ≥ 12 for CHARLS, ≥ 3 for HRS, ≥ 5 for MHAS, 
≥ 4 for SHARE, and ≥ 3 for ELSA [ 25 ]. Items on both the CES-D and 
Euro-D scales were dichotomously coded, with affirmative responses 
indicating the presence of depressive symptoms. Detailed descriptions of 
IC measurements across the five cohort studies are provided in Supple -
mentary Material S1.
2.8. Assessment of hip fracture
In four cohorts (CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, and ELSA), the occurrence of 
hip fractures was ascertained through standardized self-report questions 
administered at each follow-up interview. Specifically, participants 
were asked either: “ Since the last interview, have you experienced a hip 
fracture? ” or “ Since the last interview, has a physician diagnosed you 
with a hip fracture? ” A response of “ yes ” to either question was classified 
as an incident hip fracture event [ 26 ], whereas in SHARE, hip fractures 
were physician-diagnosed. Once a participant reported such an event, 
their follow-up was censored at that time point, as the primary outcome 
of interest had occurred. Participants who responded “ no ” were 
considered free of the outcome and continued to contribute person-time 
at risk until one of the following events: (1) a subsequent interview in 
which a hip fracture was reported, (2) death, (3) loss to follow-up, or (4) 
completion of the prespecified study period without a hip fracture. This 
approach ensured complete capture of incident cases within the obser -
vation window and minimized misclassification by consistently 
applying the same outcome definition across cohorts.
2.9. Covariates
To account for potential confounding factors, a total of 12 covariates 
were included in the analysis. These comprised both sociodemographic 
and health-related characteristics. Sociodemographic variables included 
age, sex (male or female), educational attainment (categorized accord -
ing to the highest level of formal education completed), and marital 
status (classified as married or unmarried). Lifestyle behavior was rep -
resented by smoking status (yes and no). In addition, a range of clinically 
relevant comorbid conditions known to influence fracture risk were 
incorporated. These included the presence of hypertension, diabetes 
mellitus, cancer, chronic lung disease (e.g., chronic obstructive pulmo -
nary disease, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis), heart disease 
(including ischemic heart disease and heart failure), stroke, and osteo -
arthritis. All comorbidities were assessed based on self-reported physi -
cian diagnosis during the baseline or follow-up assessments. The 
inclusion of these variables allowed for more robust adjustment of the 
multivariable models, thereby reducing residual confounding and 
strengthening the validity of the observed associations.
2.10. Statistical analysis
Baseline characteristics for each cohort (CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, 
SHARE, and ELSA) were summarized, with continuous variables re -
ported as means and compared using t-tests, and categorical variables 
presented as counts and percentages, compared using χ ² tests, consid -
ering a two-sided P < 0.05 as statistically significant. Univariable

analyses initially explored potential confounders of incident hip frac -
ture, followed by multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression 
models to assess the association between intrinsic capacity (IC) and hip 
fracture, reporting hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals 
(CIs). The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld 
residuals with global and univariate tests, where P > 0.05 indicated no 
violation. Three models were constructed: Model I (unadjusted), Model 
II (adjusted for age and sex), and Model III (further adjusted for age, sex, 
education, marital status, smoking status, hypertension, diabetes, can -
cer, chronic lung disease, heart disease, stroke, and arthritis). Results 
from Model III were pooled across cohorts using a common-effects meta- 
analysis.
Four sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of 
the main findings after adjustment for all covariates. First, age was 
modeled as a continuous variable rather than a categorical variable. 
Second, participants with a history of cancer, stroke, or chronic lung 
disease were excluded to minimize potential confounding by severe 
comorbidities. Third, locomotion was redefined using gait speed, with 
impairment defined as the lowest quintile (20%) of gait speed, instead of 
the original locomotion indicators. Due to the unavailability of gait 
speed data in MHAS and SHARE, this analysis was restricted to CHARLS, 
HRS, and ELSA. Fourth, vitality was redefined using grip strength, with 
preserved vitality defined as values in the highest quartile, rather than 
using body mass index. Because grip strength data were unavailable in 
MHAS, this analysis was restricted to CHARLS, HRS, SHARE, and ELSA.
In addition, subgroup analyses were performed to examine potential 
effect modification by age ( < 80 vs. ≥ 80 years), sex (male vs. female), 
educational attainment (below high school vs. high school or higher), 
marital status (unmarried vs. married), and the presence of chronic 
conditions. All analyses were performed using R software (version 
4.4.3). Furthermore, we conducted a meta-analysis to synthesize the 
associations between intrinsic capacity (IC) and the risk of hip fractures 
across five independent national cohort studies. By pooling the effect 
estimates from these cohorts, we aimed to increase the statistical power 
and obtain a more precise and generalizable assessment of the rela -
tionship between IC and hip fracture risk, thereby minimizing the po -
tential influence of random variation within individual studies.
3. Results
3.1. Baseline characteristics of study cohorts
Baseline characteristics of participants from five longitudinal aging 
cohorts (CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, SHARE, and ELSA) are presented in 
Table 1 . The mean age of participants was approximately 70 years in 
MHAS, SHARE, and ELSA, while CHARLS participants had a mean age of 
67 years, and HRS participants were older, with a mean age of 75 years. 
The proportion of male participants varied across cohorts, ranging from 
41.57% in HRS to 54.76% in CHARLS. Mean intrinsic capacity (IC) 
scores were above 4 points in all cohorts: 4.56 in CHARLS, 5.44 in HRS, 
5.31 in MHAS, 5.48 in SHARE, and 4.92 in ELSA. The prevalence of hip 
fracture was comparable in MHAS (1.62%), SHARE (1.40%), and ELSA 
(1.82%), but higher in HRS (3.73%) and CHARLS (4.64%).
Additionally, baseline characteristics were compared between IC 
level groups (decreasing vs. normal), with the normal group defined as 
having an IC score of 6 and the decreasing group as having an IC score 
less than 6. Across CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, and SHARE, participants in the 
decreasing IC group were significantly older, more likely to be female, 
had a higher prevalence of below-high-school education, were less likely 
to be married, and exhibited a higher prevalence of stroke and arthritis 
compared to the normal IC group. In contrast, in the ELSA cohort, the 
decreasing IC group was significantly younger than the normal group, 
with no significant differences in chronic disease prevalence between 
the two groups. Detailed results are presented in Supplementary 
Tables S2 – S6.

3.2. Univariable analyses for hip fractures
Univariable analyses of risk factors for hip fracture across the five 
cohorts (CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, SHARE, and ELSA) are presented in 
Supplementary Table S7. Age and osteoarthritis were consistently sig -
nificant predictors of hip fracture in all cohorts (P < 0.05). Marital status 
was significantly associated with hip fracture in CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, 
and SHARE (P < 0.05) but not in ELSA (P ≥ 0.05). Sex and educational 
attainment were significant predictors in HRS and SHARE (P < 0.05), 
but no significant associations were observed in CHARLS, MHAS, or 
ELSA.
3.3. The association between IC and hip fractures
Table 2 presents the association between intrinsic capacity (IC) and 
hip fracture risk using Cox proportional hazards regression across five 
cohort studies (CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, SHARE, and ELSA). In the unad -
justed model (Model I), higher IC was significantly associated with a 
reduced risk of hip fracture in all cohorts (P < 0.05). After adjustment 
for age, sex, and other covariates in Model II, the association was 
attenuated in MHAS and SHARE. In the fully adjusted model (Model III), 
higher IC remained significantly associated with a lower hip fracture risk 
in all cohorts: CHARLS (HR = 0.75, 95% CI [0.67, 0.84]), HRS (HR =
0.65, 95% CI [0.53, 0.78]), MHAS (HR = 0.77, 95% CI [0.63, 0.95]), 
SHARE (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.72, 0.95]), and ELSA (HR = 0.74, 95% CI 
[0.57, 0.98]), all with P < 0.05. A common-effects meta-analysis pooling 
results across the five cohorts yielded a combined HR of 0.76 (95% CI 
[0.71, 0.81], I² = 10.7%, P = 0.345), indicating low heterogeneity and a 
robust association ( Fig. 2 ).
3.34 Subgroup and Sensitivity Analyses Subgroup analyses were 
conducted to explore potential effect modification. No statistically sig -
nificant interactions were observed. Importantly, the inverse association 
between higher IC and the risk of hip fracture remained robust among 
women, as well as among participants without a history of cancer, lung 
disease, or stroke. In the CHARLS, HRS, and SHARE cohorts, this 
protective association was particularly evident in individuals younger 
than 80 years and in those without arthritis (Supplementary 
Tables S13 – S17).
Sensitivity analyses further supported the robustness of these find -
ings. When age was modeled as a continuous variable in the multivari -
able Cox proportional hazards models, the results were materially 
unchanged across all five cohorts (Supplementary Table S18). Likewise, 
exclusion of participants with baseline cancer, chronic lung disease, or 
stroke did not materially alter the observed associations between IC and 
hip fracture risk (Supplementary Table S19). Additionally, alternative 
definitions of locomotion and vitality were applied to evaluate measure- 
specific effects. When gait speed was used in place of the original 
locomotion indicator, the association between intrinsic capacity and hip 
fracture risk remained consistent in CHARLS (HR = 0.753, 95% CI: 
0.673 � 0.842), HRS (HR = 0.626, 95% CI: 0.525 � 0.745), and ELSA (HR 
= 0.703, 95% CI: 0.565 � 0.875) (Supplementary Table S20). Likewise, 
substituting grip strength for the original vitality proxy yielded com -
parable effect estimates in CHARLS (HR = 0.750, 95% CI: 
0.674 � 0.835), HRS (HR = 0.625, 95% CI: 0.526 � 0.742), SHARE (HR =
0.824, 95% CI: 0.730 � 0.931), and ELSA (HR = 0.660, 95% CI: 
0.520 � 0.838) (Supplementary Table S21). Collectively, these findings 
support the robustness of the primary results.
4. Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the association 
between intrinsic capacity (IC) and the risk of hip fracture among adults 
aged 60 years and older using harmonized data from five large, multi -
national aging cohorts. We found a consistent inverse association: 
higher IC was associated with a lower risk of incident hip fracture across 
cohorts. These findings suggest that IC may serve as a useful integrated 
early indicator of physiological reserve that identifies individuals at 
lower risk of hip fracture. Notably, our observation is consistent with 
previous studies reporting that inverse associations between IC and 
adverse health outcomes such as mortality and falls [ 27 – 30 ].
We observed notable differences in baseline characteristics across 
cohorts. Participants from China were the youngest, with a mean age of 
67 years; however, their mean IC score (4.56) was lower than that of 
participants in Western cohorts, despite prior evidence suggesting that

IC generally declines with advancing age [ 23 ]. Further analysis revealed 
that impairments across the five domains of IC — psychological function, 
hearing, vision, vitality, and cognition — were more prevalent in the 
Chinese cohort than in other national cohort studies. Consistent with our 
findings, previous research has also reported a higher prevalence of 
hearing loss in China compared with other countries [ 31 ]. This disparity 
may partly explain why, despite being younger, individuals in the Chi -
nese cohort exhibited lower IC scores than those from other countries. In 
addition, these differences are likely to reflect a combination of socio -
economic, environmental, healthcare access, and historical factors 
rather than age alone. For example, the higher prevalence of reported 
hearing impairment in CHARLS is consistent with findings from previous 
epidemiological comparisons. Moreover, compared with developed 
countries, Chinese individuals tend to place less emphasis on their 
health conditions [ 32 ] and demonstrate weaker health awareness [ 33 ], 
which may contribute to poorer health status among older adults in 
China and, consequently, lower levels of intrinsic capacity. This seem -
ingly paradoxical finding may, in part, reflect historical differences in 
economic development, healthcare infrastructure, and population 
health literacy between China and developed countries [ 34 ]. Therefore, 
such cohort differences highlight the value of multinational studies and 
underscore the need for context-specific reference values and interven -
tion strategies when implementing IC-based screening in diverse set -
tings. Collectively, these results underscore the importance of early IC 
screening and targeted interventions in China to enhance IC and pro -
mote healthy aging. Recent multidomain intervention studies have 
demonstrated that IC can be preserved or even improved, particularly 
through strategies focusing on physical activity, cognition, and vitality, 
thereby improving health outcomes in older adults [ 35 ].
In our study, we observed that higher intrinsic capacity (IC) was 
associated with a reduced risk of hip fracture, with each one-unit in -
crease in IC score corresponding to a 24% lower risk. These findings 
underscore the importance of maintaining IC in older adults. The 
mechanisms underlying the association between IC and hip fracture risk 
are likely multifaceted. IC may influence hip fracture risk through 
several pathways. First, higher IC is linked to a reduced risk of falls and 
frailty [ 36 ].Specifically, a study consisting of 319 participants reported 
that higher IC significantly lowered the risk of falls, with the 
adjusted-OR being 0.33(95%CI:0.16 � 0.82) [ 37 ], suggesting that IC may 
lower fracture risk by mitigating these key mediators. Second, IC is 
inversely associated with sarcopenia [ 38 ]. A recent study involving of 6, 
554 individuals reported that higher IC was significantly associated with 
a lower risk of sarcopenia (OR = 0.85, 95%CI:0.76 � 0.95) [ 38 ]. As, 
sarcopenia is a well-established risk factor for fractures, higher IC may 
reduce fracture risk by preserving muscle mass and strength. Third, IC 
may promote optimal sleep duration in older adults [ 39 ], which in turn 
enhances mental and physical functioning, thereby reducing fracture 
susceptibility. Collectively, these pathways imply that declines in IC 
elevate hip fracture risk by increasing the propensity for falls, frailty, 
and sarcopenia, as well as compromising overall physiological 
resilience.
Hip fractures in older adults not only carry high morbidity and 
mortality but also impose substantial medical and societal burdens. 
Evidence indicates that interventions targeted IC can maintain or 
enhance IC, especially in domains of locomotion, cognition, and vitality, 
even among older adults with declining self-care capacity [ 40 , 41 ]. A 
systematic review further showed that multi-domain intervention can 
preserve intrinsic capacity- such as grip strength, gait speed and BMI 
[ 42 ]. Therefore, incorporating routine IC assessment and interventions 
into primary care or community-based programs — for example, through 
annual health checkups — may facilitate primary prevention of hip 
fractures and reduce the health and economic burden associated with 
aging populations. Routine, brief intrinsic capacity (IC) assessment in 
primary care or community settings can enable early identification of 
older adults at risk of fractures and guide timely preventive strategies 
targeting locomotion, vitality, and cognition. Our findings show a 
consistent inverse association between IC and hip fracture risk, sup -
porting the integration of IC assessment into geriatric care and primary 
prevention programs. A practical approach is a simple, harmonized 
five-domain IC tool (locomotion, vitality, cognition, psychological ca -
pacity, and sensory function), completed in 5 – 10 min during annual 
wellness visits or comprehensive geriatric assessments. Individuals in 
the lowest IC quartile could be offered multidomain interventions, 
including resistance and balance training, nutritional optimization 
(protein and vitamin D), cognitive stimulation, depression management, 
and hearing or vision correction. In resource-limited settings, even a 
two- or three-domain screening (e.g., gait speed, handgrip strength, 
brief cognitive testing) may serve as a rapid triage tool, shifting care 
from reactive fracture treatment toward proactive preservation of 
functional reserves. Future randomized controlled trials are needed to 
evaluate whether screening strategies, combined with corresponding 
interventions, can more effectively improve intrinsic capacity in older 
adults.
This study has several notable strengths. First, it provides valuable 
insights into the association between intrinsic capacity (IC) and hip 
fracture risk, shedding light on potential mechanisms underlying disease 
progression and long-term outcomes. Second, it is the largest multina -
tional investigation to date of the IC – hip fracture relationship, including 
37,267 participants from nationally representative cohorts from Asia, 
Europe, and North America. Third, all cohorts were drawn from na -
tionally representative samples, further strengthening the external val -
idity of the results. Fourth, sensitivity analyses, including the use of 
alternative definitions of intrinsic capacity and other methodological 
variations, confirmed the robustness of the observed associations. 
Finally, meta-analytic pooling of results across these cohorts allowed us 
to synthesize evidence and mitigate variability between studies, 
providing additional confirmation of the findings.
However, a few limitations to this study are worthy of note. First, hip 
fractures in SHARE were physician-reported but identified by self-report 
in CHARLS, HRS, MHAS, and ELSA; thus, some underascertainment of 
fracture incidence is possible. However, any misclassification is ex -
pected to be non-differential and would therefore likely have attenuated 
the effect estimates. Future studies employing objective assessments, 
such as imaging verification, are warranted. Second, measurement of IC

observational design and the possibility of bidirectional relationships, 
causality between IC and hip fracture cannot be inferred. Longitudinal 
studies using causal inference methods are needed to further validate 
these findings.
In conclusion, higher intrinsic capacity (IC) is associated with a 
reduced risk of hip fracture among older adults, with particularly pro -
nounced protective effects observed in women and in individuals 
without cancer, chronic lung disease, or stroke. Integrating brief IC as -
sessments into routine primary care and community-based interventions 
may offer a feasible strategy to identify at-risk individuals and help 
mitigate the burden of hip fractures in the context of global population 
aging.

Abstract
Background:frailty shows an upward trajectory with age, and higher levels increase the risk of mortality. However, it is less
knownwhethertheshapeoffrailtytrajectoriesdiﬀersbyageatdeathorwhethertherateofchangeinfrailtyisassociatedwith
mortality.
Objectives:toassesspopulationfrailtytrajectoriesbyageatdeathandtoanalysewhetherthecurrentlevelofthefrailtyindex
(FI) i.e. the most recent measurement or the person-speciﬁc rate of change is more predictive of mortality.
Methods: 3,689 individuals from three population-based cohorts with up to 15 repeated measurements of the Rockwood
frailty index were analysed. The FI trajectories were assessed by stratifying the sample into four age-at-death groups:<70,
70–80, 80–90 and>90 years. Generalised survival models were used in the survival analysis.
Results: the FI trajectories by age at death showed that those who died at<70 years had a steadily increasing trajectory
throughoutthe40yearsbeforedeath,whereasthosewhodiedattheoldestagesonlyaccrueddeﬁcitsfromage ∼75onwards.
Higher level of FI was independently associated with increased risk of mortality (hazard ratio 1.68, 95% conﬁdence interval
1.47–1.91),whereastherateofchangewasnolongersigniﬁcantafteraccountingforthecurrentFIlevel.TheeﬀectoftheFI
level did not weaken with time elapsed since the last measurement.
Conclusions: Frailty trajectories diﬀer as a function of age-at-death category. The current level of FI is a stronger marker for
risk stratiﬁcation than the rate of change.
Keywords: frailty,trajectories,mortality,age at death,older people
Key Points
• Frailtyshowsanupwardtrajectorywithage,butitisunknownwhetherpopulationfrailtytrajectoriesdiﬀerbyageatdeath.
• Less is also known whether it is the level or the rate of change that is more predictive of mortality.
• Those who died at<70 years had the highest levels and rates of change in frailty from midlife onwards.
• Those who died at the oldest ages only accrued increase in frailty from age∼75 onwards
• The current level of FI is as a stronger marker for risk stratiﬁcation than the rate of change.

Introduction
Aging is a highly heterogeneous process with substantial
between-individualvariationinhealthandfunctioning.One
way to capture this heterogeneity is to measure the level of
frailty. Frailty is a clinically recognised condition associated
with decreased physiological reserves and functioning across
multiple organ systems [1]. It is a major public health
concernandisassociatedwithavarietyofadverseoutcomes,
suchashospitalisations,disabilityanddeath[ 2].Whilethere
isyetnowidelyacceptedconsensusontheoperationalisation
of frailty, the two principal models are the frailty phenotype
(FP) and the Rockwood frailty index (FI). The FP views
frailty as a physical syndrome and categorises individuals as
robust, pre-frail, and frail based on weak grip strength, slow
walking speed, exhaustion and low energy expenditure [3].
The FI is based on a broader, multidimensional deﬁnition
of frailty; it is a continuous score that measures the accu-
mulationofhealthdeﬁcitsacrossmedical,physiologicaland
(psycho) social domains [4]. Due to these properties, the
FI also allows for feasible assessment of population frailty
trajectories and identiﬁcation of subtle changes therein.
Population estimates from longitudinal studies [ 5],
including ours [6], have unequivocally shown that the FI
showsanupwardtrajectorywithage.Afewstudieshavealso
looked at frailty trajectories in relation to death across old
age [7–9] and at the end of life [10], and found that higher
or rapidly increasing frailty trajectories were associated with
worsesurvival.Itisthuspertinenttoassesspopulationfrailty
trajectories considering not only time to death, but also
age at death, to assess whether those who die at younger
ages have diﬀerent frailty trajectories from those who die
at older ages. Ascertaining such diﬀerences will aid in
understanding individual diﬀerences in frailty trajectories
and their relationship to mortality. Another understudied
question in the relationship between frailty trajectories and
mortality is whether the person-speciﬁc rate of change is
associated with mortality, and if so, whether it captures the
risk better than the current (most recent) level of frailty.
Towards these goals, we ﬁrst wanted to examine whether
people of diﬀerent age at death have distinct FI trajectories
before death across adulthood and into old age by analysing
FItrajectoriesinfourage-at-deathgroups( <70,70–80,80–
90 and>90 years). We next assessed whether the level and
rate of change in FI diﬀer across the age-at-death groups,
andlastlyanalysedwhetheritisthecurrentlevelofFIorthe
person-speciﬁc rate of change in FI that is more predictive
of all-cause mortality.

facilities. The strengths of this study also include complete
coverage of mortality, frequent repeated measurements of
frailty and the ability to track frailty trajectories for up to
40 years before death.
Insummary,thisstudyﬁndsthatfrailtytrajectoriesdiﬀer
as a function of age-at-death category, the most prominent
feature being that there is a delay in the accrual of deﬁcits
among those who die at very old age. As frailty assessment
is becoming more widely used in clinical decision-making
processes, our results suggest that regular frailty assessments
are useful in informing decisions, with the most recent
assessment being more informative than the past change.
Higherleveloffrailtyinamiddle-agedoryounger-oldadult
givescauseforaclosermonitoringandcareneedassessments,
whereas higher frailty in older age is relatively less alarming.

Abstract
Background: intrinsic capacity (IC) is a construct encompassing people’s physical and mental abilities. There is an implicit
link amongst IC domains: cognition, locomotion, nutrition, sensory and psychological. However, little is known about the
integration of the domains.
Objectives:to investigate patterns in the presentation and evolution of IC domain impairments in low-and-middle-income
countries and if such patterns were associated with adverse outcomes.
Methods:secondary analyses of the ﬁrst two waves of the 10/66 study (population-based surveys conducted in eight urban
andfourruralcatchmentareasinCuba,DominicanRepublic,PuertoRico,Venezuela,Peru,MexicoandChina).Weapplied
latenttransitionanalysisonICtoﬁndlatentstatuses(latent clusters)ofICdomainimpairments.Weevaluatedthelongitudinal
associationofthelatentstatuseswiththeriskoffrailty,disabilityandmortality,andtestedconcurrentandpredictivevalidity.
Results: amongst 14,923 participants included, the four latent statuses were: high IC (43%), low deterioration with
impaired locomotion (17%), high deterioration without cognitive impairment (22%), and high deterioration with cognitive
impairment(18%).Atotalof61%oftheparticipantsworsenedovertime,35%werestable,and3%improvedtoahealthier
status.
Participants with deteriorated IC had a signiﬁcantly higher risk of frailty, disability and dementia than people with high IC.
There was strong concurrent and predictive validity. (Mortality Hazard Ratio=4.60, 95%CI 4.16; 5.09; Harrel’s C=0.73
(95%CI 0.72;0.74)).
Conclusions: half of the study population had high IC at baseline, and most participants followed a worsening trend. Four
qualitatively diﬀerent IC statuses or statuses were characterised by low and high levels of deterioration associated with their
risk of disability and frailty. Locomotion and cognition impairments showed other trends than psychological and nutrition
domains across the latent statuses.

Key Points
• Literature on the relationship between the intrinsic capacity domains is scarce.
• Our study identiﬁed and validated four latent statuses or clusters of intrinsic capacity impairments.
• Both the deterioration level and the type of domain aﬀected (notably cognition and locomotion) are linked to clinical
outcomes.
• About 3% of the study population transitioned to a higher intrinsic capacity status.
Background
Intrinsiccapacity(IC)istheaggregateofphysicalandmental
capacitiespeoplecandrawuponastheyage[
1].Understand-
ing IC is crucial for healthy longevity because it informs
about the preservation of central physiological systems that
operate to allow older adults to be functional. The concept
andmeasurementofICareunderconstructionasthereisno
consensus on a deﬁnitive IC operationalisation.
Studies have found that IC encompasses the locomo-
tive,cognitive,psychological,nutritionalandsensory(vision
and hearing) domains [2–4]. The authors used a reﬂective
structural IC model, which implies that one could remove
one of the domains and still be able to measure IC and
that the correlations amongst the domains should be high
[
5]. However, those implications have not been suﬃciently
discussed in the ageing ﬁeld.
The construct of IC is relevant from the research and
the healthcare points of view. Assessing IC in care settings
is helpful as an indicator of the core physiological elements
that allow older adults to be and do what is meaningful for
them [
6, 7]. Monitoring IC in individuals and populations
enables the detection of early functional declines for timely
interventions [3, 8, 9], as has been demonstrated in the
INSPIRE-Icope care cohort in the south of France [10].
If IC permeates the health systems, it might help to
switch the disease-centred paradigm into a person-centred
one.Re-organisinghealthservicesusingtheICdomainsand
its clinical pathways might improve the healthcare provi-
sion for older people [
6]. For instance, the World Health
Organisation’sIntegratedCareforOlderPeople(ICOPE)is
astrategytofosterjoined-upcareforolderadults[ 11].Pub-
lications from China, [12] France, [7] Hong Kong [13]a n d
Taiwan [14] have used ICOPE to assess IC in older adults.
However, evidence from low-and-middle-income countries
(LMIC) is still limited.
OlderadultsarelikelytobeimpairedinmorethanoneIC
domain [7, 15]. For instance, the percentage of older adults
with at least one IC domain impairment ranged between
43% and 94%, with a mean of 74% in eight previous
publications from around the world [7, 12, 13, 15–19].
It would be helpful to know the presentation pattern
of those impairments. Multidomain interventions could be
designed and planned to target the most common pat-
terns. So far, studies have reported clusters of IC domain
impairmentsonlycross-sectionallyandcircumscribedtoone
country[
21,22].Examinationofdatafromtheglobalnorth
and the global south could expand our knowledge of the
natural history of IC impairments in older adults.
Therefore, this study aims to investigate patterns in the
presentation and evolution of IC domain impairments in
LMIC using data from the 10/66 dementia research group
(10/66DementiaResearchGroup(DRG))studyandifsuch
patternsareassociatedwithadverseoutcomesandasserttheir
concurrent and predictive validity.
Methods
Participants
The 10/66 DRG population-based studies of ageing and
dementia included people aged 65 years and over living
in selected geographic areas of Peru (urban Lima and
rural Canete), Mexico (urban Mexico City and rural
Morelos state), China (urban Xicheng and rural Daxing)
and India (urban Chennai and rural Vellore), and urban
sites in Cuba (Havana/Matanzas), Dominican Republic
(Santo Domingo), Puerto Rico (Bayamon) and Venezuela
(Caracas).
Baselinesurveyswerecarriedoutbetween2003and2007,
andthefollow-upbetween2008and2010inmostcentres.A
detaileddescriptionofthe10/66cohortshasbeenpublished
elsewhere [23, 25]. We did not include India data because
follow-up was unavailable. The sample of the rest of the
countries was included in the ﬁnal analyses.
The baseline cohort was deﬁned by systematically door-
knocking all households in each selected geography (catch-
ment area). Eligibility criteria: residents aged 65 and over
living in the catchment area. No direct exclusion criteria
were applied, but the design excluded high-income urban
districts.
Data was gathered via household interviews, including
medical history, healthcare utilisation and lifestyle-related
factors; a cognitive assessment; a physical examination;
and an informant interview. The King’s College London
and the local research ethics committee approved the
study.
Informed consent was collected on paper, and literate
participants signed their approval. The information sheet
was read to illiterate participants by a literate, independent
witness who provided attestation. For participants without
thecapacitytoconsent,agreementfortheirparticipationwas
obtained from next of kin. The ethics committees approved
these procedures.
