2012 developed a PROMPT model for the prediction of 
6-month mortality in community-dwelling older adults. 
At 10%-70% cutpoints, PROMPT achieved a sensitivity 
of 0.80%-83.4%. The models’ discriminatory power was 
further supported by the fact that over half of patients 
with estimated 6-month mortality > 30% died within a 
12-month follow-up period [34]. Maurer et al., 2023 per-
formed an external validation of a Predictive OpTimal 
Trees in Emergency Surgery Risk (POTTER) model, pre -
dicting 30-day mortality. POTTER is available as a mobile 
telephone app and outperforms all traditional risk pre -
diction approaches. The model achieved a c-statistic of 
0.80, with its worst performance in the ≥ 80 years cohort 
(c-statistic = 0.71) and its best in the 65–74 years cohort 
(c-statistic = 0.84). The group concluded that POTTER 
could be useful in emergency surgery departments [37]. 
Suzuki et al., 2020 developed a multiple logistic regres -
sion model to predict 180-day all-cause mortality. The 
model showed good discriminatory power with a c-statis-
tic of 0.820. The group remarked on the models’ potential 
application in deciding the direction of therapy, palliative 
care or hospital referrals [18]. Thongprayoon et al., 2023 
utilised a clustering approach (unsupervised consensus 
clustering) to allocate patients and their post-transplant 
outcomes, such as mortality, graft failure and acute all -
graft rejection. Graphical mean cluster consensus scores 
suggest good model performance [47]. Venturini et al., 
2021 developed five tree models designed for the pre -
diction of various clinical outcomes, including mortal -
ity, intensive care unit admission and intensive care unit 
discharge. The accuracy scores recorded were as follows; 
conditional RF (0.70), RF (0.79), ordinal forest (0.77), par-
titional tree (0.65), and conditional inference tree (0.79). 
While these results show good discriminatory power, 
external validation is needed before implementation into 
clinical care [19].
Studies predicting hospitalisation, admission, and transfer 
outcomes
Belmin et al., 2022 utilised a previously developed 
machine learning algorithm to predict emergency 
department admissions using questionnaire data col -
lected during home visits, achieving a sensitivity of 83%. 
The system was successfully implemented, and the group 
concluded that it could have a use in lowering the num -
ber of emergency department visits within the study 
cohort [11]. Bories et al., 2022 built three machine learn -
ing models to predict hospitalisation for bleeding effects. 
The RF, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machine achieved 
predictive accuracy of 0.64, 0.68 and 0.64, respectively, in 
a sample of 7,462 participants [23]. Considine et al., 2019 
utilised multivariable logistic regression to predict emer -
gency interhospital transfer from subacute to acute care 
in a cohort of 1717 participants. The model achieved a 
median AUC of 0.77. The group concluded that while the 
results from the model are encouraging, further devel -
opment and testing is necessary before implementing 
for external validation [26]. Friz et al., 2022 developed 
four machine learning models with good discriminatory 
power to predict 30-day readmission; adaptive boosting 
(AUC = 0.803), gradient boosting (AUC-ROC = 0.782), 
XGBoost (AUC-ROC = 0.776), RF (AUC-ROC = 0.786). 
All four models outperformed the traditionally used 
LACE index, which achieved an AUC of 0.504; how -
ever, they require external validation before introducing 
into a clinical setting [32]. Ren et al., 2022 developed an 
RF model for predicting various hospital complications 
within 30  days of admission and investigating feature 
importance from three traditionally used risk scores [43]. 
Sax et al., 2021 developed five machine learning models 
to predict serious adverse events within 30 days of emer -
gency department admission. Logistic regression, Least 
Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), 
decision tree, RF, and XGBoost models achieved c-statis -
tic of 0.80, 0.80, 0.65, 0.83, 0.85, respectively. The group 
concluded that using machine learning is an improve -
ment on using traditional approaches [45]. Zarkowsky 
et al., 2021 developed a multivariable statistical model 
and a multilayer perceptron to predict the appropriate -
ness of short-stay discharge and survival at 30 days. Boot-
strap model validation with 1000 repetitions generated 
an AUC-ROC of 0.71. The study found that selecting 
patients for short-stay discharge is possible without risk 
to the patient [51].
Studies predicting cardiovascular outcomes
Chung et al., 2020 developed two ANN models to predict 
i) favourable/poor clinical outcome ii) modified Rankin 
Scale at 3 months in a sample of participants with acute 
ischemic stroke. Both models performed well, predict -
ing clinical outcomes with an AUC-ROC of 0.974 and 
predicting modified Rankin Scale at 3  months with a 
low error, MSE = 0.24. In conclusion, the group showed 
the usefulness of these two ANN models and remarked 
that they could benefit clinicians, assisting with thera -
peutic decision-making. It should be noted that this 
analysis included only 31 participants [25]. Falsetti et 
al., 2021 developed an XGBoost model for the predic -
tion of 3 clinical outcomes, all three models showing 
good discriminatory power: stroke/transient ischaemic 
attack (AUC-ROC = 0.931), therapeutic failure (AUC-
ROC = 0.974), and major bleeding (AUC-ROC = 0.930).

tively. The results achieved with the GA-KPLS and SVM 
models are particularly high compared to others, which 
could be explained by a small participant count of just 
149. The authors concluded that while the performance 
of the models was encouraging, external validation in 
another dataset/in a live clinical setting is required [52].
Studies predicting other clinical outcomes
Bowen et al., 2021 used a multilevel mixed model to 
predict pain perception in the last 7  days. The model 
included 58 continuous features and showed that poor 
sleep is highly associated with pain perception in the last 
7  days. It should be noted that a sample size of just 15 
community-dwelling older adults was used in this study, 
which is a significant limiting factor when considering 
how generalisable the results are in the larger geriatric 
care setting [12]. Chen et al., 2020 predicted survival in 
patients with early-stage uterine papillary serous car -
cinoma using a proportional subdistribution hazards 
regression predictive model. The model showed great 
risk stratification ability as the participants placed in the 
high-risk-of-death group had higher incidence of death 
(p < 0.001). The group concluded that the model showed 
promising results [24]. Ford et al., 2021 developed three 
models (logistic regression, naïve Bayes, RF) to detect 
dementia in patients where the symptoms were identified 
in primary care, but a formal diagnosis was not made. All 
three models achieved similar AUC-ROC results in the 
range of 0.87–0.90 with coded variables and 0.90–0.94 
when keywords were added. The study showed the ben -
efit of using machine learning for the retrospective diag -
nosis of dementia, assuring that records are up to date 
and that good quality of care is provided to patients [30]. 
Ko et al., 2014 aimed to develop two machine learning 
models, decision trees and linear discriminant analy -
sis, to classify colonoscopy indications from EHR data. 
The overall accuracy for classifying colonoscopy indi -
cation was 71%, 73%, and 68% for decision trees, linear 
discriminant analysis model 1 and linear discriminant 
analysis model 2, respectively. The study concluded 
that while these results are promising, external valida -
tion is necessary before deploying in clinical care [35]. 
Li Kuan Ong et al., 2023 developed three multivariate 
analysis models to predict the risk of late genitourinary 
toxicity in older adults with prostate cancer receiving 
radiotherapy. Models 1, 1a and 2 achieved AUC of 0.63, 
0.64, and 0.81, respectively [36]. Ocagli et al., 2021 devel-
oped an RF model to predict 4AT delirium scores. The 
RF model predicted 4AT scores with an RMSE of 3.29. 
The study showed that RF is a valid method for predict -
ing 4AT scores and assessing the factors associated with 
delirium [39]. Pompei et al., 1994 aimed to develop and 
validate a logistic regression model for predicting the 
risk of delirium by classifying participants into one of 
three ascending risk groups. The model achieved good 
discriminatory power with AUC-ROC of 0.74 [42]. Rossi 
et al., 2021 defined a multivariable Cox analysis predic -
tive model to stratify patients into three groups based 
on the risk of developing myeloid neoplasms. The model 
achieved c-index scores of 0.851 and 0.889 in the internal 
and external validation cohorts. These results, coupled 
with a reasonable sample size of 1,794 patients, suggest 
a good generalisability of the results [13]. Shardell et al., 
2021 predicted sex-specific serum 25-hydroxyvitamin 
D thresholds that best discriminated incident slow gait 
using weighted decision trees [46]. Venerito et al., 2022 
developed three machine learning approaches to predict 
a 3-month giant cell arthritis flare-up. RF outperformed 
logistic regression and decision trees, with accuracy 
scores of 71.4%, 70.4%, and 62.9%, respectively. AUC-
ROC RF outperformed logistic regression and decision 
trees 0.76, 0.73, and 0.65, respectively. The authors con -
cluded that their approach is highly reproducible and 
capable of being a benefit to a clinician caring for an 
older adult [49].
Discussion
Our review identified 37 studies which utilised a 
machine learning approach to predict a clinical out -
come in adults aged ≥ 65  years. The two-grouped 
meta-analysis consisted of a total of eight studies using 
different machine learning models to predict mortal -
ity within 6  months in the first group and mortality 
within a period over 6  months for the second group. 
Supported by an AUC-ROC summary estimate of 0.80 
(95% CI: 0.76 – 0.84) for mortality within 6 months and 
0.81 (95% CI: 0.76 – 0.86) for mortality over 6 months,

we found that machine learning models display good 
discriminatory power in predicting mortality. While 
the future of utilising machine learning in geriatric 
care looks favourable, caution must be applied before 
proclaiming it the new gold standard. This systematic 
literature review and meta-analysis identified some 
key issues facing machine learning applications in ger -
iatric settings.
First, many studies have very low numbers of partici -
pants, some as low as under 100 participants. Machine 
learning models benefit greatly from large datasets 
numbering thousands of observations, with a low per -
centage of missing data. Second, many studies are uti -
lising datasets of participants with varying levels of 
heterogeneity. Studies which use highly heterogene -
ous populations cannot be generalised to the general 
population of older adults. Third, most studies do not 
validate their findings externally. External validation 
studies incorporating a large number of participants 
are necessary before machine learning can be applied 
in the wider geriatric care setting. Fourth, ideally, 
machine learning models could be applied to any Elec -
tronic Healthcare Record (EHR)/clinical database and 
make live predictions as new data is introduced. How -
ever, this will prove challenging since many EHR differ 
fundamentally in data structures. Therefore, EHRs and 
clinical databases must be standardised to utilise these 
approaches fully. Fifth, some machine learning algo -
rithms require much larger amounts of high-quality 
data to make accurate predictions than traditional sta -
tistical approaches. Sixth, most machine learning algo -
rithms need to be optimised, and the optimal model 
tuning would be user dependent, which may introduce 
additional challenges in assessing each model’s perfor -
mance and risk of bias. Finally, we found significant 
inconsistencies in reporting machine learning study 
findings. Many studies report limited information on 
model development and performance metrics with 
no insights into 95% CI. We recommend that journals 
specialising in this niche take special care in encour -
aging authors to be detailed in reporting their model 
development approach and encourage them to supply 
a full view of model performance metrics.
In 2020, a systematic literature review was carried 
out by Choudhury et al. 2020, in which the authors 
identified 35 eligible studies concerning machine 
learning in geriatric care for chronic diseases. Similar 
to the findings in this review, the group concluded that 
while the applications of machine learning in geriatric 
settings look promising, more validation studies are 
needed, and machine learning needs to be standard -
ised and tailored to geriatric settings carefully [14].
Limitations and strengths
Our approach has several limitations. First, the search 
was limited to English, meaning relevant literature in 
other languages was not considered. Second, the review 
could have missed some studies due to unusual termi -
nology. To mitigate this, significant time was spent iden -
tifying all synonyms of keywords and working with an 
experienced subject librarian when designing the search 
strategy. Third, due to limited literature in the field, only 
eight studies were included in the meta-analysis. Fourth, 
there is much heterogeneity between the patients from 
the studies included in the meta-analysis, and several 
patients had co-morbidities such as heart failure. Addi -
tionally, we could not calculate an  I2 due to the studies 
failing to report the standard error. Fifth, we could only 
pool studies by one outcome (mortality) as there were 
inconsistent definitions and sparse data to pool stud -
ies for other clinical outcomes. Further to this point, 
further grouping of patients into cohorts with simi -
lar comorbidities is necessary but was not carried out 
as part of this meta-analysis, given the limited number 
of papers. Grouping patients into such cohorts would 
greatly improve the generalisability of our results. Sixth, 
inconsistent reporting of the model development process 
and inconsistent reporting of model performance meant 
that some studies appropriate for meta-analysis were not 
included. For instance, not all performance metrics can 
be converted to AUC-ROC, especially without specific 
data on the number of subjects in the derivation/valida -
tion cohorts. Finally, the predictions were performed on 
retrospective data, mostly from electronic health records; 
validating these models on prospectively collected data 
from other sources is critical for reproducibility. Our 
study’s strengths include following PRISMA guidelines, 
having our protocol approved and registered by PROS -
PERO, using Covidence software (increased rigour, accu -
rate documentation), using a highly appropriate quality 
of study tool (PROBAST) and utilising multiple literature 
databases.
Conclusion
Given the vast amounts of clinical data collected from 
patients, there is considerable potential in utilising 
machine learning in predicting clinical outcomes in 
older adults. This review showed that machine learning 
models exhibit high discriminatory power, often out -
performing traditional statistical approaches. It should 
also be considered that as datasets become larger and 
machine learning models become more sophisticated, 
their performance will increase further. As this field 
of research develops, we believe it is crucial that spe -
cific attention is dedicated to a comprehensive model

performance analysis for each model. More large-scale 
validation studies are needed to show that machine 
learning can predict clinical outcomes in older adults 
underrepresented in our findings, such as predict -
ing risk factors for dementia, identifying risk factors 
for multimorbidity, and screening subgroups of older 
adults vulnerable to falls and fractures.

Abstract
Objective To investigate the predictive value of Machine Learning (ML) for the occurrence of frailty in Chinese elderly 
and to identify significant factors associated with frailty.
Methods This study utilized data from the 2020 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), focusing 
on 7880 elderly individuals. Six machine learning (ML) algorithms were employed: Logistic Regression (LR), K-Nearest 
Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT), LightGBM, and Random Forest (RF). The 
performance of these models was assessed using several metrics including the Area Under the Receiver Operating 
Characteristic Curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, Negative Predictive Value (NPV), Positive Predictive Value (PPV), 
and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). To compare the differences in ROC curves among different models, the Delong 
test was applied, followed by Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple comparisons and control for Type I error. 
Additionally, the Brier score was used to evaluate the calibration of the prediction model.Permutation Importance and 
SHAP analysis were conducted to interpret feature contributions.
Results AUC values ranged from 0.722 to 0.816, with LightGBM achieving the highest predictive performance and 
demonstrating the greatest net benefit across different threshold probability ranges. Feature importance analysis 
revealed Multimorbidity, Depression, Self-rated Health, Social Events, and Drinking as the top predictors. Permutation 
Importance indicated differences in ranking between LightGBM and Random Forest, with SHAP analysis showing 
LightGBM’s ability to capture nonlinear effects, while Random Forest exhibited a more balanced global interpretation.
Conclusion ML algorithms can effectively predict the occurrence of frailty in Chinese elderly and identify significant 
factors associated with frailty. For datasets with complex feature interactions, LightGBM is preferable, while Random 
Forest offers improved stability and variance control. These findings support ML-based frailty screening and 
intervention strategies for aging populations.

Introduction
 The aging population is accelerating worldwide, and 
in Asia, China has become the country with the larg -
est number of elderly people. According to the seventh 
national census report released by the National Bureau 
of Statistics of China, by the end of 2020, the popula -
tion aged 60 and above in China reached 264 million, 
accounting for 18.7% of the total population. By 2050, the 
proportion of the elderly aged 65 and above is expected 
to reach 30% of the total population [ 1]. According to 
survey statistics, the average life expectancy of the elderly 
in China has increased from 77.3 years in 2019 to 78.2 
years in 2021. The healthy life expectancy of the elderly 
in China was 68.7 years in 2018, which means that these 
elderly people live with diseases for an average of 8–9 
years [2].
Frailty is a recognized risk factor for adverse health out-
comes in the aging population [3]. Frailty is a transitional 
state between robust health and disability, characterized 
by fatigue, reduced muscle mass and strength, and other 
physiological function declines [ 4]. This is a reversible 
dynamic pathological process and has become a signifi -
cant challenge for healthy aging [ 5]. The global preva -
lence of frailty ranges from 4.0% to 59.1%, and in China, 
it ranges from 7.0% to 28.0%, showing an increasing trend 
year by year [ 6, 7]. Adverse outcomes associated with 
frailty include poor quality of life, falls, fractures, func -
tional decline and disability, hospitalization, and even 
death [8, 9]. However, if properly treated, frailty is revers-
ible [10].
The reversibility of frailty is an important factor that 
promotes its early detection research. In fact, a tool that 
can detect frailty at an early stage, or even better, predict 
it, can greatly help us manage potential causes, which is 
crucial for preventing the elderly from developing more 
severe diseases (such as disability). Machine Learning 
(ML) is one of the most promising methods for develop -
ing such tools [ 11]. Predictive models help identify high-
risk groups before adverse events occur [ 12]. Recently, 
Machine Learning (ML) methods such as Support Vector 
Machines (SVM) and Random Forests (RF) are increas -
ingly applied to predictive models and show better per -
formance than traditional methods [ 13, 14], significantly 
reducing the manpower costs of healthcare [15].
We already know that frailty screening tools vary based 
on different definitions of frailty [ 16]. There are essen -
tially two understandings of frailty; one view considers 
it as a wasting syndrome (weight loss, reduced activity, 
slower gait speed, weaker grip strength, and fatigue), with 
the most commonly used definition of frailty being FFP 
[17]. Another view considers frailty as an accumulation 
of deficits [ 18], with the most commonly used defini -
tion of frailty being FI, a more comprehensive approach. 
Moreover, a recent review of machine learning systems 
for predicting frailty in the elderly indicates that, out of 
41 studies, only four studies were about Chinese elderly 
people, which defined frailty in the elderly using the 
FRAIL scale, Fried, and FI respectively, and only one 
study used the large sample data of CLHLS before 2019 
to construct FI [19].
During the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic, countries 
adopted measures such as lockdowns and maintaining 
social distance to mitigate the spread of the virus. These 
measures disrupted individuals’ daily lives, including 
physical activity and sleep patterns, leading to a long-
term deterioration in the health status of the elderly [ 20]. 
A narrative review study shows that COVID-19 indeed 
increases the degree of frailty in the elderly. Compared 
with the situation before the pandemic, the incidence 
of frailty in the elderly population increased in the first 
and second years of the pandemic [ 21].The situation 
after COVID-19 shares common characteristics with the 
frailty syndrome. Similarly, neurological, cardiovascu -
lar, and musculoskeletal diseases after COVID-19 may 
worsen functional status and lead to the manifestation 
and progression of frailty [22].
In our current work, we analyzed the latest China 
Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 
data obtained during the COVID-19 pandemic. We chose 
this dataset because it best represents the frailty charac -
teristics of the elderly population in China at this stage. 
Six ML models, including KNN, logistic regression, deci -
sion tree (DT), random forest (RF), LightGBM, and SVM, 
were established in order to predict frailty and identify 
significant factors associated with frailty.
Research data and methods
Data sources
The data for this study are derived from the 2020 China 
Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a 
nationally representative social science survey [ 23]. This 
comprehensive interdisciplinary survey is collaboratively 
conducted by Wuhan University and Peking Univer -
sity. The CHARLS baseline survey spans 150 regions in 
China, including 450 villages and city communities, and 
involves 10,257 households encompassing 17,708 indi -
viduals, reflecting the overall conditions of the elderly 
population in China. To ensure the representativeness of 
the sample, a multi-stage PPS random sampling method 
based on implicit stratification was employed [24].
All experimental methods in this study adhered to the 
principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and 
the guidelines established by the relevant ethics review 
committees. Data collection, processing, and analysis 
were conducted in accordance with internationally rec -
ognized standards and best practices in the field. The 
study received approval from the Biomedical Ethics 
Committee of Peking University (IRB00001052-11015).

Each participant provided informed consent by signing 
two forms, one retained by the participant and the other 
stored in the CHARLS office [25].
The inclusion criteria focused on elderly individuals 
aged 60 and above. Samples with missing demographic 
variables or FI scores were excluded. Ultimately, 7,880 
samples were included in this study.
Outcome variable
The Frailty Index (FI) is utilized to evaluate the frailty 
status of the elderly. This study refers to the FI standards 
established by Samuel, with criteria for the included 
variables as follows: (1) Manageable Health Impact: The 
selected indicators should be elements that can be man -
aged and have a significant impact on health. For exam -
ple, uncontrollable factors like the appearance of white 
hair with age are excluded. (2) Increasing Prevalence 
with Age: The prevalence of the indicator should increase 
with age. (3) Avoid Early Saturation: The indicator should 
not reach saturation at an early age, such as presbyopia, 
which typically saturates around age 55 in older adults, 
making it unsuitable as a frailty indicator. (4) Systematic 
Coverage: The frailty indicators should adhere to the 
principle of systematicity, covering various dimensions of 
health.
Samuel’s standard suggests including at least 30–40 
indicators in the frailty index. A minimal inclusion 
(around 10 or fewer) may result in unreliable outcomes. 
Essentially, the more indicators included, the more accu -
rate the FI’s calculation will be. Previous studies have 
validated that a frailty index computed from 30 to 40 
related indicators is sufficiently accurate for prediction 
[26]. Furthermore, research indicates that the FI can be 
constructed using most readily accessible survey indica -
tors in health surveys [27].
This study’s FI is adapted from the previously validated 
40-item FI developed by Samuel. Based on Samuel’s stan-
dard, the controllable risk factors influencing elderly 
frailty include socioeconomic status, unhealthy lifestyle, 
disease, dietary behavior, psychological depression, sleep 
disorders, and cognitive impairment, among others. Ulti -
mately, 36 indicators were selected to construct the FI 
warning model, which includes:
(1) Disease: 13 chronic diseases: hypertension, 
dyslipidemia (hyperlipidemia or hypolipidemia), 
diabetes or hyperglycemia, cancer and other 
malignant tumors, chronic pulmonary disease, liver 
disease, heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, gastric 
disease or digestive system disease, memory-related 
disease, arthritis or rheumatism, asthma. 2 forms 
of disabilities: physical disability, brain damage or 
intellectual impairment. 3 categories of visual and 
auditory conditions: blindness or partial blindness, 
deafness or partial deafness, dumbness or severe 
stuttering. 2 types of health evaluations: self-rated 
health, body pain.
(2) Disability: The Katz-ADL and Lawton-IADL scores, 
including 11 indicators, assess independent living 
ability and instrumental daily living functions. These 
cover dressing independently, bathing independently, 
eating independently, moving independently (getting 
up, going to bed), using the toilet independently, 
controlling bowel and bladder function, handling 
housework, preparing meals, shopping, managing 
finances, and making phone calls [28].
(3) Depression: The CESD10 scale is used for evaluation 
[29, 30].
(4) Cognition: Cognitive function is measured using the 
approach employed in the Health and Retirement 
Study (HRS) in the United States [31]. The variables 
are evaluated based on their type, with values 
assigned accordingly. The calculation method of FI 
is the number of health deficits divided by the total 
number included (34 in this study), with a range of 
0–1. The larger the value, the more frail it indicates, 
with FI ≥ 0.25 defined as frail.
Data preprocessing
To ensure dataset completeness and reliability, we con -
ducted a systematic missing data analysis before model 
training. Using the missdata() function, we computed 
missing rates for all variables and identified high-miss -
ing-rate variables, including occupational status (23.5%) 
and parent-child relationship satisfaction (18.7%). Instead 
of direct deletion, we classified variables into continuous 
and categorical types to apply appropriate imputation 
strategies. Continuous variables were imputed using the 
median value, preserving data distribution while mini -
mizing bias. Categorical variables with missing data were 
retained without imputation to avoid introducing arti -
ficial distortions.This preprocessing step ensured data 
integrity and sample representativeness, allowing for 
robust Frailty Index (FI) calculations while preventing 
excessive data reduction. Additionally, missingness anal -
ysis confirmed that the missing data were randomly dis -
tributed (MCAR), mitigating concerns about systematic 
bias impacting model predictions.
Socio-demographic factors
The sociodemographic variables included in this study 
encompass age, gender, level of education, region, mari -
tal status, and living situation. Specific classifications for 
these variables are as follows:
Gender: Classified as female or male.
Education Level: Classified as illiterate, primary 
school, or junior high school and above.

Song and Liu BMC Geriatrics         (2025) 25:1003 
Region: Classified as urban or rural.
Marital Status: Classified as married, divorced, 
widowed, or single.
Living Situation: Classified as living alone or not.
Age: Treated as a continuous variable.
Health status
For health status, we selected Healthself-assessment, 
multimorbidity,. Specifically, self-rated health is catego -
rized as very poor, poor, fair, good, or very good; multi -
morbidity is categorized as yes or no.
Behavioral factors
Behavioral factors include smoking, drinking, duration 
of nighttime sleep, nap duration, social activities, MVPA, 
and the frequency of physical activity. Specifically, the 
duration of nighttime sleep is classified into three cate -
gories: short (< 6 h), moderate (6–8 h; reference group), 
and long (> 8 h); nap duration is evaluated based on the 
response to the question: “How long do you typically nap 
in the past month?” Respondents are segmented into four 
groups: no nap (0  min), short nap (< 30  min), moder -
ate nap (30–90 min), and long nap (> 90 min); smoking, 
drinking, and social activities are classified as either pres -
ent or absent; the frequency of physical activity is clas -
sified as 0 times per week, 1–4 times per week, or more 
than 4 times per week.
MVPA: The CHARLS questionnaire categorizes the 
physical activity of the elderly into three intensities: high, 
moderate, and low, which includes the count and dura -
tion of physical activity at different intensities per week 
[32]. Physical activity exceeding 3 h per day at various 
intensities is recorded as “180 minutes. ” Only physi -
cal activity of different intensity types is permitted and 
quantified to a maximum of 21 h per week to prevent 
misclassification of the samples into the high-intensity 
physical activity group. Based on the assigned metabolic 
equivalents (METs), different types of physical activ -
ity are observed at different intensity levels in the Sum -
mary of Physical Activity (8.0 for high-intensity physical 
activity, 4.0 for moderate-intensity physical activity, and 
3.3 for low-intensity physical activity) [ 33]. The energy 
expenditure of one week of physical activity is calculated 
using the formula (1 week of physical activity energy 
expenditure = metabolic equivalent of physical activity 
corresponding to the type of intensity * number of days 
of physical activity corresponding to intensity per week * 
time) [34]. In line with the International Physical Activity 
Scale, the physical activity of the elderly is divided into 
three levels: high (>3000 METs/week), moderate (600–
3000 METs/week), and low (< 600 METs/week) intensi -
ties [35]. MVPA refers to moderate to vigorous physical 
activity.
Mental health factors
Mental health factors include cognitive function scores, 
life satisfaction, and parent-child relationships. Cogni -
tive function scores are evaluated following the meth -
odologies of the American Health and Retirement Study 
(HRS). Participants are subjected to in-person evalua -
tions across four dimensions of cognitive function, spe -
cifically orientation, memory, calculation, and drawing. 
The cumulative cognitive score is the sum of orientation 
(5 points), calculation (5 points), memory (20 points), 
and drawing (1 point), yielding a total score of 31 points. 
Life satisfaction and parent-child relationships are each 
classified as very poor, poor, fair, good, or very good.
Built environment factor
For the built environment, we selected the indicator 
“Wheelchair Accessible” . Wheelchair accessible is catego-
rized as either “yes” or “no” .
Statistical methods
In our frailty prediction study, we trained six types of 
machine learning models: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), 
Logistic Regression, Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest 
(RF), LightGBM, and Support Vector Machine (SVM). 
Logistic Regression was used as the baseline model for 
comparison. These algorithms were developed by repeat-
edly splitting the data to identify feature collections that 
optimally discriminate between outcome classes, utiliz -
ing a 5-fold cross-validation technique. The models were 
then tested using reserved data, with 60% of the data allo-
cated for training (including cross-validation and model 
tuning) and the remaining 40% designated as the test set.
Given the lower occurrence of frailty among the elderly 
compared to those without frailty in our study, handling 
class imbalance was crucial. While various methods are 
available, data sampling techniques are most commonly 
used, particularly the SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-
sampling Technique) method. After data cleaning, the 
data was first split into training and testing sets. Overs -
ampling was then performed on the training set using the 
SMOTE method to avoid the risk of data leakage and to 
ensure the reliability of the model results [36, 37].
To optimize the LightGBM model, we conducted a 
systematic hyperparameter tuning process using Grid -
SearchCV, combined with 5-fold cross-validation, to 
maximize ROC AUC as the primary performance met -
ric. The hyperparameter search space was defined as fol -
lows: n_estimators ranged from 1 to 100 in increments of 
10, max_depth ranged from 1 to 10 in increments of 1, 
and learning_rate ranged from 0.01 to 0.1 in increments 
of 0.01. The search was performed using GridSearchCV 
with scoring=’roc_auc’ , ensuring model selection was 
based on maximizing discrimination ability. The best 
hyperparameter configuration was determined using

best_params_, which selected n_estimators = 91, max_
depth = 8, learning_rate = 0.08 as the optimal combina -
tion. To prevent overfitting, we applied early stopping 
criteria, monitoring validation AUC, and ensured model 
stability by setting random_state = 1. Given the compu -
tational complexity of hyperparameter tuning, we opti -
mized the model using parallel processing (n_jobs=−1), 
allowing efficient parameter exploration within a rea -
sonable runtime.The performance of the models was 
evaluated using several metrics: Area Under the Receiver 
Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC), sensitivity, speci -
ficity, Negative Predictive Value (NPV), Positive Predic -
tive Value (PPV), and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). 
To compare the differences in ROC curves among the six 
models, we employed DeLong’s test. Given that multiple 
pairwise comparisons were conducted, we applied Bon -
ferroni correction to adjust the significance level, setting 
the threshold at 0.00333 to control for Type I error. This 
ensured that the identified differences between models 
remained statistically robust and minimized the risk of 
false positive findings. Additionally, DCA, a new method 
for evaluating the predictive ability of different models, 
calculates an analytical measure called net benefit using 
the true positives and false positives of a model, thus 
placing the advantages and disadvantages of the model 
on the same scale [38].
We assessed the probabilistic accuracy of the best-
performing model using the Brier score, defined as the 
mean square difference between observed and predicted 
outcomes. The Brier score ranges from 0 to 1.00, with 0 
representing the best calibration [39].
To further explain the performance of different 
machine learning models, we utilized two complemen -
tary feature importance analysis methods: SHapley 
Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Permutation Impor -
tance. SHAP , a game theory-based method, provides 
individualized explanations by assigning importance 
values to features based on their contribution to a spe -
cific prediction. It employs Shapley values to quantify 
the impact of each feature, with values closer to zero 
indicating a smaller effect and values farther from zero 
denoting stronger influence. Meanwhile, Permutation 
Importance assesses the global contribution of features 
by randomly shuffling individual predictor values and 
measuring the resulting change in model performance, 
typically using the AUC metric. Features that cause 
greater performance deterioration when shuffled are 
considered more crucial for prediction. By integrating 
SHAP and Permutation Importance, our study enhances 
the interpretability of frailty prediction models, ensuring 
robust assessments of feature relevance from both local 
(individual-level) and global (dataset-wide) perspectives.
Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 23.0 and Python 
3.8 software. Continuous variables were profiled, and 
the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to verify if the 
test data followed a normal distribution. Measurements 
adhering to a normal distribution were represented as 
(x ± s), and the t-test was used for mean comparisons 
between two groups, while analysis of variance was 
employed for mean comparisons among several groups. 
Measurements not adhering to a normal distribution or 
variance were depicted as M (Q1, Q3), and the rank sum 
test was used for comparisons within or among groups. 
Categorical data were represented as n (%), and the χ2 
test or Fisher’s exact test was used for analysis among two 
or more groups. Differences were considered statistically 
significant at P < 0.05.
Results
Participant characteristics
The final valid sample of this study includes 7880 elderly 
people: 4125 are females (52.35%), with an average age of 
(69.05 ± 6.82) years, and 2066 (26.22%) suffer from frailty. 
There are 4413 illiterates (56.00%), 6464 living in rural 
areas (82.03%), 6012 married (76.29%), 707 with excel -
lent self-rated health (8.97%), and 4450 who did not par -
ticipate in any social events within a month (56.47%). The 
weekly MVPA time is (221.36 ± 63.97) min, the depres -
sion score is 9.23 ± 6.61, the cognitive function score is 
11.54 ± 7.06, the nighttime sleep duration is (5.87 ± 2.23) 
h, and the nap sleep is (46.05 ± 48.79) min. There is no 
statistically significant difference in the variables of 
region, living alone, and drinking ( P > 0.05), and there 
is a statistically significant difference in other variables 
(P < 0.001). For specific basic characteristics, see Table 1.
Predicting frailty in Chinese older adults using ML models
The dataset in this research was partitioned into a train -
ing subset and a testing subset at a 6:4 ratio. Following 
this, the minority samples were oversampled using the 
SMOTE algorithm. The training process was carried out 
on the training subset, and its ability to generalize was 
assessed on the testing subset. Recursive feature elimina -
tion was performed on the training subset using the RF 
algorithm as a classification model. The AUC score was 
obtained from various combinations of feature selection 
through three-fold cross-validation, identifying 21 as the 
ideal number of features. The rank-sum test results indi -
cated no statistically significant difference in the continu-
ous variables between the training and testing subsets 
(P > 0.05). Likewise, the chi-square test revealed no signif-
icant difference for other categorical variables (P > 0.05).
With respect to predicting frailty, the AUC values 
of the Decision Tree and LightGBM were the lowest 
(AUC = 0.722) and the highest (AUC = 0.816), respec -
tively, among the six ML models (Fig.  1). Furthermore, 
Delong’s statistical comparison showed that, with the 
exception of the SVM model, there were differences in

Feature importance and variables interpretation
In frailty prediction, the LightGBM model ranks the 
importance of features as shown in Fig.  3. According to 
this model, comorbidity, depression, self-rated health, 
social activities, and drinking are the five most impor -
tant features for predicting frailty. Notably, comorbidity, 
depression, smoking, drinking, nap duration, and age 
are positively correlated with the occurrence of frailty, 
while self-rated health, social activities, frequency of 
physical exercise, cognitive function score, MVPA, night-
time sleep duration, life satisfaction, and education level 
are negatively correlated with the occurrence of frailty. 
Retired elderly people have a higher likelihood of frailty 
occurrence than those who are not retired. These find -
ings are crucial for the identification and intervention of 
frailty in the elderly.
In addition to SHAP analysis, we conducted Permuta -
tion Importance to further validate feature contributions. 
Permutation Importance, which measures the reduc -
tion in model performance when a feature’s values are 
randomly shuffled, offers a complementary global per -
spective on feature relevance. Our analysis revealed that 
depression ranked highest in permutation importance, 
reinforcing its critical role in frailty prediction. Multi -
morbidity followed closely, confirming previous findings 
from SHAP rankings. Social activities, self-rated health, 
and smoking also showed substantial importance, align -
ing with established frailty risk factors. Interestingly, 
some variables exhibited minor or negative importance in 
permutation analysis, such as cognitive function and age. 
This suggests that these features may have complex inter-
actions with frailty or may contribute indirectly rather 
than as primary predictors. The combined use of SHAP 
and permutation importance ensures a more robust and 
interpretable frailty prediction model, highlighting key

Discussion
To our knowledge, this is the first study to predict frailty 
in Chinese elderly people using CHARLS data combined 
with machine learning methods during the COVID-
19 pandemic. In terms of data selection, previous stud -
ies have shown that the sources of databases used for 
frailty prediction vary greatly, whether in China or other 
regions of the world [ 19]. No database has been used in 
more than two studies, which makes comparing results 
more complex [19]. Replicating results is another key step 
for researchers to compare and improve current results. 
Therefore, we hope that our research conforms to the 
characteristics of frailty in Chinese elderly people at the 
current stage, providing a reference for future research -
ers to compare and improve.
The task of predicting frailty in the elderly was carried 
out with the support of six ML algorithms. It was found 
that the LightGBM model performed best in terms of 
AUC value, which is the most commonly used indicator 
for evaluating the performance of prediction models [40]. 
DCA analysis also showed that within different thresh -
old probability ranges, the LightGBM model also has 
the greatest net benefit. DCA is also used to evaluate the 
clinical value of models and has been applied in many 
medical studies, showing great clinical utility [41].
Given the multiple comparisons among six machine 
learning models, we applied Bonferroni correction to 
ensure statistical rigor and control for Type I error. After 
adjusting the significance threshold to 0.00333, pairwise 
comparisons confirmed statistically significant differ -
ences in predictive performance (Table 3). This validation 
strengthens the conclusion that ensemble learning meth -
ods, particularly LightGBM and Random Forest, dem -
onstrate superior reliability compared to simpler models 
such as Decision Tree and KNN.
Furthermore, both LightGBM and Random Forest 
demonstrate high predictive performance, with AUC 
values ranging from 80% to 82%. However, their deci -
sion-making mechanisms differ significantly: Light -
GBM employs a boosting strategy, iteratively refining 
weak learners to reduce bias, whereas Random Forest

While the current study demonstrates the effectiveness 
of LightGBM, future research could explore alternative 
ensemble learning strategies and incorporate advanced 
feature selection techniques to further optimize frailty 
prediction models. Additionally, age-specific subgroup 
analyses may provide deeper insights into model gen -
eralizability across different population cohorts. The 
application of Bonferroni correction in future compara -
tive studies can further ensure statistical robustness 
when assessing model performance across varied clinical 
datasets.
Machine learning (ML) methods are highly effective 
at uncovering complex patterns and interactions within 
data, but they are often criticized for their “black box” 
nature [ 42]. This study employs SHAP (SHapley Addi -
tive Explanations) technology because it can empirically 
reveal the importance of each feature to the model out -
put. SHAP values highlight which features significantly 
impact the model’s prediction for each data point and 
whether these impacts are positive or negative. This 
enhances the interpretability of the model by helping us 
understand why specific predictions are made [43].SHAP 
values have been successfully utilized for ML interpre -
tation in the medical research field. For instance, the 
feature importance and SHAP values of the XGBoost 
algorithm revealed that systolic blood pressure, diastolic 
blood pressure, age, and body mass index play crucial 
roles in predicting three types of physical frailty [ 44]. 
While this method has been applied in various fields of 
ML interpretation, it has not yet been extensively used 
in exploratory studies on predicting frailty occurrence 
among elderly individuals in China. Therefore, the results 
of this study can provide valuable insights for improv -
ing frailty prediction models for the Chinese elderly 
population.
This study explained the significant contributions to 
the model prediction results through SHAP analysis. 
The results showed that Multimorbidity, Depression, 
Self-rated Health, Social events, and Drinking are the 
five most important features for predicting the occur -
rence of frailty. The summary plot intuitively displays 
the contribution of each feature to the model prediction 
results. These findings reveal the key factors affecting 
the occurrence of frailty, which is crucial for early iden -
tification and intervention of frailty. In addition to SHAP 
analysis, we incorporated Permutation Importance to 
ensure robust feature interpretability.Further analysis of 
the interpretability of these models reveals distinct dif -
ferences in Permutation Importance and SHAP values: 
LightGBM ranks key features differently from Random 
Forest. For example, Multimorbidity is ranked slightly 
lower in LightGBM but appears more significant in 
Random Forest, suggesting that Random Forest focuses 
more on holistic feature combinations, whereas Light -
GBM emphasizes individual strong variables.SHAP val -
ues provide individual-level explanations, showing that 
LightGBM captures nonlinear effects more effectively, 
with smoother feature importance distributions, while 
Random Forest exhibits more evenly distributed feature 
dependencies, making it ideal for global importance 
assessments.Depression consistently emerged as a top 
predictor, reinforcing prior research that links mental 
health with frailty development. However, Multimor -
bidity ranked slightly lower in permutation analysis, 
suggesting potential interactions or nonlinear effects. 
Additionally, smoking showed greater importance in 
permutation ranking than in SHAP analysis, indicating 
its potential confounding effect or indirect association 
with frailty. Given the differences between boosting and 
random forest models, permutation importance offers 
unique insights into feature dependencies that SHAP 
alone might overlook. These findings emphasize the need 
for multi-angle interpretability methods when design -
ing frailty prediction models, ensuring a comprehensive 
understanding of the predictors contributing to frailty 
development. For datasets with complex feature interac -
tions, LightGBM is more suitable, while Random Forest 
is the better choice when reducing variance and enhanc -
ing model robustness is the priority. Researchers can 
select the optimal model based on application needs to 
ensure both predictive stability and interpretability.
This study found that Multimorbidity is the most 
important factor affecting the occurrence of frailty in the 
elderly, and it is positively correlated with the occurrence 
of frailty in the elderly. As the elderly age, they accumu -
late two or more diseases, which accounts for 55% to 98% 
of the population over 65 years old. This is consistent 
with the 96.9% Multimorbidity result of this study [ 45, 
46]. Previous research evidence suggests that there is a 
certain degree of overlap in the biological causes of frailty 
and Multimorbidity, and there may be a bidirectional 
causal relationship between them. Frailty may make the 
elderly prone to multiple chronic diseases, but frailty may 
also stem from the coexistence of multiple diseases [ 17, 
47]. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 obser-
vational studies on frailty and Multimorbidity, the possi -
bility of physical frailty due to multiple diseases increased 
nearly twofold. According to longitudinal studies, Mul -
timorbidity is associated with an increased risk of frailty 
[48].
Depression in the elderly is also positively correlated 
with the occurrence of frailty. Previous studies have 
also found a positive correlation between depression 
and frailty [ 49]. Researchers have found that depressive 
symptoms in frail patients are associated with a higher 
incidence of frailty (OR = 3.13; 95% CI = 1.37–7.13) [ 50].

In terms of pathophysiological mechanisms, Interleu -
kin-6 (IL-6) may play a role, as studies show that patients 
with depression have elevated levels of inflammatory 
cytokines [51, 52]. High levels of inflammatory cytokines 
enter the blood-brain barrier and act on skeletal muscles, 
adversely affecting muscle strength, mass, and cognitive 
function, leading to the development of frailty [53].
Self-rated health in the elderly is negatively correlated 
with the occurrence of frailty. Previous studies have also 
found that frailty is positively correlated with poor health 
status (p ≤ 0.05). Elderly people with poor health status 
have a lower level of education, leading to a significant 
reduction in self-management ability ( P ≤ 0.001), and a 
higher degree of frailty (P ≤ 0.001) [54].
Social events among the elderly are also negatively cor -
related with the occurrence of frailty. Previous research 
has also shown that social activities, such as visiting 
friends, seeking advice, and engaging in intellectual activ-
ities, can reduce the decline in Instrumental Activities 
of Daily Living (IADL) [ 55]. Participating in meaningful 
social events contributes to the well-being of the elderly 
[56]. For the elderly, in order to maintain their mental 
health, participating in meaningful social activities can 
increase physical activity and reduce cognitive decline 
[57].
Our research also indicates that drinking is positively 
correlated with the occurrence of frailty. This is incon -
sistent with previous studies, some of which found that 
moderate drinking can reduce the risk of frailty in elderly 
men and women, and that consuming 1–7 alcoholic bev -
erages per week is associated with a reduction in the 
degree of frailty in women (OR = 0.49, p < 0.001) [ 58]. 
Another Mendelian randomization study found no sig -
nificant causal relationship between alcohol use and the 
risk of frailty [ 59]. Other research has found that the risk 
of frailty is lowest among moderate drinkers who drink 
3–4 days per week, possibly showing a U-shaped rela -
tionship [ 60]. Heavy drinkers may be a high-risk group 
for physical frailty, sick abstainers or those not intend -
ing to start drinking are classified as non-drinkers, and 
healthy drinkers who continue to drink are classified as 
current drinkers, resulting in a significantly lower risk 
of frailty among drinkers [ 61]. Therefore, no definitive 
conclusions can be drawn about the clear relationship 
between heavy drinking and frailty. This is a problem that 
needs to be further addressed in future research.
This study also has several limitations. First, the cur -
rent definition of frailty is not unified, and we use the FI 
of the well to assess frailty in the elderly, which may lead 
to bias in the assessment results. A standard definition 
of frailty is needed to make the data methods effective 
and comparable. In the case of cross-sectional studies, 
we cannot establish a causal relationship between the 
factors included and the results (frailty). Secondly, the 
scope of this study’s data survey was during the COVID-
19 pandemic in 2020, and new data after the pandemic 
has not yet been released. Subsequently, with the release 
of data after COVID-19, a new longitudinal data model 
can be constructed. Finally, despite taking some mea -
sures to ensure good model performance, once the 
model is established, it still needs to be validated using 
an independent external queue. Additionally, while we 
systematically optimized key hyperparameters such as n_
estimators, max_depth, and learning_rate, other hyper -
parameters—such as num_leaves, min_child_samples, 
and subsampling techniques—were not included in this 
study. Future research could explore their impact to fur -
ther refine the predictive capacity of LightGBM. Despite 
these limitations, this study shows that the constructed 
model can be used for the prediction and further inter -
vention of frailty in the elderly.
Conclusion
This study constructed a prediction model for the occur -
rence of frailty in the elderly in our country using six 
ML algorithms, and the prediction model based on the 
LightGBM algorithm has superior comprehensive per -
formance compared to other models. Therefore, the 
research results can provide a theoretical reference 
for accurately identifying high-risk groups from mul -
tiple dimensions and implementing appropriate early 
interventions.

Abstract
Background As the population continues to age, the prevalence of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) has increased 
steadily. Studies have shown that older adults with chronic diseases are more likely to develop MCI than those 
without chronic conditions, suggesting that chronic diseases may play a significant role in the onset of MCI. Therefore, 
this study is designed to develop a predictive model for MCI among older individuals with chronic diseases in China 
and to identify the major factors influencing the occurrence of MCI.
Method The training and internal validation data are from the 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study 
(CHARLS), using retrospective data with 4,712 older adults with chronic diseases. The external validation data are from 
the General Hospital of Southern Theater Command in Guangdong, using prospective data with 1,000 cases. This is an 
observational study. Univariate logistic regression was used to select statistically significant predictors, and ultimately, 
a combination of LASSO regression and random forest results identified 9 optimal predictors, which were used to 
construct the nomogram. The model’s discrimination, calibration, clinical applicability, and generalizability were 
assessed using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA), and 
internal validation.
Results Age, education level, child satisfaction, marital status, depressive symptoms, ADL score, income, SCD, and the 
number of chronic diseases were identified as significant predictors of MCI in older adults with chronic diseases. The 
AUC values exceeded 0.7 across the training, internal validation, and external validation sets.The calibration curves 
closely align with the diagonal, and the P values of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test are all greater than 0.05, indicating 
strong consistency between the predicted and actual outcomes. The DCA further demonstrates that the model has 
significant clinical utility.

Background
By 2035, China’s older population is projected to exceed 
400 million, comprising one-third of the total popula -
tion, highlighting the country’s growing aging challenge 
[1, 2]. The aging population, coupled with extended life 
expectancy, has contributed to a steady increase in the 
prevalence of chronic diseases, significantly impacting 
the health and daily lives of residents. Data showed that 
approximately 75.8% of older adults suffer from at least 
one chronic condition, with hypertension and coronary 
heart disease being the most common. Chronic diseases 
are now the leading contributors to the global disease 
burden [3], accounting for more than 70% of China’s total 
disease burden [ 4], leading to an increase in the demand 
for public health resources and medical expenditures. 
The treatment of chronic diseases is generally costly 
and often requires lifelong management [ 5]. These dis -
eases not only impose a significant economic burden on 
patients but also severely affect the quality of life of older 
adults.
As the population ages, the prevalence of Alzheimer’s 
disease (AD) is increasing. AD, characterized by cogni -
tive decline and behavioral changes, is the most com -
mon form of dementia. In 2018, the global number of AD 
patients worldwide reached 50 million and is projected 
to exceed 152 million by 2050 [ 6]. AD severely affects 
daily functioning in older adults and imposes substan -
tial economic and caregiving burdens on families and 
society [ 7]. Evidence suggests that AD is preceded by a 
transitional stage during which cognitive decline begins 
gradually. Once this stage is surpassed, cognitive dete -
rioration accelerates, significantly impairing daily activi -
ties [8]. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represents this 
transitional phase. As of 2020, there were over 38.77 mil -
lion MCI patients in the older adult population [9]. These 
patients exhibit mild memory impairment but have not 
yet met the clinical diagnostic criteria for dementia and 
are in the early stages of dementia development [ 10, 11]. 
Studies have shown that 15% to 28% of older adults with 
MCI progress to dementia within three years, with the 
likelihood rising to 70% within five to ten years [ 11, 12]. 
Current pharmacological treatments for AD provide only 
symptomatic relief, with no effect on halting or reversing 
disease progression [ 13]. The clinical practice guidelines 
for MCI released by the American Academy of Neurol -
ogy indicate that 14.4% to 55.6% of MCI patients can 
restore nervous system integrity and reduce the risk of 
AD through intervention [ 14]. Consequently, research 
has increasingly focused on early identification and 
intervention during the MCI stage, widely considered 
the “golden window” for dementia prevention.Studies 
have shown that patients with chronic diseases are more 
likely to experience cognitive decline due to factors such 
as chronic inflammation and immune dysfunction [ 15]. 
Older adults with chronic conditions are at greater risk 
of developing MCI than their healthy peers [ 16]. Chronic 
conditions may increase the risk of MCI by affecting 
brain structure and function, including through vascu -
lar damage [ 17], metabolic disorders [ 18], and inflam -
matory responses [ 19]. These conditions not only lead 
to a decline in physiological function but also increase 
the risk of MCI [ 20]. Existing prediction models fail to 
adequately reflect the cognitive risk in older adults with 
chronic diseases. Therefore, early identification of cogni -
tive decline in older patients with chronic diseases, along 
with timely intervention and treatment, holds significant 
clinical importance in delaying or even reversing cogni -
tive decline.
In the medical field, risk prediction models are com -
monly used to assess the impact of various risk factors 
on the occurrence of outcome events. These models help 
identify high-risk populations and enable the develop -
ment of personalized interventions in advance. Signifi -
cant increases in MCI incidence were observed during 
the epidemic period, likely linked to the viral pandemic 
[21]. The 2020 data, focused mainly on the epidemic. 
This dataset could not provide sufficient predictors for 
the gradual return to normal life following the end of 
the epidemic phase. Therefore, this study uses 2018 data, 
which are considered the most accurate representation 
of cognitive characteristics in older adults during a nor -
mal phase. Using the China Health and Retirement Lon -
gitudinal Study (CHARLS) database, this study aims to 
develop a risk prediction model for MCI in older adults 
with chronic diseases, identify high-risk groups through 
early screening, and provide effective management and 
personalized interventions for high-risk individuals.
Materials and methods
Data sources
The data for the training set and internal validation set 
in this study are sourced from the 2018 CHARLS, using 
retrospective data to construct and validate the model, 
ultimately including 4,712 older adults with chronic dis -
eases. The external validation set data are obtained from 
the General Hospital of Southern Theater Command in 
Conclusion The nomogram prediction model deeloped in this study demonstrated good predictive performance 
and may serve as a useful tool to help identify older adults with chronic diseases who are at increased risk of MCI. 
These findings may inform future strategies for individualized risk assessment and early management.

Guangdong Province, using prospective data for external 
validation, with 1,000 cases of older adults with chronic 
diseases included. This study is an observational study. 
CHARLS, organized by the Research Center for Healthy 
Aging and Development and the National School of 
Development at Peking University, is a nationally repre -
sentative survey of individuals aged 45 years and above 
in China. It aims to provide comprehensive health data 
for the older population, covering domains such as cogni-
tive health and socioeconomic status, thereby supporting 
the development of effective health management policies 
for older adults. The survey adopts a multistage stratified 
cluster sampling design, covering 28 provinces (includ -
ing municipalities and county-level cities), 150 counties 
or districts, and 450 villages or communities, represent -
ing approximately 85% of the national population. All 
data are collected through face-to-face interviews, ensur -
ing strong representativeness [ 22]. The data are publicly 
accessible through the official website  (   h t t p : / / C H A R L S 
. p k u . e d u . c n     ) . The original CHARLS study protocol has 
been approved by the Biomedical Ethics Review Com -
mittee of Peking University (IRB00001052-11015), and 
written informed consent is obtained from all partici -
pants prior to the interviews.
The external validation data are sourced from more 
than 20 departments for older adults with chronic dis -
eases, including cardiology, respiratory medicine, and 
nephrology, at the hospital. According to the require -
ment that external validation samples account for 20% of 
the total sample size [ 23], the minimum number of cases 
needed for external validation in this study is 4,712 × 20% 
= 942. Under the guidance of head nurses in each depart-
ment, the research team strictly adheres to the inclusion 
and exclusion criteria and conducts face-to-face inter -
views, ultimately collecting 1,000 cases of older adults 
with chronic diseases as the external validation sample. 
The external validation protocol has been approved by 
the Ethics Committee of Scientific Research at the Gen -
eral Hospital of Southern Theater Command of PLA 
(NZLLKZ2025106).
To ensure data accuracy and reliability, this study 
includes individuals aged ≥ 60 years who are diag -
nosed with at least one chronic disease. Participants 
are excluded if more than 20% of their data are missing, 
if their cognitive function assessment is incomplete or 
invalid, or if sex information is unavailable.
Data collection
Cognitive functioning scale
The CHARLS survey adopts the same methods as the 
U.S. Health and Retirement Study (HRS) to assess cog -
nitive function [ 24]. In CHARLS, cognitive function is 
evaluated across four domains: orientation, calculation, 
word recall, and drawing [ 25]. The total score ranges 
from 0 to 31, with higher scores indicating better cogni -
tive performance. The orientation section requires par -
ticipants to answer questions about the current season, 
day of the week, year, month, and date. The calculation 
section assesses mental arithmetic through a serial sub -
traction task in which participants subtract 7 from 100 
five consecutive times, receiving 1 point for each correct 
answer and 0 points for an incorrect answer. The word 
recall section has a maximum of 20 points; participants 
are presented with 10 Chinese words and asked to recall 
them within 2 min, followed by delayed recall after 4 to 
10 min. Each correctly recalled word is awarded 1 point. 
The drawing section evaluates visuospatial ability by ask -
ing participants to copy two overlapping pentagrams, 
with 1 point awarded for each correctly reproduced fig -
ure [26].
In this study, MCI is defined using the Age-Associated 
Cognitive Decline (AACD) criterion. Specifically, individ-
uals are classified as having MCI if their cognitive func -
tion score falls at least one standard deviation (SD) below 
the mean for their respective age group [27]. Accordingly, 
participants aged 60 years and older are categorized into 
5-year age groups, and those meeting the AACD thresh -
old within each group are identified as having MCI.
Methodology for determining chronic diseases
In CHARLS, chronic disease is defined across a range of 
conditions, including hypertension, dyslipidemia (e.g., 
hyper- or hypolipidemia), diabetes or elevated blood glu -
cose, malignancies (excluding mild skin cancer), chronic 
lung diseases (e.g., chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and 
pulmonary heart disease, excluding tumors or cancer), 
liver diseases (excluding fatty liver, tumors, or cancer), 
heart diseases (e.g., myocardial infarction, coronary heart 
disease, angina, heart failure), stroke (including infarc -
tion and hemorrhage), kidney disease (excluding cancer), 
digestive system disorders (excluding cancer), emotional 
and mental health issues, memory-related diseases (e.g., 
Alzheimer’s disease, brain atrophy), arthritis or rheuma -
tism, and asthma, among others. The diagnosis was based 
on self-reports. The participants were asked whether 
a doctor had diagnosed them with each condition. A 
response of ‘‘yes’’ was given a score of 1, and ‘‘no’’ was 
given a score of 0. The scores were summed to determine 
the total number of chronic conditions [28].
Independent variables
Through an extensive literature review and consultations 
with geriatricians, neurologists, and epidemiologists 
specializing in aging and MCI, this study identifies 30 
factors associated with an increased risk of MCI. These 
factors are categorized into four main domains: sociode -
mographic characteristics, lifestyle, health status, and
