ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

machine, and extreme gradient boosting. Model performance was evaluated 
using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), 
calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Feature contributions were 
elucidated using SHAP values.
Results: Incident cardiovascular disease occurred in 1,246 participants 
(22.0%) within the training cohort. Multivariable analysis identified 
hypertension (adjusted OR 1.80), waist circumference (adjusted OR 1.05 per 1-
cm increment), dyslipidaemia (adjusted OR 1.42), and liver disease (adjusted OR 
1.60) as principal independent predictors. Among ten algorithms evaluated, 
random forest demonstrated superior performance: validation set AUC 0.829 (95% 
CI 0.809-0.848), accuracy 0.770, sensitivity 0.681, specificity 0.795. The model 
exhibited excellent calibration and yielded maximal net clinical benefit across 
the 10%-85% risk threshold spectrum. SHAP analysis revealed waist 
circumference as the predominant contributor, followed by triglycerides, age, 
and hypertension. Psychobehavioural factors (depression, sleep duration) 
demonstrated independent predictive value. A web-based risk calculator was 
developed, providing real-time individual 9-year cardiovascular disease 
probability estimates.
Conclusion: The random forest model accurately predicts cardiovascular 
disease risk in the Chinese middle-aged and elderly population, with waist 
circumference emerging as the most critical predictor. Translated into an online 
assessment tool, this model facilitates community-based screening and 
individualized prevention, offering a pragmatic risk stratification approach for 
resource-constrained settings.

Introduction
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) has emerged as the foremost cause of 
mortality worldwide. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 documented 
approximately 20.5 million CVD-attributable deaths, representing 32.4% of 
global mortality, with ischaemic heart disease and stroke accounting for 9.2

ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

million and 7.6 million deaths respectively, whilst contributing 430 million 
disability-adjusted life-years lost [1]. This public health challenge assumes 
particular gravity in China. The Report on Cardiovascular Health and Diseases 
in China 2024 estimates the current prevalence exceeds 350 million cases, 
encompassing 14 million stroke survivors, 12 million individuals with coronary 
heart disease, 9 million with heart failure, and a striking 245 million with 
hypertension[2]. In 2022, the CVD mortality rate reached 324.49 per 100,000, 
constituting the leading cause of death amongst both rural (48.12%) and urban 
(46.74%) residents [2]. Despite declining age-standardised mortality rates, 
accelerated population ageing continues to amplify the absolute disease 
burden—by 2020, adults aged ≥60 years numbered 264 million (18.70% of the 
population), with projections estimating 40 million CVD patients by 2030 [3]. 
Within this epidemiological context, accurate identification of high-risk 
individuals and implementation of early intervention strategies constitute pivotal 
imperatives for disease control.
Risk prediction models represent the cornerstone of precision CVD 
prevention. Since the seminal 1998 Framingham Heart Study risk score[4], such 
tools have gained widespread adoption in clinical decision-making. The 
American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Pooled Cohort 
Equations (PCE) [5], the European Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE) 
system[6], and the WHO cardiovascular risk charts have been extensively 
deployed across Western populations. However, the cross-population 
generalisability of these models exhibits substantial limitations. A validation 
study encompassing 95,649 Chinese adults demonstrated systematic risk 
overestimation and suboptimal calibration of the Framingham score in Chinese 
cohorts [7]. External validation of PCE equations in Chinese populations yielded 
similarly disappointing results [8], with predictive discordance attributable to 
ethnic genetic heterogeneity, lifestyle patterns, risk factor prevalence profiles, 
and healthcare system disparities [9].
In response to the inadequate localisation of international tools, Chinese 
investigators have undertaken systematic endeavours. Leveraging data from 
127,000 participants in the China Prediction for Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular 
Disease Risk (China-PAR) study, researchers developed a 10-year 
atherosclerotic CVD risk prediction instrument for adults aged 35-79 years, 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPTARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

achieving an external validation C-statistic of 0.794 [10]. The Kailuan cohort and 
China Patient-centered Evaluative Assessment of Cardiac Events (PEACE) 
Million Persons Project have subsequently established indigenous prediction 
frameworks[11-13]. Nevertheless, these models predominantly employ Cox 
proportional hazards or logistic regression, with performance constrained by 
statistical assumptions. Conventional methodologies inadequately capture non-
linear relationships and interaction effects amongst high-dimensional variables 
[14], whilst demonstrating limitations in handling missing data and 
multicollinearity [15, 16]. A systematic review incorporating 32 traditional CVD 
prediction models revealed a median external validation C-statistic of merely 
0.74 (IQR 0.70-0.78), with uniformly suboptimal calibration [17].
Machine learning algorithms demonstrate superiority in addressing complex 
non-linear associations, yet their "black-box" opacity impedes clinical translation. 
Ensemble methods such as random forest and gradient boosting machines, 
despite exhibiting exceptional predictive performance, possess opaque internal 
decision architectures that provoke trust and ethical concerns in high-stakes 
medical scenarios [18, 19]. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) technologies 
offer a resolution to this dilemma. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), 
grounded in game-theoretic Shapley value principles, provides unified feature 
contribution quantification for arbitrarily complex models [20, 21]. Compared with 
traditional feature importance metrics, SHAP satisfies mathematical properties 
including additivity, symmetry, dummy variable consistency, and efficiency, 
whilst facilitating both global feature ranking and individualised patient-level 
explanations[22]. This methodology has been validated across oncological 
prognostication [23], diabetic complication assessment [24], and intensive care 
unit mortality prediction [25]. Nevertheless, systematic application of 
interpretable machine learning to long-term CVD risk prediction in China's 
middle-aged and elderly populations remains conspicuously absent.
The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) furnishes 
an optimal platform to address this lacuna. Initiated in 2011, the programme 
encompasses 28 provinces, 150 counties, and 450 communities, employing 
multistage probability sampling to recruit approximately 23,000 residents aged 
≥45 years, with follow-up assessments conducted biennially to triennially [26]. 
The survey architecture incorporates multidimensional data spanning

ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

demographic characteristics, socioeconomic indicators, functional health status, 
lifestyle behaviours, anthropometric measurements, and biomarkers [27]. Its 
nationally representative sampling framework, variable breadth, and 
longitudinal design provide a robust foundation for comprehensive prediction 
model development.
The present investigation leverages CHARLS 2011-2020 longitudinal data to 
systematically compare ten machine learning algorithms for long-term CVD risk 
prediction in China's middle-aged and elderly demographic, employs SHAP 
methodology to elucidate model decision mechanisms and critical risk 
determinants, and translates the optimal model into an online individualised risk 
assessment platform. This study integrates conventional risk factors with 
psychosocial determinants, ensures model generalisability through nationally 
representative cohort derivation, enhances clinical utility via interpretability 
analysis, and ultimately transforms research outputs into pragmatic tools, 
thereby furnishing scientific evidence and decision support for precision CVD 
prevention and control amongst China's ageing population.
Methods
Study Design and Data Source
This population-based prospective cohort study utilised data from the China 
Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) [26]. Administered by the 
National School of Development at Peking University, CHARLS employed 
multistage stratified probability-proportional-to-size (PPS) sampling to recruit 
approximately 17,000 community-dwelling residents aged ≥45 years and their 
spouses from 450 village or urban committees across 150 counties (districts) in 
28 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities.
Baseline assessment was conducted in 2011, with subsequent follow-up 
waves completed in 2013, 2015, 2018, and 2020, constituting a 9-year 
observation period. This investigation integrated longitudinal data from all five 
temporal nodes for cardiovascular disease long-term risk prediction model 
development and validation. The study protocol received approval from the 
Biomedical Ethics Review Committee of Peking University (approval number: 
IRB00001052-11015), with written informed consent obtained from all 
participants.
Participant Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

The baseline survey enrolled 17,708 participants. Exclusion criteria 
comprised: (1) physician-diagnosed myocardial infarction, coronary heart 
disease, angina pectoris, congestive heart failure, or stroke at baseline; (2) 
indeterminate baseline cardiovascular disease history; (3) absence of blood 
biochemistry assays; (4) >20% missingness in core predictor variables; (5) loss 
to follow-up or incomplete outcome ascertainment during the observation period. 
Given systematic deficiencies in mortality documentation during the 2015 and 
2018 survey waves, effective sample sizes for corresponding periods underwent 
calibration. Ultimately, 8,080 participants were enrolled in the model 
development cohort, with detailed selection workflow presented in Figure 1.

Outcome Definition and Adjudication
Incident CVD served as the primary outcome, encompassing first diagnosis 
of cardiac events (coronary heart disease, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, 
congestive heart failure, or other cardiac conditions) or stroke. This composite 
definition reflects our focus on overall atherosclerotic cardiovascular burden 
rather than individual disease entities. We recognize that grouping 
pathophysiologically diverse conditions—ischemic heart disease, heart failure 
with potentially disparate origins, and cerebrovascular events—may dilute 
subtype-specific risk associations. Nevertheless, this approach aligns with 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPTARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

primary prevention goals: identifying individuals requiring global cardiovascular 
risk modification rather than targeting specific disease trajectories. Outcome 
ascertainment relied on participant self-report of physician diagnosis via 
standardised questionnaires, a methodology validated in prior CHARLS cohort 
investigations [28, 29]. CVD events were adjudicated exclusively when participants 
without baseline disease history reported new diagnoses at subsequent follow-
up assessments, with event timing defined as the corresponding visit date.
Candidate Predictor Variables and Selection Strategy
Seventy-seven baseline candidate variables were initially incorporated, 
encompassing demographic characteristics (age, sex, geographical region, 
marital status, educational attainment), medical history (hypertension, 
dyslipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, hepatic disease, asthma), lifestyle behaviours 
(smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, sleep duration), 
anthropometric measurements (height, weight, waist circumference, body mass 
index), psychological assessment (10-item Centre for Epidemiologic Studies 
Depression Scale [CESD-10]), and laboratory parameters (lipid profile, 
glycaemia, hepatorenal function).
Feature Selection Strategy
We employed a two-stage variable selection process integrating 
epidemiological principles with machine learning considerations. Initial 
univariable logistic regression identified candidate predictors associated with 
CVD incidence (P<0.05). Qualifying variables then entered multivariable logistic 
regression with stepwise selection (P<0.05) to identify independent predictors.
This approach served dual objectives. First, it yielded a parsimonious set of 
interpretable predictors with established clinical relevance. Second, it reduced 
dimensionality for machine learning models, minimizing overfitting risk while 
preserving statistically and biologically plausible features. Although tree-based 
algorithms inherently perform feature selection through recursive partitioning, 
pre-filtering enhanced computational efficiency and ensured clinical face validity.
We assessed collinearity for variables with correlation coefficients >0.7 
using variance inflation factors (VIF). When VIF exceeded 5, we retained 
variables with stronger clinical relevance or practical measurement feasibility. 
This consideration benefits both traditional regression—where multicollinearity 
inflates coefficient standard errors—and machine learning algorithms where

correlated features may dilute variable importance estimates.
Eleven predictors were ultimately selected: geographical region, 
hypertension, dyslipidemia, hepatic disease, asthma, CESD-10 depression score, 
age, sleep duration, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, and waist circumference.
Data Pre-processing and Quality Control
We addressed missing data using multiple imputation by chained equations, 
generating five imputed datasets through 20 iterations each. Imputation 
methods were tailored to variable type: predictive mean matching for continuous 
measures, logistic regression for binary variables, and polytomous regression 
for the four-level geographical region variable. Following established guidelines, 
the outcome variable served as a predictor in the imputation models but was not 
itself imputed, thereby preserving the predictor-outcome associations in the 
original data. Trace plot inspection confirmed algorithm convergence across all 
chains. Statistical tests supported the missing-at-random assumption, with 
missingness patterns significantly linked to geographical region (χ² = 84.884, p 
< 0.001) and urban-rural residence (χ² = 21.568, p < 0.001), yet unrelated to 
cardiovascular outcome status (χ² = 2.993, p = 0.084). We pooled estimates 
across imputed datasets according to Rubin's combination rules[15, 30, 31] .
Continuous variables underwent Shapiro-Wilk normality assessment: 
normally distributed data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation with 
intergroup comparisons via t-tests; non-normally distributed data were reported 
as median (25th-75th percentile) with Mann-Whitney U or Kruskal-Wallis H tests. 
Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, with 
intergroup comparisons via χ² or Fisher's exact tests. Two-tailed tests were 
applied with significance threshold α=0.05.
Model Construction and Training
The cohort was partitioned into training (n=5,656, 70%) and validation 
(n=2,424, 30%) sets via stratified random sampling based on CVD occurrence 
status. Ten machine learning models were constructed in parallel: logistic 
regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), gradient boosting machine 
(GBM), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), light gradient 
boosting machine (LightGBM), categorical boosting (CatBoost), adaptive 
boosting (AdaBoost), neural network (NN), and k-nearest neighbours (KNN).
All models were trained on identical feature sets and data partitioning

ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

strategies. Hyperparameter optimisation employed 10-fold cross-validation with 
grid search ranges informed by literature review and exploratory analysis. For 
instance, random forest tree quantity (n_trees) was searched across 100-1,000, 
with tree depth (max_depth) constrained to 5-20 layers; XGBoost learning rate 
ranged from 0.01 to 0.3.
Handling of Class Imbalance
Among the 5,657 participants in the training cohort, 1,246 (22%) 
experienced incident CVD during follow-up. While this represents a modest 
imbalance in outcome distribution, we elected not to employ synthetic 
resampling techniques (e.g., SMOTE) or algorithmic class weighting. This 
decision was guided by three considerations. First, the observed event rate 
approximates the true epidemiological burden of CVD in middle-aged and older 
Chinese adults, and preserving this natural prevalence is essential for 
generating well-calibrated absolute risk estimates suitable for clinical 
implementation. Second, artificial manipulation of class distributions—while 
potentially improving classification metrics—can introduce systematic 
miscalibration, particularly in the probabilistic outputs required for shared 
decision-making. Third, tree-based ensemble learners, which constituted the 
majority of candidate algorithms, exhibit documented resilience to moderate 
outcome imbalance through recursive partitioning mechanisms. Empirical 
validation of this approach was provided by calibration plots demonstrating close 
agreement between predicted and observed risks across probability strata, 
alongside decision curve analyses confirming net benefit over reasonable 
threshold ranges.
Model Performance Evaluation and Selection
A multidimensional evaluation framework was employed: (1) Discrimination: 
area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) with 95% 
confidence intervals, with inter-model comparisons via DeLong's test; (2) 
Classification metrics: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score; 
(3) Calibration: calibration plots with Hosmer-Lemeshow χ² test for quantifying 
calibration error; (4) Clinical net benefit: decision curve analysis (DCA) 
assessing model performance relative to "treat all" and "treat none" strategies 
across risk threshold spectra.
All metrics were computed separately for training and validation sets. Model

ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

selection prioritised algorithms demonstrating maximal validation set AUROC, 
optimal calibration, and sustained positive net benefit across the 20%-80% risk 
threshold range. For models with comparable AUROCs (overlapping 95% 
confidence intervals), classification metrics were further compared. Statistical 
analyses utilised R version 4.2.0, with two-tailed significance threshold P<0.05.
Statistical Software
Analyses employed R 4.2.0. Core packages: mice (multiple imputation), 
catboost and lightgbm (ensemble learning), caret (unified ML framework), pROC 
and rms (discrimination and calibration), dcurves (decision curve analysis), 
shapviz v0.5.0 and kernelshap (SHAP interpretability), DynNom with Shiny (web 
calculator). 
Model Interpretability Analysis
Interpretability analysis employed the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) 
framework. SHAP, grounded in game-theoretic Shapley value concepts, 
quantifies each feature's marginal contribution to predictions. Global SHAP 
value aggregation identified critical risk factors and their relative importance, 
whilst individual-level SHAP visualisation elucidated risk composition for 
specific patients, informing personalised intervention strategies.
Online Risk Assessment Tool Development
The validated optimal model was deployed as an interactive risk calculator 
using the Shiny framework. The front-end interface comprised 11 standardised 
input fields corresponding to core predictor variables in the final model. The 
back-end embedded the trained model (serialised in .rds format), executing data 
pre-processing, model prediction, and result visualisation. The system outputs 
individualised 9-year absolute CVD risk probability (0-100%). The web calculator 
runs on encrypted cloud infrastructure accessible across devices. We frame it as 
a screening facilitation and decision support tool that complements, rather than 
replaces, clinical judgment. Recalibration was deemed unnecessary: the 
validation sample—drawn from the same national sampling frame—exhibited 
adequate calibration without systematic bias requiring intercept adjustment. 
Users encounter an upfront interpretive statement emphasising that predicted 
probabilities capture statistical patterns in the training population and must be 
contextualised within broader clinical assessment.

Baseline Characteristics of Study Participants
The study enrolled 8,080 CHARLS participants completing 9-year follow-up, 
partitioned into training (n=5,657, with 1,246 [22.0%] incident CVD cases) and 
validation (n=2,423) sets at a 7:3 ratio. Supplementary Table S1 reports baseline 
distributions across 77 candidate predictor variables in the training set, 
alongside univariable and multivariable logistic regression results comparing 
CVD and non-CVD groups.
Demographic and Geographical Distribution Characteristics
Gender composition differed between CVD and non-CVD groups, with female 
proportions of 55.9% and 51.8%, respectively. Whilst univariable analysis 
demonstrated lower CVD risk amongst males (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.75-0.96, 
P=0.009), this association lost statistical significance following multivariable 
adjustment (adjusted OR [aOR]=1.00, 95% CI 0.61-1.63, P=0.988). Geographical 
distribution exhibited pronounced regional disparities: relative to northeastern 
China, eastern (aOR=0.56, 95% CI 0.42-0.76, P<0.001), central (aOR=0.66, 95% 
CI 0.47-0.91, P=0.012), and western regions (aOR=0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.74, 
P<0.001) demonstrated significantly reduced CVD risk, suggesting elevated 
cardiovascular disease burden in northeastern provinces. Urban-rural 
differentials achieved statistical significance in univariable analysis but failed to 
reach significance threshold following multivariable adjustment (aOR=0.93, 
P=0.389).
Medical History

Web-Based Risk Assessment Tool
Leveraging the validated random forest model, a web-based CVD risk 
calculator was developed (Figure 5C; accessible 
at https://zxy08887.shinyapps.io/make_web/). The tool requires input of eleven 
variables: demographic information (age, geographical region), medical history 
(hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hepatic disease, asthma), physical examination 
parameters (waist circumference), laboratory investigations (triglycerides, HDL-
C), and lifestyle factors (nocturnal sleep duration, CESD-10 score). The system 
computes 9-year CVD incidence probabilities on demand. Three target use cases 
guide its design: first, screening in community and primary care settings to 
identify candidates for enhanced risk management; second, clinical decision 
support where predicted probabilities augment physician assessment without 
superseding it; third, informed self-evaluation by the general public, coupled 
with explicit recommendations for professional consultation before 
interpretation. A standardised preamble alerts all users that risk estimates 
reflect cohort-specific statistical patterns drawn from Chinese adults aged 45+ 
and do not constitute diagnostic conclusions.
Discussion
Leveraging 9-year longitudinal data from the nationally representative 
CHARLS cohort, this investigation systematically compared the performance of 
ten machine learning algorithms for cardiovascular disease risk prediction 
among middle-aged and older Chinese adults. The random forest model 
demonstrated optimal performance, achieving a validation AUC of 0.829, 
significantly exceeding that of conventional logistic regression (AUC=0.792). 
Through SHAP interpretability analysis, we identified waist circumference, 
triglycerides, age, and hypertension as the most influential predictors, whilst 
elucidating non-linear effect patterns and individualised contributions of each 
factor. The web-based risk assessment tool developed from this model enables 
instantaneous generation of individual 9-year CVD incidence probabilities, 
providing a pragmatic solution for community screening and clinical decision-
making.

Comparison of Model Performance with Existing Literature
The predictive performance of our random forest model (AUC=0.829) is 
comparable to or superior to recent domestic and international machine 
learning-based CVD prediction studies. Ambale-Venkatesh and 
colleagues[32]compared six machine learning algorithms for 10-year ASCVD risk 
prediction using the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohort, with 
the optimal model (gradient boosting machine) yielding an AUC of 0.742, inferior 
to our findings. Dinh et al[33] constructed a deep neural network model using UK 
Biobank data, achieving an AUC of 0.774 for 5-year CVD risk prediction. By 
contrast, our study maintained superior discriminative capacity despite a longer 
prediction horizon (9 years), suggesting model robustness. Notably, the deep 
learning model developed by Kakadiaris and colleagues [34] attained an AUC of 
0.848 for 5-year CVD risk prediction; however, that investigation incorporated 
imaging parameters such as coronary artery calcium scoring, whereas our study 
achieved comparable performance utilising solely readily accessible clinical 
variables, rendering it more amenable to primary care settings.
Within Chinese population-based research, our results align closely with 
selected machine learning prediction models. Li et al [35] employed XGBoost 
algorithms with data from over 100,000 participants in the Kailuan cohort to 
predict 10-year CVD risk, reporting a C-statistic of 0.812. Nevertheless, their 
predictor variables included laboratory indices such as uric acid and 
homocysteine, entailing higher data acquisition costs. Zhang and colleagues [36] 
utilised China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB) data to construct a random forest model 
predicting 10-year CVD risk with an AUC of 0.803, approximating our findings. 
However, the CKB cohort concentrated predominantly on specific geographical 
regions, whereas the national representativeness of CHARLS confers broader 
generalisability to our results. More importantly, most existing studies prioritise 
model performance comparisons whilst lacking in-depth elucidation of model 
decision-making processes, thereby constraining clinical acceptability.
Complementary evidence from Japanese population-based cohorts further 
contextualizes our findings within an East Asian framework. Using data from 
7,389 participants in the Suita study, Vu and colleagues constructed stroke 
prediction models across five machine learning algorithms, with random forest 
again emerging as the top performer (AUC 0.73) [37]. SHAP decomposition

Our random forest model demonstrated superiority over the conventional

ensemble learning across multiple decision trees. Furthermore, our study 
incorporated psychobehavioural factors including depressive symptoms and 
sleep duration, extending beyond traditional risk factor paradigms. It merits 
emphasis that improvements in model performance require careful balance with 
interpretability and clinical practicability, which precisely underscores the 
significance of implementing SHAP analysis in this investigation.

SHAP analysis revealed waist circumference as the most influential 
predictor of 9-year CVD risk, a finding consonant with the central role of

surrogate measure of visceral adipose tissue accumulation, waist circumference 
more accurately reflects metabolically active fat distribution compared with 
BMI[39]. Visceral adiposity precipitates insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, 
endothelial dysfunction, and prothrombotic states through secretion of 
inflammatory cytokines (interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor-α), adipokines 
(leptin, adiponectin), and free fatty acids, ultimately promoting atherogenesis[40]. 
Asian populations exhibit a propensity for greater visceral fat accumulation even 
at lower BMI levels, potentially accentuating the predictive value of waist 
circumference for CVD risk [41]. In our investigation, each 1-cm increment in 
waist circumference conferred a 5% increased CVD risk (adjusted OR=1.05), 
with SHAP analysis demonstrating accelerated effect magnitude in higher value 
ranges, suggesting that even modest weight reduction might yield substantial 
cardiovascular benefits in individuals exceeding waist circumference thresholds. 
This observation substantiates the clinical relevance of Chinese adult waist 
circumference cut-points (≥90 cm for men, ≥85 cm for women) in CVD risk 
stratification[2].
The importance of triglycerides as the second most influential predictor was 
corroborated in this study. Epidemiological evidence demonstrates that 
hypertriglyceridaemia associates independently with CVD risk, potentially 
mediated through the atherogenic effects of remnant lipoproteins[42]. Mendelian 
randomisation studies support a causal relationship between triglycerides and 
CVD[43]. The Chinese Guidelines on Prevention and Treatment of Dyslipidaemia 
in Adults recommend borderline-high and elevated triglyceride cut-points of 1.7 
mmol/L and 2.3 mmol/L, respectively [44]. Clinical practice should implement 
stratified intervention strategies according to patient triglyceride levels—
lifestyle modifications for borderline elevation, with potential pharmacotherapy 
for marked elevation. Notably, HDL-cholesterol ranked lower in SHAP 
importance in our study, diverging from Western population research 
emphasising HDL as a protective factor, potentially reflecting distinctive lipid 
profile characteristics and genetic backgrounds in Chinese populations[45].
Hypertension and age, as classical risk factors, were reaffirmed in this 
investigation. Hypertension accelerates atherosclerotic progression through 
mechanical stress-induced endothelial injury, inflammatory pathway activation,

Independent Contributions of Psychobehavioural Factors
This investigation identified depressive symptoms and sleep duration as 
possessing independent predictive value for CVD risk. Although 
psychobehavioural variables ranked modestly relative to traditional risk factors, 
their inclusion enhanced model discrimination, indicating clinically relevant 
predictive information beyond conventional metabolic and cardiovascular 
markers. Critically, SHAP-derived importance quantifies statistical contribution

association aligns with epidemiological evidence documenting bidirectional 
relationships between the conditions. Hypothesised mechanisms linking 
depression to cardiovascular risk include HPA axis dysregulation with sustained

states[50].Furthermore, depressed individuals frequently exhibit adverse lifestyle 
behaviours (smoking, sedentariness, poor dietary habits), further amplifying 
CVD risk [51]. Among middle-aged and older Chinese adults, depression 
recognition and treatment rates remain suboptimal[52]. Our findings suggest that 
incorporating convenient depression screening (such as the CES-D scale) into 
CVD risk assessment may facilitate identification of overlooked high-risk 
individuals.

Clinical Value of SHAP Interpretability
This investigation implemented SHAP technology to achieve transparent 
interpretation of machine learning models, bridging the chasm between 
predictive performance and clinical acceptability. Whilst traditional machine 
learning models demonstrate high predictive accuracy, their "black box" 
characteristics impede clinicians' comprehension of prediction logic, thereby 
constraining application [19]. The SHAP methodology, grounded in game-
theoretic Shapley values, allocates marginal contributions to individual 
prediction outcomes for each predictor variable, possessing desirable 
mathematical properties including theoretical consistency and additivity [21]. 
Compared with conventional feature importance methods (such as Gini 
importance), SHAP not only provides global ranking but, more importantly, 
generates individualised interpretations—for any given patient, the model 
explicitly identifies which factors elevate risk, which exert protective effects, and 
the specific magnitude of each factor's contribution[56].
In clinical practice, such individualised interpretation holds substantial 
significance. For instance, for a patient with elevated waist circumference but 
normal blood pressure, SHAP force plots can intuitively demonstrate how waist 
circumference dominates the high-risk state, thereby guiding physicians to 
formulate targeted weight reduction programmes. Conversely, for elderly 
patients with well-controlled other factors, SHAP analysis may reveal that risk

Clinicians and lay users alike should recognise these factors as contributing to 
probabilistic risk estimates—not as discrete causal levers amenable to 
intervention. Embedding this distinction into the web interface itself is critical 
to avoid misreading statistical outputs as mechanistic guidance.
Clinical Application Prospects and Practical Implications
The web-based risk assessment tool developed from the optimal model 
translates research findings into clinically pragmatic solutions. Requiring input 
of merely 11 readily accessible variables, the tool generates individual 9-year 
CVD incidence probabilities within seconds, applicable across diverse clinical 
scenarios. In community health centres or township health facilities, primary 
healthcare workers can utilise this tool to conduct cardiovascular risk screening, 
identify high-risk populations, and facilitate timely referrals to tertiary 
institutions. In general hospital outpatient settings, clinicians can integrate the 
tool into electronic medical record systems, achieving automated risk 
assessment and early warning to support clinical decision-making. In health 
management and medical examination institutions, the tool can provide 
personalised health consultation and lifestyle guidance for middle-aged and 
elderly individuals. Moreover, the public can access this tool via the internet for 
self-health assessment, enhancing cardiovascular disease prevention awareness.
The clinical value of this tool also manifests in cost-effectiveness 
considerations. Compared with traditional risk assessment instruments, our 
model does not depend on expensive laboratory tests (such as apolipoproteins, 
high-sensitivity C-reactive protein) or imaging examinations (such as coronary 
artery calcium scoring). Most variables can be obtained through medical history

outperformed "treat all" or "treat none" strategies, confirming clinical net 
benefit. Particularly under resource-constrained circumstances, this model can 
optimise resource allocation by concentrating limited intervention measures on 
genuinely high-risk populations, achieving precision prevention.
However, clinical application of the model necessitates cautious 
consideration. Firstly, risk prediction constitutes only one component of clinical 
decision-making and cannot completely supplant physicians' professional 
judgment and comprehensive assessment. Secondly, the model was developed 
in middle-aged and elderly populations; applicability to younger adults or special 
populations (such as pregnant women) requires further validation. Thirdly, the 
purpose of risk assessment is to initiate preventive interventions; subsequent 
follow-up management and patient adherence remain equally important. Finally, 
with evolving medical knowledge and changing risk factor profiles, the model 
requires periodic recalibration and updating to maintain predictive accuracy. 
Therefore, we recommend implementing this tool as a clinical decision support 
system rather than a replacement instrument in actual application, whilst 
establishing complementary quality control and effectiveness evaluation 
mechanisms.
Composite CVD endpoints trade specificity for power: while grouping 
coronary events, heart failure, and stroke increases incident cases for model 
training, it conflates conditions with partially distinct vascular mechanisms and 
risk factor hierarchies. Hypertension dominates stroke prediction; dyslipidemia 
drives coronary disease; heart failure reflects a spectrum from ischemic to non-
ischemic etiologies. This heterogeneity may attenuate individual predictor 
effects and obscure the model's relevance to specific clinical presentations. 
Subtype-stratified analyses warrant future attention. For primary prevention—
where treatment decisions target modifiable risk factors shared across 
outcomes—composite CVD prediction nonetheless remains appropriate and 
widely applied.

Principal Strengths
The primary strength of this investigation resides in the representativeness 
of the data source. As a national cohort study, CHARLS encompasses 
community-dwelling populations across 28 provinces, providing a broad 
population foundation for model construction, partially offsetting the limitations 
of previous research predominantly confined to specific regions or healthcare 
institution patients. The 9-year follow-up period accumulated sufficient endpoint 
events, enabling the model to capture long-term CVD incidence risk, which 
possesses practical reference value for clinical decision-making.
Regarding predictor variable selection, the study integrated demographic 
characteristics, physiological indicators, biochemical parameters, and 
psychobehavioural factors, constructing a relatively comprehensive risk 
assessment framework that transcends traditional models' predominant reliance 
on biochemical indices. The model development process systematically 
compared ten machine learning algorithms, selecting the optimal model through 
cross-validation—this methodological design enhances result robustness.
Implementation of SHAP technology represents a salient feature of this 
investigation. This methodology achieves model decision process interpretability 
whilst maintaining machine learning's high predictive performance, partially 
alleviating concerns regarding "black box" models in clinical applications. SHAP 
analysis not only provides feature importance ranking but also generates 
individualised risk attribution; this transparency facilitates enhanced clinical 
acceptability. Furthermore, the web-based risk assessment tool developed in this 
study translates research findings into practical products, providing convenient 
pathways for clinical application. The study employed rigorous statistical 
methods in data processing (multiple imputation) and model evaluation (AUROC, 
calibration curves, decision curves), demonstrating satisfactory methodological 
quality.
Limitations
Several methodological considerations merit acknowledgement. Our 
reliance on self-reported physician diagnoses for CVD ascertainment introduces 
potential misclassification despite CHARLS quality assurance protocols. Linkage 
with administrative health databases or mortality registries would strengthen 
endpoint validation in future iterations. The CHARLS sampling architecture—

probabilistic recruitment of community-dwelling adults aged ≥45 years—
systematically underrepresents younger populations, institutionalized 
individuals, and geographically concentrated high-risk cohorts. Stringent 
eligibility criteria requiring complete 9-year follow-up and comprehensive 
baseline biochemistry further constrained our analytical sample; participants 
lost to follow-up, frequently those experiencing adverse health trajectories or 
facing healthcare access barriers, were necessarily excluded. Such selection 
may attenuate observed risk gradients.
Predictor availability was circumscribed by survey instrumentation, 
precluding integration of genetic architecture (polygenic scores) or emerging 
biomarkers (high-sensitivity troponin, NT-proBNP). While these additions might 
enhance discrimination, our emphasis on routine clinical measures aligns with 
pragmatic implementation priorities. Biennial assessment cycles permitted only 
baseline modelling; risk factor trajectories—blood pressure fluctuations, lipid 
responses to therapy, weight dynamics—remain uncharted. Time-varying 
covariate models could capture such evolution but substantially compound 
analytical and implementation complexity.
The decade separating baseline data collection (2011-2012) from 
contemporary practice has witnessed considerable epidemiological shifts: 
evolving risk factor distributions, recalibrated diagnostic criteria, and expanding 
therapeutic landscapes. Regional variations in healthcare infrastructure, 
socioeconomic gradients, and dietary patterns transcend our geographical 
categorization, introducing unmeasured heterogeneity that likely varies across 
deployment settings. External validation in independent cohorts remains 
outstanding; planned collaboration with complementary Chinese platforms (CKB, 
CHARLS sister studies) should illuminate generalizability boundaries. 
Populations demonstrating substantially different baseline profiles or CVD 
incidence necessitate local recalibration—preserving the predictor hierarchy 
while adjusting intercepts, as discrimination transportability typically exceeds 
that of absolute risk estimates. Our web platform accommodates such coefficient 
refinement. Prospective performance monitoring should trigger recalibration 
upon detecting meaningful calibration degradation.
Random forest implementation demands greater computational 
infrastructure than traditional approaches; resource-constrained primary care

settings may find logistic regression-based scoring systems more tractable. 
Finally, as an observational investigation, reported associations cannot establish 
causality. Bidirectional relationships warrant consideration—depression and 
sleep disturbances may represent prodromal CVD manifestations rather than 
purely etiological factors—and unmeasured confounding persists despite 
multivariable adjustment.
Future Research Directions
Based on these findings, several directions merit further exploration. 
Independent external cohort validation represents a critical step in assessing 
model generalisability. Model predictive performance should be evaluated 
across different regions, urban-rural settings, ethnicities, and socioeconomic 
populations, with necessary model recalibration according to validation results.
Dynamic risk prediction constitutes an important avenue for enhancing 
model accuracy. Utilising repeated measurement data from multiple follow-up 
waves (longitudinal changes in blood pressure, lipids) to update individual risk 
assessments can achieve "dynamic monitoring and timely warning". Statistical 
methods such as joint models or Landmark models can construct such dynamic 
prediction frameworks, though their implementation demands higher technical 
requirements.
Integration of multi-omics data (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics) and 
emerging technologies (wearable devices, medical imaging artificial intelligence) 
holds promise for constructing multimodal fusion precision prediction models. 
With precision medicine advances, multilevel biological information integration 
may achieve more refined risk stratification. However, balance must be sought 
among data acquisition costs, technical complexity, and clinical accessibility.
Prospective intervention trials represent a necessary component for 
validating model clinical value. Prediction models established through 
observational research require verification through randomised controlled trials: 
whether risk-stratified intervention strategies based on models truly reduce CVD 
incidence and mortality, and their cost-effectiveness ratios. Only through 
intervention trials can final confirmation be obtained regarding whether model-
guided clinical decisions improve patient outcomes.
Intelligent upgrading of clinical decision support systems represents an 
approach to enhancing model practicability. Deep integration of risk prediction

models with electronic medical record systems, combined with natural language 
processing technology to automatically extract predictor variables from medical 
record text, can achieve automated risk assessment and personalised 
intervention recommendation, alleviating healthcare worker burden.
Model fairness and ethical considerations warrant attention. Assessment is 
needed regarding whether models exhibit systematic prediction biases across 
different population subgroups, avoiding algorithmic exacerbation of health 
inequities. Particularly for ethnic minorities and low socioeconomic status 
populations, model applicability and fairness must be ensured. Other explainable 
artificial intelligence methods (such as LIME, attention mechanisms) merit 
exploration. Through comparison of different interpretation method merits, 
standardised frameworks for interpretability assessment can be established, 
which holds substantial significance for promoting responsible artificial 
intelligence application in the medical domain.
Conclusions
In summary, leveraging long-term follow-up data from the nationally 
representative CHARLS cohort, this investigation successfully constructed a 
long-term CVD risk prediction model applicable to middle-aged and elderly 
Chinese populations. The random forest algorithm demonstrated optimal 
performance, with predictive capacity significantly exceeding traditional 
statistical methods. Through SHAP explainable artificial intelligence technology, 
we not only quantified the relative importance of predictor factors but also 
elucidated non-linear effect patterns and individualised contributions, bridging 
the contradiction between machine learning's "high performance" and "black 
box" characteristics. Waist circumference, triglycerides, age, and hypertension 
emerged as the most critical predictors, whilst independent contributions of 
psychobehavioural factors including depressive symptoms and sleep duration 
expanded the dimensions of CVD risk assessment. The web-based risk 
assessment tool developed in this study possesses characteristics of convenience, 
rapidity, and low cost, applicable across diverse scenarios including community 
screening, clinical decision-making, and self-health management, providing 
scientific evidence and pragmatic solutions for precision prevention of 
cardiovascular disease in China's middle-aged and elderly populations. Future 
work necessitates further validation of model external validity in independent

Explainable Machine Learning for 10-Year Prediction of Cognitive Impairment in 
a Rural Chinese Population    
Abstract 
Cognitive impairment (CI) is an emerging public  health challenge in rural aging  populations, 
where access to formal cognitive testing is limited. Using data from 4,781 adults in the Rural 
Chinese Cohort Study (RCCS) with 10-year follow-up and the Shenzhen Aging-related Disorder 
Cohort (SADC) with baseline cognitive assessment, this study developed an interpretable 
machine learning model for long-term CI risk prediction  and evaluated its cross -population 
transportability using eight routinely collected indicators. Among nine algorithms, the Random 
Forest model showed the most balanced performance, with AUCs of 0.721 (95% CI: 0.596, 
0.846) in the RCCS internal validation set for 10-year incident CI prediction and 0.690 (95% CI: 
0.664, 0.717) in the SADC baseline-CI evaluation, acceptable calibration, and positive net 
benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 10% to 40%.  SHAP identified age, 
education, and systolic blood pressure as the main predictive contributors. Subgroup analyses 
showed heterogeneous discrimination, while sensitivity analyses supported broadly consistent 
performance under alternative data partitioning and MICE imputation. Mediation analysis 
suggested a primarily direct association between baseline age and later CI.  These findings 
indicate that a simple, interpretable mo del based on widely available clinical indicators may 
support preliminary risk stratification and targeted cognitive screening in resource-constrained 
rural settings. 
Introduction 
Cognitive impairment (CI) represents an intermediate state between normal ag ing and dementia and is 
partially reversible1. It is a key precursor of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease and 
is associated with loss of functional independence, reduced quality of life, and increased mortality among 
older adults, imposing substantial burdens on families and health  systems2,3. As the global population 
ages, the prevalence of CI and the rate at which it progresses to dementia continue to rise 4. A 2020 
nationally representative study estimated that 15.07 million adults aged 60 years or older in China had

burdens worldwide. With rapid population aging, these numbers are expected to increase markedly by 
2050, further intensifying the health-care and societal burden associated with cognitive decline5-7. Early, 
accurate, and scalable risk stratification has therefore become a public health priority, particularly among 
populations where cognitive screening remains limited. 
The World Health Organization’s Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 
for 2017-2025 identifies rural elderly adults as a priority population for screening and intervention 8. In 
China, more than 45% of adults aged 60 years or older reside in rural areas 9. In these settings, lower 
educational attainment 10, limited health literacy 11, insufficient access to primary care 12, poor chronic 
disease control13, and reduced family support due to labor migration contribute to elevated CI risk14. The 
prevalence of CI remains consistently higher in rural than in urban settings, at 15.4% versus 11.7%, 
alongside higher  disability and misdiagnosis rates 5. Shortages of trained personnel and validated 
screening tools in rural primary care further delay diagnosis and intervention 15. Conventional cognitive 
assessments such as the Mini -Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment 
(MoCA), while widely used in clinical settings, are often difficult to implement in rural communities. 
Standard cognitive questionnaires may be difficult to administer in older adults with limited formal 
education or literacy, particularly in rural settings. These barriers can reduce participation and contribute 
to under-detection, underscoring the need for interpretable prediction models based on accessible data 
and feasible workflows in primary care16. 
Existing CI prediction models exhibit several limitations. Many rely on cross -sectional or short -
term cohorts of 3 years or less, use traditional logistic regression with limited  feature selection, and 
frequently overlook modifiable physiological factors such as blood pressure and glucose17. Few models

with 10 or more years of follow-up for model development, interpretability, and independent population-

To address these gaps, the present stu dy was designed to develop and validate a pragmatic, 
interpretable machine learning model for predicting 10-year incident CI in rural older adults, leveraging 
over a decade of prospective data from the Rural Chinese Cohort Study (RCCS) 18. This objective was 
achieved through a multi-faceted approach, incorporating a robust feature selection process, independent 
baseline-CI evaluation in an urban cohort, and the application of SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) 
to ensure the model's clinical transparency by identifying key predictors. Beyond the primary goal of 
prediction, the study further sought to elucidate underlying mechanisms by investigating the potential 
mediating role of metabolic factors in the longitudinal relationship between aging and cognitive decline. 
Results 
Study Participants 
Table 1 summarizes the baseline characteristics of the 4,781 RCCS participants included in model 
development and internal validation, among whom 726 were classified as having CI at the 10 -year 
follow-up. Compared with participants who remained cognitively normal, participants with CI were older 
and more often female, illiterate, and unmarried. In terms of lifestyle behaviors, participants with CI were 
less likely to report current smoking, alcohol drinking, or tea consumption, while reporting lower levels 
of physical activit y, shorter daily television viewing time, and shorter sleep duration (all P<0.05). In 
addition, systolic blood pressure (SBP), fasting blood glucose (GLU), and body mass index (BMI) were 
higher in the CI group, as were the prevalences of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), stroke, 
and use of anti -hypertensive medication (all P<0.05). Total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), and

Model Development and Evaluation 
After comprehensive evaluation across multiple performance metrics, the  RF model showed the most 
balanced overall performance among the nine candidate algorithms ( Supplementary Table S6, 
Supplementary Figure S1 ). In 10 -fold cross -validation, the RF model achieved an area under the 
receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.717, with a 95% CI of 0.640 to 0.795. The final RF 
model showed an AUC of 0.721, with a 95% CI of 0.596 to 0.846, in the RCCS internal validation set 
for 10-year incident CI prediction. When applied to the independent SADC for baseline -CI evaluation, 
the model showed moderate discrimination, with an AUC of 0.690 and a 95% CI of 0.664 to 0.717, as 
shown in Figure 3A-C. The corresponding threshold-based classification metrics with 95% confidence 
intervals, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value 
(NPV), are reported in Table 2. Beyond discrimination, the RF model also showed acceptable calibration 
(Figure 3D and 3E) and positive net benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 10% to 40% 
in both the RCCS internal validation set and the SADC baseline-CI evaluation (Figure 3F and 3G).   
To distinguish the statistical threshold selected using the Youden index from potential 
implementation thresholds, an implementation-oriented threshold-probability analysis was conducted in 
the RCCS internal validation set (Supplementary Table S7). Increasing the threshold from 15% to 20%, 
25%, and 30% reduced the proportion of participants classified as high risk from 29.7% to 23.8%, 4.7%, 
and 1.2%, respectively. This reduction in screening burden was accompanied by lower sensitivity, from

Subgroup analyses were performed by sex, age group, education level, hypertension status, and T2DM 
status (Table 3). AUC values ranged from 0.571 to 0.700, indicating heterogeneous discrimination across

Sensitivity Analyses 
Sensitivity analyses using alternative RCCS data partitions and datasets imputed by multiple imputation 
by chained equations (MICE) showed broadly comparable performance patterns (Supplementary Table 
S9). Under the 80% training and 20% internal validation split and the 60% training and 40% internal 
validation split, validation AUCs remained similar to that observed in the primary 70% training and 30% 
internal validation split. In the RCCS MICE-imputed analysis, model performance was also materially 
unchanged. Applying the same MICE procedure to the SADC and re-evaluating the final RCCS-derived 
RF model yielded comparable SADC baseline -CI performance. Decision curve analyses under these 
sensitivity settings showed broadly similar net-benefit patterns (Supplementary Figure S3), suggesting 
that the main findings were not meaningfully affected by alternative data -partitioning or imputation 
assumptions. 
Model Explainability 
Model interpretability was examined using SHAP app lied to the final RF model retrained on the full 
RCCS dataset. Age, education, and SBP were the most influential contributors, with mean absolute SHAP 
values of 0.045, 0.018, and 0.013, respectively. Higher BMI values were associated with negative SHAP 
values, suggesting a lower predicted probability of CI. In contrast, longer sleep duration was associated 
with positive SHAP values  (Figure 4A and 4B). To evaluate the consistency of these model -derived 
associations, SHAP directions were compared with coefficients from multivariable LR (Table 4 ). 
Education, SBP, BMI, sex, sleep duration, and T2DM remained statistically significant in the regression 
model and showed directions of association consistent with SHAP outputs. Age and TC were not retained 
in the multivariable LR comparison but still exhibited positive SHAP contributions, suggesting potential 
nonlinear or interaction effects captured by the RF mod el. The overall concordance between SHAP -

Mediation Analysis  
As shown in Supplementary Table S11, GLU and TG showed statistically significant but very small 
indirect associations between baseline age and 10-year incident CI, whereas no indirect associations were 
observed for TC, HDL -C, or LDL -C. The total and direct associations between age and CI remained

statistical terms, with limited and inconsistent evidence for metabolic mediation. 
Discussion 
This study developed and internally validated a machine-learning model for 10-year CI prediction using 
the RCCS cohort and assessed its cross-population transportability in the SADC baseline-CI evaluation. 
Among the tested algorithms, RF showed the most balanced overall performance, with acceptable 
calibration and positive net benefit across selected threshold -probability ranges. SHAP analysis 
identified age, education, and SBP as the main contributors to model output. In  the SADC, the model 
retained moderate discrimination for baseline-CI evaluation. 
CI appears more prevalent in rural than in urban populations 19, a disparity that has been attributed 
to several contextual factors including lower educational attainment, limited capacity for vascular risk 
control within primary care, social fragmentation associated with labor migration, occupational exposure 
to neurotoxicants, and restricted access to digital health resources 20-23. These contextual constraints 
underscore the need for pragmatic approaches that can support earlier identification in rural communities 
without relying solely on specialist -led cognitive assessment. The final model uses routinely collected

ARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESS
 
indicators covering demographic, vascular, metabolic, and lifestyle domains, which supports its potential 
integration into rural primary -care workflows. The web -based tool, together with SHAP -based 
explanations, may help primary-care providers generate and communicate individualized risk estimates 
rapidly. However, the tool is intended to serve as an upstream triage aid, with formal cognitive testing 
remaining necessary for confirmatory assessment. A more appropriate workflow is a two-step process in 
which the mo del first identifies individuals who may warrant further assessment, followed by 
confirmatory MMSE or MoCA testing and clinical follow -up where appropriate. The cutoff selected 
using the Youden index should therefore be interpreted as a statistical threshold for model-performance 
reporting. Implementation thresholds should be adapted to local screening capacity, population 
prevalence, and the acceptable balance between false positives and missed CI cases. This approach aligns 
with broader policy priorities for early detection, dementia prevention, and community-based cognitive 
and mental health services under Healthy China 2030 and SDG 3 24. Future implementation studies can 
further evaluate how this workflow affects screening efficiency, resource allocation, and patient 
outcomes in rural primary care settings25,26. 
The RF algorithm provided the most balanced overall performance across the modeling stages. This 
may reflect its ability to capture nonlinear associations and interactions in epidemiologic tabular data 
with mixed variable types and potential multicollinearity, while requiring relatively limited preprocessing 
and hyperparameter tuning 27-29. RF is compatible with SHAP ana lysis, which decomposes individual 
predictions into feature-level contributions and supports transparent interpretation of model output 30,31. 
Compared with more computationally intensive or prompt -dependent AI approaches, tabular machine 
learning models such as RF may be more readily deployable in rural primary care settings32.  
The main predictors identified by SHAP were broadly consistent with established epidemiologic

evidence. Age and lower educational attainment were among the strongest contributors to model output, 
consistent wit h the roles of aging and cognitive reserve in cognitive decline 33,34. SBP was also an 
important predictor, supporting the relevance of vascular risk profiles to cognitive vulnerability. This 
finding aligns with evidence linking elevated blood pressure to cerebral small -vessel disease, impaired 
white matter perfusion, microbleeds, and brain atrophy35-37. These results suggest that the model captured 
a combination of life -course, educational, and vascular -risk information that is clinically plausible in 
rural aging populations. 
Metabolic and lifestyle -related indicators also co ntributed to model prediction. GLU and TG 
showed statistically significant but very small indirect associations in the binary CI mediation analysis, 
but these findings were not consistently supported when continuous MMSE scores were used as the 
outcome and should therefore be interpreted as exploratory 38,39. T2DM showed a similar association to 
glucose, consistent with the broader link between metabolic health and cognition 40. The inverse 
association between BMI and cognitive risk may be compatible with the late -life obesity paradox, in 
which low BMI may reflect frailty, undernutrition, or prodromal disease 41. Sleep duration may capture 
behavioral or health-related vulnerability, consistent with prior studies reporting a U-shaped association 
with cognitive outcomes42,43. TC was retained because of its routine availability and practical relevance, 
although its association with cognition may be nonlinear and may depend on age, lipid subfractions, and 
broader metabolic context 44. Collectively, these predictors may inform cognitive health priorities in 
community settings. Lower educational attainment supports the value of cognitive stimulation and health 
literacy activities, va scular and metabolic predictors highlight the need to integrate cognitive health 
awareness into vascular and metabolic risk management, and sleep duration suggests that sleep hygiene 
education may be a feasible and low-cost component of community-based prevention.

This study has several strengths. To our knowledge, it is among the first studies to develop an 
interpretable CI risk stratification model for rural Chinese older adults using routinely available 
indicators, based on a rural cohort with approximately 10 years of follow-up. The final model used only 
eight primary -care or community -health indicators, supporting practical use as a preliminary risk -
stratification tool without requiring advanced imaging, specialized biomarkers, or extensive 
neuropsychological batteries. SHAP explanations and the online calculator may improve transparency 
and usability, supporting potential implementation in resource-constrained rural settings.  
Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. Selection bias may have affected model 
development and evaluation because the analytic sample included only participants who survived and 
completed follow-up cognitive testing; these participants differed from excluded individuals in several 
baseline characteristics, as s hown in Supplementary Table S2. The model was developed in one rural 
setting, and although the SADC provided an independent baseline -CI evaluation, its transportability, 
particularly its 10-year prognostic performance, requires further validation in indepe ndent longitudinal 
cohorts. Variable-importance rankings should be interpreted cautiously because model -specific metrics 
are not directly comparable, and RF Gini -based importance can be influenced by variable type, the 
number of possible split points, and correlated predictors.  Mediation findings should be interpreted 
cautiously and regarded as exploratory because residual confounding cannot be fully excluded in 
observational mediation analyses, biochemical mediators may be subject to measurement error, and age, 
as a non-manipulable exposure, limits causal interpretation. 
Another important limitation concerns the model ’s limited discriminatory performance. The AUC 
of 0.721 in the RCCS internal validation set and 0.690 in the SADC baseline -CI evaluation indic ate 
modest discrimination and limited accuracy for individual -level classification.  In the RCCS cohort,

This study established an interpretable machine learning model based on eight routinely available 
health indicators to estimate 10 -year CI risk among rural older adults. The model offers a feasible 
approach for early risk stratification and may assist primary -care providers in identifying individuals 
who could benefit from confirmatory cognitive testing and preventive follow -up. Its reliance on 
accessible predictors, transparent interpretation, and online implementation aligns with the practical 
constraints of rural health systems. Further validation across diverse rural populations and evaluation 
within real-world care pathways will help determine its broader applicability and implementation value. 
Methods 
Study Participants  
The model was developed using data from the RCCS , which is a population -based longitudinal study 
initiated in Henan Province, China, during 2007 -2008, enrolling 20,194 baseline participants aged ≥18 
years at baseline examination. Data were collected by trained staff through interviewer -administered 
questionnaires, standardized physical examinations, and laboratory tests. Data included

ARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESS
 
sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle behaviors, medical and family history, anthropometric 
measurements, and fasting biochemical indicators. Data collec tion for the first follow -up in 2013-2014 
and the second follow -up in 2017 -2018 was consistent with the baseline assessment, except that the 
second follow-up additionally incorporated cognitive function testing for adults aged 60 years or older. 
Eligible participants for the current analysis were those who had reached 60 years or older by the 10 -
year follow-up, totaling 11,016 individuals. Participants were excluded sequentially as follows: 688 were 
lost to follow-up at the 10-year examination, 2,297 died before the 10-year examination, 3,011 attended 
the follow -up but did not complete cognitive assessment owing to non -participation or inability to 
perform the test, and 239 had missing data on key baseline variables. Finally, 4,781 participants were 
included in the model development and internal validation analyses. 
The SADC is a community -based prospective study established in 2017 -2018 in Luohu District, 
Shenzhen, recruiting 9,411 adults aged 60 -92 years 45. Comprehensive baseline data were collected 
through questionnaires, physical examinations, laboratory testing, and cognitive assessments. For the 
independent baseline -CI evaluation in the present study, baseline variables aligned with the final 
predictor set were extracted, and participants with complete data on these indicators were included to 
form the effective independent baseline -CI evaluation sample. Because longitudinal incident CI data 
were not available in the SADC, this dataset was used to eva luate cross-population transportability for 
baseline-CI classification. The study followed the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction 
Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis reporting guidelines. Participant selection for both cohorts 
is detailed in Figure 6. 
The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhengzhou University and the Ethics 
Committee of the Shenzhen Center for Disease Control and Prevention under approval numbers

R2017001 and R2018020, respectively. All procedures involving human participants were conducted in 
accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants 
prior to data collection.

Outcome ascertainment 
In the RCCS development cohort, cognitive function was assessed during the second follow -up survey 
approximately 10 years after baseline and was used to define the long -term prediction outcome. In the 
SADC, cognitive function was assessed at cohort baselin e and was used for baseline -CI classification. 
In both cohorts, CI was measured using the Chinese version of the MMSE  and defined according to 
education-adjusted thresholds 46: ≤17 for individuals without formal education, ≤20 for those with 
primary education, and ≤24 for those with junior high school education or above47. 
Candidate predictors 
Candidate predictors comprised baseline variables collected in the RCCS and were grouped into six 
domains: (1) sociodemographic characteristics: age, sex, education level, marital status, and per capita 
monthly income; (2) lifestyle behaviors: smoking status, alcohol and tea consumption, physical activity, 
television viewing time, other sedentary activities, and sleep duration; (3)  medical history: physician -
diagnosed hypertension, T2DM, stroke, coronary heart disease, heart failure, myocardial infarction, 
cancer, kidney disease, and use of antihypertensive or lipid -lowering medications; (4) family history: 
hypertension, hyperlipide mia, diabetes, coronary heart disease, and stroke in first -degree relatives, 
including parents, siblings, or children; (5) anthropometric and clinical measurements: height, weight, 
waist circumference, BMI, SBP, DBP, and pulse rate; and (6) biochemical ind icators: GLU, TC, TG, 
HDL-C, and LDL-C. 
Feature Selection and Model Development

The RCCS dataset was randomly partitioned, with 70% of participants assigned to the training set and 
30% assigned to the internal validation set. All procedures for feature selection and model development 
were performed using the training set. A multi -step feature selection process was applied to create a 
cautious and parsimonious model. Robust candidate predictors were first identified from the intersection 
of features selected by both LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm48,49. These candidate predictors 
were then ranked using three model -specific approaches: standardized LR coefficients, XGBoost gain 
values, and RF Gini importance. Because these importance measures are model-specific and not directly 
interchangeable, final feature selection was based on a triangulation framework incorporating data-driven 
importance evidence, clinical relevance, measurem ent feasibility, public-health relevance, and existing 
literature. 
Nine supervised machine learning algorithms were trained on the final predictor set, including LR, 
RF, gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), XGBoost, LightGBM, AdaBoost, decision tree, Gaussian 
naïve Bayes (GNB), and support vector machine (SVM). Model tuning and evaluation were conducted 
using 10-fold cross-validation within the training set. 
Model Evaluation 
The final model ’s performance was evaluated in terms of discrimination, calibration, threshold-based 
classification performance, and clinical utility. Discrimination was quantified using the AUC, and 
calibration was assessed using calibration plots and the Brier score. Point estimates and 95% confidence 
intervals were reported  for the AUC and threshold -based classification metrics, including accuracy, 
sensitivity, specificity, PPV , NPV , F1 score, and κ coefficient. Confidence intervals for model -
performance metrics were estimated using bootstrap resampling.  For threshold -based performance 
reporting, the statistically optimized cutoff was determined using the Youden index. Specifically,

ARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESS
 
predicted probabilities were traversed from 0 to 1 with an increment of 0.001, and sensitivity, specificity, 
PPV , NPV , F1 score, and accuracy were calculated at each candidate cutoff. The cutoff maximizing the 
Youden index, defined as sensitivity + specificity -1, was selected as the primary statistical threshold for 
model-performance reporting in each evaluation dataset.  Clinical utility was furth er examined using 
decision curve analysis (DCA) in the RCCS internal validation set for 10 -year CI prediction and in the 
SADC for baseline-CI classification. To distinguish the statistical cutoff selected using the Youden index 
from potential implementatio n thresholds, an implementation -oriented threshold -probability analysis 
was conducted in the RCCS internal validation set. Predicted probabilities generated by the final RF 
model were evaluated at several plausible thresholds, including 10%, 12%, 15%, 20%,  25%, and 30%. 
For each threshold, the number and proportion of participants classified as high risk, true positives, false 
positives, false negatives, true negatives, sensitivity, specificity, PPV , NPV , and the number needed for 
confirmatory assessment were calculated. The number needed for confirmatory assessment was defined 
as the number of participants classified as high risk divided by the number of true-positive cases. 
Subgroup Analyses 
Subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate variation in RF mode l performance across key 
demographic and clinical strata, including sex, age group, education level, hypertension status, and 
T2DM status. Using predicted probabilities generated by the final RF model, discrimination and 
probabilistic performance were asse ssed within each subgroup using AUC and Brier score. These 
analyses were intended to describe heterogeneity in model performance across clinically relevant strata 
and to inform the need for future recalibration or subgroup-specific threshold evaluation. 
Sensitivity Analyses 
Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the model in relation to missing data

ARTICLE IN PRESS
 
and sampling variability. For the missing -data sensitivity analysis, MICE was applied consistently to 
both the RCCS and SADC, and the  RF model was re -evaluated using the imputed datasets, with the 
SADC retained as an independent baseline-CI evaluation dataset without model re-tuning or refitting. To 
further evaluate the sensitivity of the model to random data partitioning, the RF model was re-trained 
using alternative training/internal -validation splits of 80%/20% and 60%/40%. Performance metrics 
across these partitions were compared with those from the main 70%/30% split to assess internal stability 
with respect to sampling variation. 
Model Interpretability and Application 
Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP, which decompose s the model output into additive 
contributions from each predictor. Consistent with methodological principles, SHAP values represent 
associative contributions to the model ’s prediction function rather than causal effects 50. Global SHAP 
explanations were used to assess the relative importance and directionality of predictors, while individual 
SHAP force plots illustrated how specific feature patterns contributed to predictions for representative 
participants. To ensure interpretative consistency, the SHAP-derived directionality of major predictors 
was cross-checked against multivariable LR coefficients. The model was also translated into a web-based 
risk calculator to support practical application in primary-care settings. 
Mediation Analyses 
Mediation analyses were conducted within the RCCS cohort to evaluate whether biochemical indicators 
measured at the 2013 -2014 first follow -up statistically mediated the association between baseline age 
and cognitive outcomes assessed at the 10-year follow -up. A two -step regression framework with 
bootstrapping was used to estimate indirect and direct effects. Because age is a non-manipulable exposure, 
all estimates were interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal pathways. All m odels were

adjusted for key baseline confounders, including sex, education level, marital status, hypertension, 
T2DM, BMI, sleep duration, physical activity, and baseline biochemical indicators. Robustness was 
examined by repeating the analysis using continuous MMSE scores as the outcome. 
Statistical analysis 
Data management and statistical analyses were conducted using Python version 3.8 and R version 4.2.   
Following the procedures detailed in preceding subsections, feature selection used LASSO and Boruta,  
and nine supervised algorithms were compared under tenfold cross-validation. Model performance was 
evaluated by discrimination, calibration, and decision -curve analysis, and the statistical classification 
threshold was selected using the Youden index. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness, 
including missing -data imputation and alternative training -validation splits. SHAP values quantified 
variable contributions, while mediation analyses evaluated statistical pathways between baseline age, 
biochemical indicators, and cognitive outcomes. Continuous variables were summarized as mean (SD) 
or median (IQR), and categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. A two -sided 
P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.
